Characters: Esther Longtree

Definition from research

"the cross was growing, too, in her womb" makes Esther's pregnancy a burden borne, the cross carried inside her.

Her thoughts run to guilt and lost innocence, and a litany, "Jesus, the angels, God in heaven, the stars," sets the holy names loose in a flood of murder and mystery, the sacred adrift among the dead.

Allusions: Angels and Archangels

Definition from research

She has "wandered like some penitential palmer with sea shells on his hat," the pilgrim to the Holy Land marked by scallop shells, penance made visible, and a "Crusader's castle" sets her among the medieval holy wars.

"There were halos where there were no moons," a light of holiness that shines from itself, not borrowed or reflected.

"Angels rolling away the stones of tombs" recalls the empty grave of Easter and the stone rolled back.

"a white bird lifted its archangelic wing" lends the highest order of angels to a bird stirring in the wind, and "an old cross-beam breaking upon the waves" carries a faint echo of Noah's ark.

Her long prayer, "Forgive the cloud which knows not what it whispers," on through "I fell from star to star. My life was one long act of falling," gathers divine forgiveness, the Fall, and the downward pull of all things into one plea, a breaking body asking pardon for a secret "none can tell and live."

Around this the chapter also gathers echoes from beyond Christianity, a Roman epitaph, Carthage, a "forgotten Ramadan," a winding horn, but the mourning frame stays Christian, a burial in a "grey New England churchyard."

Allusions: Genesis · Judaism · Revelation and the Apocalypse · The Bible

Definition from research

The first thing the tally makes plain is scale. Religion is not one theme among many in the novel; it is the language the book is written in. Nearly every page reaches for scripture, from Genesis to Revelation, and where the Bible runs out Young reaches further, to Islam and the Talmud, to Buddhism and Ubuntu, to the Greek underworld. Her characters think in psalms and parables because that is the only vocabulary wide enough for what they are asking. When they meet death, love, guilt, or the plain question of what is real, they reach for the sacred stories, because those are the stories a culture keeps for exactly these moments. The book's religiosity is not piety. It is the sound of people using the largest words they have.

religion-chapters-26-to-28:
Chapters 26 to 28

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Chapter 26 · Guide 26 The Department of the Dead · Wheel Chapter 26 · Index Chapter 26 · Chapter 27 · Guide 27 The Two Watches · Wheel Chapter 27 · Index Chapter 27 · Chapter 28 · Guide 28 Impalpable Butterflies · Wheel Chapter 28 · Index Chapter 28

Definition from research

No Christian references appear in these chapters.

The religious question underneath

These three chapters name no scripture, but they are where Mr. Spitzer comes nearest to the question Chapter 29 states openly: whether anything rises after death. The question of resurrection runs under all three, carried by his work, his watches, and his butterflies. Chapter 29 then gives it the language of the Bible: Joseph’s coat, Aaron’s breastplate, the Word made Flesh.

Chapter 26: The Department of the Dead

Mr. Spitzer’s law practice is a ministry to the dead: wills, deeds, archives, lost heirs. He tends the afterlives that property gives people. The two Boston spinsters who each believe they are Cleopatra, one leaving her fortune to Siamese cats who seem likely to live forever, are a comic version of eternal life secured by a legal instrument. Immortality here is an estate held in trust.

The chapter closes on the thought that to reach the upper world one must first travel through the lower. That is the shape of the descent stories behind the whole book. In Book Six of the Aeneid, the Sibyl warns that going down to the underworld is easy and that climbing back is the real task: hoc opus, hic labor est, the words Joachim takes as his own motto in Chapter 55. In Christian tradition the same shape belongs to the creed, the descent into hell before the rising on the third day. Mr. Spitzer, who believes in no heaven except as a state of mind, keeps the shape of the journey without its promise.

He asks what Peron would have done in his place, and decides Peron would have dragged Catherine into the living sunlight even if it killed her. Faithful watching at a bedside set against a rescue that might be fatal: the chapter is asking what it means to save someone.

Chapter 27: The Two Watches

Mr. Spitzer carries calling cards and an old passport so that, if he dies, he will be identified as himself and not as his brother. It is a comic precaution with a theological edge. Belief in resurrection has always raised the question of which self will rise, and Mr. Spitzer no longer knows which self he is.

His two watches, his brother’s still running and his own stopped near the hour of Peron’s death, put him in two times at once: ordinary time that keeps moving, and a stopped time in which the death is always happening. That is the condition of mourning, and it is the condition the promise of resurrection speaks to: an end to the stopped hour.

The stranger who asks whether he wants to die and then leads him safely through the traffic plays the part of the unrecognized guide, the stranger who turns out to be a rescuer, a figure that runs from the Book of Tobit to the road to Emmaus. Mr. Spitzer says no while nodding yes, and is saved anyway.

Chapter 28: Impalpable Butterflies

The butterfly has stood for the soul since the Greeks, who used one word, psyche, for both. Christian art took it up as an emblem of the resurrection: the crawling caterpillar as earthly life, the chrysalis as the tomb, the winged creature as the body raised. Mr. Spitzer abandoned his collection after Peron’s funeral, as if he could no longer bear an emblem of rising.

His observation that anyone called away at the crucial moment could never tell whether they had seen a beginning or an end is the chapter’s central religious thought. From outside, emergence and death look alike, and only faith says which one happened. Mr. Spitzer cannot say, and that uncertainty is what Chapter 29 opens into when he speaks of the butterfly as psyche and of the Word made Flesh.

He also admits that he may be only one of Catherine’s hallucinations, truly alive only in her room in the evenings. A man who exists in someone else’s dreaming is a dark inversion of the believer who lives in God’s sight: his whole being depends on a dreamer who does not truly see him.

Chapter 3

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Chapter 03 · Guide 03 The Truest Thing in the House · Wheel Chapter 03 · Index Chapter 03

Characters: Miss MacIntosh

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Ecclesiastes · The Bible · The Book of Job

Definition from research

The line about a God "Who had God's limitations," who "had left many things uncreated," is the novel's boldest theological stroke. It gives up the all-powerful Creator for a finite one, a God with edges, a creation left open and unfinished. The idea runs against orthodoxy and toward the book's steady questioning of how much of the world was ever truly made or governed.

The line that "labor was man's lot upon this earth," set beside a God who "made the furrows on the sea," leans on Ecclesiastes, work as a God-given portion and toil accepted as part of the order of things.

God as a "harness-maker" who "hung her harness with tinkling bells" pictures providence as a craftsman keeping watch, a maker who can always find his creature.

"ours was not the problem of questioning God's remotest mysteries" states the plain Christian humility that runs through the book: live rightly, and leave what cannot be known alone.

"Perhaps God's understanding never had been God's" turns even omniscience into a question, another crack in the traditional picture of God.

"whether a camel shall enter through the needle's eye or a rich man through the gates of heaven" is Jesus's saying from Matthew 19:24, the hard odds of the rich entering the kingdom.

"the argument as to how many angels might stand on a needle's point" nods to the old satire of medieval hairsplitting, learned debate spent on nothing.

"There would be no light without the darkness" makes the plain point that contrast is what lets either be seen.

"God's business had never been ours, perhaps had never been God's" holds humility and radical doubt in the same breath, and catches the book's central tension between faith and skepticism whole.

The counsel to "mind his own knitting, his own cooking, his own household duties even though he had no house" carries the ethic of plain, honest living, an echo of the call to deny oneself and take up one's cross.

"To kiss the rod was better than not to know self-discipline" urges the acceptance of discipline over the illusion that a person is free and answerable to no one.

"We must not waste our lives in the vain expectation" of what may never come recalls the Parable of the Rich Fool and the futility of hoarding hope against an empty future.

The line joining "the strength of the unicorn" to a God who would "bring us out of Egypt" layers the wild strength of the re'em (rendered "unicorn" in the King James Version), the Exodus, and the wilderness as a testing ground, deliverance longed for and not yet arrived.

"The joys of the hypocrite were but for the moment," set against "the joys of the honest man" that last, draws on Job 20:5, the brief triumph of the wicked against the lasting worth of honest living.

"What had God done? How should God answer for God's omissions?" presses the hardest question in the book, divine justice weighed against God's silence and what he has left undone.

The hope that "iniquity should not be found on our lips" until "the laborer should be paid for the sweat of his brow" voices a longing for an end to sin and a world set right.

Miss MacIntosh prefers Pilgrim's Progress "to even the Word of God." She holds that scripture "should be taken with a grain of salt," open to too many readings and thick with human exaggeration, its very angels "falling into a dark sea." Bunyan's allegory of the soul's journey suits her better than doctrine, and her wariness of the Bible as a handled, fallible thing is the book's questioning stance put plainly.

"The easiest way was the coward's way, the path of least resistance," broad and well paved, set against "the path of the brave," narrow and thorned and lonely, is Matthew 7:13-14, the wide road to ruin and the narrow one to life.

St. Simeon Stylites, the Syrian hermit who lived thirty-seven years atop a pillar, stands for extreme ascetic devotion.

Daniel, the exile who survived the lions' den for refusing to stop praying, stands for faith kept under pressure and God's protection of the faithful.

St. Augustine, bishop of Hippo, appears with his City of God, which set the heavenly society of the faithful against the earthly City of Man.

See also: Chapter 01 · Guide 01 The Endless Grayness · Wheel Chapter 01 · Index Chapter 01

Characters: Moses Hunnecker · Vera Cartwheel

Allusions: American Religious Movements · Angels and Archangels · Genesis · The Bible

Definition from research

The book invokes the Jehovah's Witnesses, a nontrinitarian, millenarian denomination known for door-to-door preaching, for refusing military service and blood transfusions, and for calling their body of belief "The Truth." They reject the Trinity, the immortal soul, and hellfire as unscriptural, and hold the wider world to be corrupt and under Satan's sway.

Moses Hunnecker makes "many calls upon God, the angels, the archangels, angel Gabriel." Gabriel is the messenger angel of Scripture, the one who announces the births of John the Baptist and of Jesus.

"the first creation when only the spirit of God had moved upon the deep" reaches back to Genesis 1:2, the Spirit of God hovering over the formless, dark waters before order and light are made.

"a cloud of pearl-breasted seagulls, all crying with angelic voices" turns ordinary birds into a chorus of angels, one of the novel's habitual liftings of the plain world toward the holy.

The preachers who cry of "harvests of dragons' teeth and reaping the whirlwind" draw on Hosea 8:7, "sow the wind, and reap the whirlwind," the prophet's warning that empty, faithless action ends in ruin.

"God is the loneliest of all," and "no God but what we dreamed, and there is no train," is one of the book's bleakest lines. The first phrase pictures a God isolated in his own divinity, unreachable, close to Christ alone on the cross. The second doubts God outright, suggesting he may be only something dreamed. The missing train completes the mood: no clear route out, no assured road to salvation.

"the world's greatest juggler, performing for the Lord's sake and glory" echoes 1 Corinthians 10:31, doing whatever one does for the glory of God rather than one's own.

"When shall the light, Peter, enter my soul again?" takes up the recurring biblical image of God's light returning to the soul after a stretch of darkness.

Vera names her whole errand in one line, "the search for life, for love, for truth that does not fail," a phrasing that leans on 1 Corinthians 13, where love takes its joy in the truth.

Noah's Ark appears as an allusion to Genesis 6 through 8, the flood, the vessel, and its landing on Ararat.

"My soul thirsts for God, for the living God" is Psalm 42:2, the psalmist's plain hunger to stand again in God's presence.

"your whole body will be full of light" comes from Matthew 6:22, the eye as the lamp of the body: a single, clear devotion fills a life with light, a divided one with darkness.

religion-the-unmaking-of-the-almighty-go:
The Unmaking of the Almighty God

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

Themes: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology

Definition from research

If the book has a single theological signature, it is the patient dismantling of the all-powerful God. Again and again the divine is given limits. God "had God's limitations," "had left many things uncreated," and His creation is called "problematical," the work of a maker filled with the "greatest remorse ever since the day of the beginning." He is "the loneliest of all." He "does not know God." At the far edge there is "no God but what we dreamed," and, flatly, "there is no God." None of this is careless blasphemy. It is a sustained reimagining. Young trades the monarch on his throne for a finite, laboring maker, a harness-maker, a carpenter, a worker who began what he could not finish. Her God has edges and His creation is left open, which is exactly the faith she claimed for herself, unable to believe in a God "too mundane" and wanting one "more imaginative" and "always on the move."

The Sacred Is Here

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Allusions: Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest

Definition from research

Miss MacIntosh carries the argument in her body. Her faith is the plainest in the book and the most radically immanent. She rejects the ornate heaven, the palace of angels, the opulent ceremonies of her employer's house, and keeps instead to "truth to nature." Her God is not a monarch on a far throne but a worker close to hand, imagined as a "harness-maker" or a plain carpenter, a craftsman who made the furrows on the sea the way a person makes anything, by hand and by labor. What Cheer, Iowa, her home, believes the same, a Christianity of endurance and daily work, wary of visions, content with the cycles of season and soil as the only scripture that can be trusted. This is the tenth idea of radical immanence stated as a character. The sacred is not guaranteed from above. It is made here, by plural people building provisional things, and Miss MacIntosh's whole moral teaching to Vera is a training in exactly that kind of attention.

Chapter 9

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Chapter 09 · Guide 09 I Am Dancing with Death · Wheel Chapter 09 · Index Chapter 09

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Allusions: Genesis · The Bible · The Book of Job

Definition from research

The "Twelfth Commandment" is Miss MacIntosh's own invention; no such commandment exists. What she hangs on it, fetch the needle, hem the handkerchief, cover our nakedness, turns her plain morality into a kind of scripture, with a glance back at the nakedness of birth and the shame of the Fall.

"naked as in that day when we came from our mothers' wombs" echoes Job 1:21, naked we come and naked we go, all things given and taken by God.

"Hope dies hard in the human breast" darkens Pope's "Hope springs eternal," trading his easy optimism for the stubborn refusal of hope to die even when it should.

Vera's refusal to believe Miss MacIntosh's childhood was unhappy is a small act of protective denial, of a piece with the stern Christian stoicism that bears suffering rather than dwells on it.

"if it was God's hand, was it still murder?" is the book's sharpest question of divine justice, asking whether an act God willed or allowed can still be a crime, and where human guilt begins and ends.

"Eve's eating an apple of the tree of knowledge" names the Fall, the disobedience in Eden that let sin and death into the world. The apple is later tradition, not the text itself.

"Who had divided the light from the darkness and created great whales" follows Genesis 1, God parting light from dark and making the great creatures of the sea.

The whales are bid to "be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters in the seas," the blessing of Genesis 1:22 on the life of the waters.

The genealogies Vera drills from the "Moody Bible," the sons of Levi, Judah, Er, Onan, and the rest, are the long descent of Jacob's line, learned by rote as the sediment of the faith. The name points to the evangelical Moody Bible Institute.

"the heave shoulder and the breast wave" are the priestly portions of Exodus and Leviticus, the breast waved and the thigh lifted before God and set aside for Aaron's line, an image the novel turns toward self-offering and dedication.

Those who "built cities in the wilderness and built arks" recall Noah's ark and David's city that housed the Ark of the Covenant, shelters raised against the flood and the wild.

"Death is not yet" is Miss MacIntosh's flat refusal to fear death before its hour, of a piece with her sober, present-facing faith.

"the canker eats the rose," with the greatest sailor swallowed by the very waters, gathers the book's images of a decaying, fallen world, beauty consumed and even the strongest taken under.

"Died Abner as a fool died" comes from David's lament in 2 Samuel 3, set here among the novel's long meditation on the many ways of dying and the one end that levels them all.

Asked how the wise man dies, Vera answers "As the fool died," refusing any comfort that wisdom might spare a person the common grave.

"When thou diest, I shall die with you" reworks Ruth's vow to Naomi in Ruth 1:17, loyalty unto death, turned here toward reckoning and reproof.

"There but for the grace of God" carries John Bradford's words at the sight of prisoners led to die, and behind them Paul's "by the grace of God I am what I am."

The Headhunter

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Miss MacIntosh

Definition from research

The Australian headhunter, a bushman by origin, is caught between two worlds and at home in neither. He is half-civilized by his own account, yet he reaches for something higher. He carves the heads of saints and patriarchs out of barnacles, and the results come out vague and cloudy, an imagination straining after religious images it does not quite grasp.

He dreams of Rome and of being taken up among the angels, though he has never been there and barely understands what he is asking for. Miss MacIntosh cannot stand him. She finds him deceitful and confused, an affront to her sense of order, and she resents his reaching after refined ideas he has not earned. His talk runs to esoteric and mythological subjects, a syncretic muddle absorbed in pieces. His fixation on Miss MacIntosh's head, its shape and its features, hints at something he senses about her before the reader does, and it foreshadows what the book will later reveal. He is not a believer and not an unbeliever, but a dreamer stranded between his wild beginnings and a refinement he cannot reach.

Everything That Matters Is Here

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology

Allusions: Genesis · Revelation and the Apocalypse

Definition from research

Radical immanence is the name for a philosophy built on that single conviction, that everything which matters is right here, in this world, and not in some beyond that would redeem or explain it. It is offered in these pages as a reading lens rather than a claim about Young's stated beliefs, though her own creed, poetic and cosmic and not theological, sits easily beside it. Read through this lens, the novel's enormous inventory of Christian reference, its thousands of allusions running from Genesis to Revelation, stops looking like the furniture of doctrine and starts looking like raw material, something the book keeps pulling down out of the sky and setting on the ground where people can handle it.

What follows takes the ten ideas of radical immanence, and the exact crossing point that completes them, and reads Young's religious imagination through each in turn. The novel answers back at every step, not because Young set out to illustrate a philosophy she never named, but because her instinct and its instinct are the same instinct: the child's turn toward what is standing just behind her.

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

Allusions: American Religious Movements · Ancient Egypt

Definition from research

Miss MacIntosh, My Darling offers no single view of Christianity. It runs a whole spectrum, from the plain working morality of Miss MacIntosh to the fevered convictions of Mr. Bonebreaker and the drifting visions of Catherine, and it keeps asking what faith does to a life. In the book's hands, belief can steady a person or unmoor one, and it rarely says which is which.

The novel names a wide range of faiths and denominations along the way: primitive Christianity, Catholicism, Presbyterianism, Free Methodism, Shouting Baptists, Jehovah's Witnesses, agnosticism, heathenism, Islam, Platonism, the gods of Egypt, totem worship, and the angels themselves.

What follows tracks the Christian references chapter by chapter, pairing each phrase from the novel with its source and its work in the text.

Miss MacIntosh carries the book's temper. Definition from research

"God pity us. God pity the small fishes and the great whales beached on this beach" is a plea for mercy over all creation, least and greatest alike, the fish and the whale stranded out of their element, an image of spiritual desolation with Jonah behind it.

"wash our sins away and leave us white as snow" is Psalm 51:7, David's prayer for cleansing.

"Our mothers and our fathers never knew us" leans on Matthew 10, where following Christ splits families apart.

"This earth is but the poor testing ground for the king rail with the bleeding throat," on through the broken crab and the dead clam to "all oxen are our brothers," repeats the trial-of-earth theme and widens it to every suffering creature, closing on a Franciscan kinship in which the ox is a brother.

The threat that "if ever I told what I had seen, she would kill me" draws on the commandment against killing and on Paul's glass seen darkly (1 Corinthians 13:12), a secret half-glimpsed and forbidden.

"Where is Tobias Smollett?" glances at the Book of Tobit, the deuterocanonical tale of Tobit, Sarah, and young Tobias guided by the angel Raphael.

"There is no God" is the flat denial of Psalm 14:1, "the fool hath said in his heart, there is no God," spoken here as Miss MacIntosh's bleakest turn.

The vision of "eyes filled... with light which came from no reflection," of a "forehead without brows or hairline" and a "viewless summit," is the first veiled sight of Miss MacIntosh's baldness, her head made a cloud-topped mountain, the biblical site of divine encounter.

"God loves you! God loves the wind, the empty places" scatters divine love across the unseen and the barren, the wind that in Scripture is also the Spirit.

"Heaven's nets are woven very wide" recalls the parable of the dragnet in Matthew 13, the net that gathers all and sorts them at the end.

Two lines, "this life was all a dream, and there was nothing" and "in another dream, we die," collapse life and death alike into dreaming and strip away the Christian afterlife, leaving dream and void where doctrine promised judgment and eternity.

"God Himself... does not know God, and the night is long which has no ending" turns even God's self-knowledge into a question and stretches the dark toward a night without end.

The string of proverbs, "Better go to hell with rags than to heaven with embroidery," "the best are often the worst," "we are all our fallen brothers," reworks the gospel reversals, the last shall be first, and the doctrine of the Fall into Miss MacIntosh's hard, humble wisdom.

"that authority which deserts the dying king" glances at kingship and abandonment, Christ's own cry of forsakenness not far behind it.

"robbing Peter to pay Paul," an idiom born of the two Roman basilicas, lands Miss MacIntosh's grand talk back among household money troubles.

"he is unworthy to live who lives only for himself" carries the gospel ethic of care for the orphan and the stranger (James 1) and the call to lose one's life for others (Mark 8), set here against the question of Sabbath rest.

"my father had fallen," "that secret was my sin," "my heart was the heart of the night" gather the language of the Fall, of sin, and of spiritual darkness around Vera's own guilt and her longing for a father to guide her.

The faith of What Cheer, Iowa, is plain and practical, close to the land and suspicious of anything ornate. The people are Christian and churchgoing, but they distrust grand ceremony, lavish vestments, and ritual for its own sake. Miss MacIntosh, who comes from there, carries the whole temperament with her: "truth to nature," and no patience for fancy.

Their religion is mostly a matter of conduct. It prizes honesty, self-reliance, hard work, and modesty, and it teaches that labor and suffering are part of God's design. The afterlife is granted but left vague. What matters is the day survived, the season turned, the work done. Even in so close a community, faith stays a lonely, private business, and no one pretends to know more than a person can know.

The chapter turns on death and the divided self. Mr. Spitzer is both living and dead, accused of being married to the worm, and the confusion foreshadows what the book will later reveal about him.

He believes in no heaven "except as a state of mind," a private, this-worldly faith.

He carries a "stain of immortal guilt" over his brother's death and longs, without hope, for absolution.

Behind the two brothers stands Cain and Abel. The book keeps asking whether Mr. Spitzer killed Peron, lives out the dead man's desires, or is only his shadow, the surviving twin marked and set wandering.

Catherine's knowledge outstrips his. "Both living and dead," she sees everything, an omniscience the book grants her as a near-divine attribute while his is only half.

Mr. Spitzer, "a soul divided," is in no place to judge another's dreams, and the passage folds in Paul's change "in the twinkling of an eye," the sparrows that fall by God's notice, and Ezekiel's wheels within wheels, images of a providence he cannot grasp.

Kept awake between "two iron beds," his own and his dead brother's, he guards against the "thief" of the gospel warning in Matthew 24, death or dissolution coming unannounced.

When Peron fell, "a bright light shining in his eyes deceived him," light turned to delusion rather than revelation.

"clouds of eyeless witnesses and dead sparrows falling" inverts two comforts, Hebrews' watching cloud of witnesses now blind, and the sparrow God marks now simply falling, a world stripped of divine attention.

religion-antisemitism-and-race:
Antisemitism and Race

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Cousin Hannah · Esther Longtree · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Society, Class, and Race

Allusions: Lynching and Racial Violence

Definition from research

The novel treats prejudice as a symptom. Its bigots are the lost, the raving, and the frightened, and their hatred looks less like conviction than like a way of imposing order on lives they cannot control by blaming someone outside. Young sets the ugliness in unreliable mouths and lets it condemn the speaker.

Racism in the book is not only spoken but built into a role. The "white detective" will investigate only the deaths of white children, since "the deaths of the little black children were not his business." Coming upon a murdered Black girl, he simply drops the case. His prejudice is a professional habit, the machinery of justice quietly refusing half the dead.

Esther Longtree lives the cost of this. Her Black lover has to flee "for fear the white people would see him and kill him," a fear the book confirms with an attempted lynching. Esther hides their child, dreads what her parents will do if they learn the baby is "coffee-colored," and travels to the "Negro section" of a Southern town to give birth, hunted and unsafe. Even mixed heritage is treated as a family scandal to be buried.

Set against the bigots are the ones who resist. Miss MacIntosh teaches Vera about the "injustices done to the Africans working in diamond mines," disputes Mr. Bonebreaker's slurs to his face, and hopes aloud for the end of the British Empire. Yet the book is honest about the cost of resistance too: her "tactful, hopeful silence" during his worst rants, and the "regret" that follows, show how hard it is to speak even for someone who knows better. Cousin Hannah, remembered as an abolitionist and a crosser of every border, is another, stranger figure of resistance, though the terms in which the novel recalls her carry their own period prejudice.

religion-one-gathered-religion-and-the-s:
One Gathered Religion, and the Search That Outlasts It

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home

Characters: Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Buddhism · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Judaism · The Bible

Definition from research

Set all of it together and a shape appears. Young is not a Christian novelist in any narrow sense, though Christianity is her deepest well. She gathers every tradition she touches, the Bible and the Quran, the Buddhist illusion of the separate self and the Ubuntu web that binds all souls, the Greek ferryman and the Hebrew prophets, into one religion of her own making. Its creed, if it has one, is the line the book keeps repeating, that "every heart is the other heart," that no one is finally alone. Its God is finite and imagining. Its sacred is close at hand. Its scripture is every scripture, reworked.

And in the end Young uses religion not to prove God or to deny Him but to hold open the search that outlasts both. Vera sets out after "truth that does not fail" and comes home to ambivalence, and that is not the book failing but the book telling the truth. The many references are not answers. They are the record of people asking, believing, doubting, and enduring, in the only words large enough for the asking. Young's own religion was poetic and cosmic and never theological, always on the move, and so is her novel, which turns every faith it touches into one more way of standing in the world and wondering what is real.

religion-islam:
Islam

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · The History of Opium · Women's Suffrage

Definition from research

Young does not treat Islam as a subject to explain so much as a colored light to write by. Islamic and "Oriental" imagery gives the novel a fluid, dreamlike backdrop for its questions about reality and illusion, freedom, and the shapes an identity can take. The imagery reaches the reader mostly through three figures: Catherine, Cousin Hannah, and, at a remove, Mr. Spitzer and Miss MacIntosh.

In Catherine's opium dreams the East is pure escape. Her room fills with "gold-turbaned Egyptians" and the "perfume of Oriental hanging gardens," and she gives orders to phantom servants as though they were flesh. Mr. Spitzer catches the same vision from outside, "moon minarets and crescents and jasper domes of desert cities." Seraglios and harems recur as images of veiled mystery and male control, and shadowy figures like the "Black Moor" and the black coachman drift between the real and the dreamed, their very gender uncertain.

For Cousin Hannah the East is a battlefield. The militant suffragette carries her war on men into "Araby" and the seraglios, riding a horse named "El-Burraq" after the Prophet's steed and going "by camel into places where no woman had ever gone before." She travels under the name "Al Hamid," fights turbaned Turks and Moroccan pirates, and casts herself as a "liberator of woman." Her best scenes turn the tables on the male gaze: disguised as an Arab king, she lifts her veil in a seraglio to show a pursuing sheik a "great, gaunt, bearded face" and drives him mad. The novel keeps unsettling the picture, letting the greatest sheik of the East turn out to be a woman, and letting a sheik beg Hannah's help because he too feels trapped by the harem, "hen-pecked" and desperate to escape. The East here is not a single patriarchy but a place where even men want out of their roles.

Miss MacIntosh will have none of it. She waves the whole exotic apparatus away as "balderdash, nonsense," measuring it against a Middle Western childhood in What Cheer, Iowa, a place with "no palm trees, no pearl divers." She prizes use and plainness over the "princely dignity" the East lends to something as ordinary as an umbrella.

So Islam in the novel is less a faith examined than a space imagined: flight for Catherine, a stage for Cousin Hannah's rebellion, nonsense to be swept aside for Miss MacIntosh. Young neither praises nor condemns the religion itself. She weaves its imagery into a larger, intensely personal story about identity, belief, and the border between the dreamed and the real.

He is afraid and reckless by turns, yet he keeps asking for protection and keeps thinking of someone waiting for him at home, as if faith and domestic hope were the same rope he is holding onto. Definition from research

The people who do not fit are, in radical immanence, not exceptions but evidence, the places where the seams of the constructed world show. Young crowds her margins with such figures. The Australian headhunter, caught between the bush and the cathedral, sculpts saints out of barnacles and dreams of a Rome he has never seen, and in his liminal confusion the reader watches belief being assembled. The bus driver named Moses prays and drinks at once, a folk faith with none of its seams hidden. Esther, of mixed heritage and endless loss, the hangman who calls himself Christian, the garden built for the blind who read the world by touch, all sit at the edges where the categories fail. They are not problems for the novel to solve. They are how the novel sees.

religion-the-whirling-child:
The Whirling Child

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

Symbols: Pregnancy, Birth, and Children

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Definition from research

Marguerite Young was raised in large part by her maternal grandmother, a deeply religious woman whose faith ran through the household like weather. When the grandmother suffered a stroke late in life, her delusions filled with angels and other such creatures, and the child at that bedside took away a lasting sense that the unearthly was not far off but close at hand, folded into the ordinary furniture of a life. Young later recalled a small ritual from those years. When someone said the old admonition, Satan, get behind me, the child would whirl around at once, hoping to catch a glimpse of him before he could hide.

The gesture is worth pausing on. The child does not look up toward a distant hell or forward to a day of judgment. She looks behind her, into this world, at close range, certain the figure is standing right there. That instinct, that the sacred and the terrible are immediately present rather than safely elsewhere, is the seed of everything the novel would later become. By the time Young described her creed to the Paris Review, she had a phrase for it. Her religion, she said, was poetic and cosmic, not theological. She could not believe in a God cut to the measure of a single denomination. Her God was more imaginative, and always on the move. The remark reads less like a rejection of religion than a relocation of it. The holy is not evicted from Young's world. It is brought down into it, scattered across birds and beasts and weather and the faces of the dead, made native to the here.

religion-indigenous-peoples-of-america:
Indigenous Peoples of America

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh

Allusions: Angels and Archangels

Definition from research

Young's Native American figures are more symbol than person, seen through a romantic haze of lost wisdom and vanished wilderness. Mr. Spitzer passes "cigar store Indians" and half-imagines an "Indian stockade," reducing living peoples to shop-front statues, and a mute guide reads the winter branches with a skill "only an Indian might have known." The recurring note is of a natural knowledge that modern, bewildered people have lost, admiring and distancing at once. The displacement behind that vanishing surfaces only glancingly, in a tramp's talk of "the wild Indian country" out west and the railroad's push into it.

The theme turns personal in Esther Longtree, whose father's people are "partly Irish and partly Indian." That "Indian streak" is thrown at her as the reason she is "unnatural," yet her grandmother, who bore children as easily as "leaves from the trees," stands for a rooted, unworried vitality that Esther, barren and haunted, has lost. Her father's people laugh at births and funerals alike, at home in life's cycles in a way the modern world is not.

The Australian headhunter belongs here too, and may owe something to Ota Benga, the Congolese man exhibited at the 1904 World's Fair and the Bronx Zoo as a "savage." Like Benga, the headhunter is taken into a Western house as a curiosity, taught manners, and set out to be looked at. He is called a head-hunter and a "wild, half-naked man of Borneo," yet he carves saints and patriarchs from barnacles and talks of cherubim and Cheops and Georgian silver, an intelligence his keepers refuse to see. Miss MacIntosh dismisses his art as "anemic cherubim" and his mind as swallowing everything and digesting nothing. His longing for "a better life" and his sad, imitative love songs echo Benga's own end, a man civilized against his will who, denied the way home, took his life.

religion-miss-georgia-macintosh:
Miss Georgia MacIntosh

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Miss MacIntosh

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Allusions: The History of Opium

Definition from research

Miss MacIntosh keeps the plainest faith in the book. She has no use for mystery or ceremony, and she distrusts anything that cannot be worked with the hands or checked against the world. The opulence of her employer's house, its phantom guests and grand rituals, strikes her as so much pretense, and the visions of angels and saints in Catherine's opium dreams she waves away as nonsense. Her God is not a monarch on a throne but a craftsman, a worker, someone closer to a carpenter than a king. She holds to "truth to nature" and expects people to "know their place" in an ordered world.

Her creed is mostly conduct: work, self-control, and the acceptance of hardship as part of the bargain. She is not an atheist, but she is no comfortable believer either. She doubts the neat Christian picture of God and the afterlife, suspects the creation was left unfinished, and wonders whether even God has regrets. She takes no solace in guaranteed salvation. What she offers instead is fortitude and plain charity, and she has no patience for self-pity dressed up as faith.

Death she treats as ordinary, neither to be feared nor made beautiful. She is wary of the drifting state between living and dying, seeing it as a place of confusion rather than revelation, and she means for her own end to be quiet and unremarkable. With Vera she is stern but caring, steering the child toward self-reliance and real work and away from the dreams that pull people loose from the ground. Her faith is finally a practical one: common sense, discipline, and a sober respect for the limits of what anyone can know.

Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary, and Unfinished Is Honest

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology

Definition from research

Young's most startling theological move is to make God himself incomplete. Miss MacIntosh entertains a creator who "left many things uncreated," who began what he could not finish, whose creation is called problematical and whose understanding may never have been his own. Traditional doctrine would flinch at this. Radical immanence recognizes it at once. To build knowing the structure has no final foundation, to treat incompletion not as failure but as the honest shape of any real work, is the fifth and sixth ideas exactly. Mr. Spitzer's music, the "unfinished song" he never plays, is the emblem of it. The song is not a failure because it is unfinished. It is truthful because it is unfinished, revision built into it from the start, the way an unfinished creation is more honest than a closed and perfect one that no one has ever actually lived inside.

Old Doc, Dr. Justice O'Leary, holds a faith as broken as his mind. He is "mad as a March hare," raving and wandering, still clinging to his calling as a healer even as his judgment fails him.

He curses the world and the God who made it. His God is not almighty but sorrowful, a maker filled with remorse for a flawed creation ever since the beginning. He doubts the old consolations. He once claimed to see something leave the room when a patient died, a "mist, a vapor," then admitted he never really heard a soul go. The silent woman he calls Sarah, crawling at his feet, seems to stand for whatever part of his life he can no longer control. He wants to help and cannot, and his failures at the bedside, especially around birth, deepen a crisis that is as much about faith as medicine. Definition from research

The novel's true subject is the search for reality in a world of dreams, and religion is where that search is fought out. Belief is the thing that either anchors a person or sets them adrift. Miss MacIntosh's plain faith is her grip on the ground; Catherine's is her flight from it. The same word, faith, names both the discipline that keeps Vera facing hard facts and the haze that dissolves her mother. religion-introduction-to-the-2nd-edition:
Introduction to the 2nd edition

Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Vera Cartwheel

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: American Religious Movements · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest

Definition from research

"My religion is poetic and cosmic and not theological."

Marguerite Young, Paris Review

Marguerite Young held a religion all her own, and it shaped everything she wrote. She came down from two figures who could hardly have agreed on anything, Brigham Young, who led the Latter-day Saint movement west, and John Knox, who drove the Scottish Reformation, and out of that unlikely descent she drew a lifelong pull toward utopias, toward faith, and toward the line where belief shades into illusion.

Her grandmother raised her and marked her early life. Late in life the old woman suffered a stroke, and her delusions filled with "angels and other such creatures," a household haunted by the fantastic. The child took it in and never quite set it down. Young was taught young to ask the angels for help and to cast Satan away, and when someone said "Satan, get behind me," she would whirl around on the spot, hoping to catch a glimpse of him before he could hide. That reflex, the sense that the unearthly stood close at hand rather than far off, runs straight through the work that followed.

The books trace the same preoccupation from every angle. Angel in the Forest: A Fairy Tale of Two Utopias (1945) digs into the Rappist and Owenite communities that rose and fell at New Harmony, Indiana, and her deep research there springs from the same fascination with utopian dreams and the search for truth. Miss MacIntosh, My Darling (1965) is a mythological journey through illusion and reality, in which Vera hunts for the Christian nursemaid who stands for solid ground and finishes by accepting that life is shot through with ambivalence instead. Harp Song for a Radical (1999), her biography of the socialist Eugene V. Debs, ties his labor movement back to the communal, mutual-aid spirit of the nineteenth-century utopian sects, the Mormons and the Shakers among them. The Complete Poems of Marguerite Young (2022) still waits for a close reading of its own, one that would test how her spirituality speaks in the earliest work.

Nature, for Young, was never simply beloved. She prized it for what it meant. Her "birds and beasts" stand in for human traits and cosmic ideas, a habit of symbolic reading she first worked out in her master's thesis on Elizabethan and Jacobean literature. Asked once by the Paris Review to name her faith, she called it "always poetic and cosmic," which is about as close as she came to a creed.

This second edition takes Miss MacIntosh, My Darling as its ground. It works through the novel reference by reference, gathering every mention of Christianity and of the other faiths and beliefs the book carries, in order to read Young's religious imagination closely and, in the end, to say what her Christianity and her religion finally amount to.

Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Definition from research

If grief cannot be fixed, what remains is to stay present with it, and this is the office both Vera and Mr. Spitzer perform. Vera is the novel's witness, the recorder who holds every contradiction, every dream and denial, without rushing them to a conclusion. Her long quest for a "truth that does not fail" ends not in an answer but in an acceptance of ambivalence, which radical immanence would call the mark of an honest witness rather than a defeat. religion-chapter-10:
Chapter 10

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Chapter 10 · Guide 10 The Wedding That Became a Funeral · Wheel Chapter 10 · Index Chapter 10

Allusions: Revelation and the Apocalypse · The Bible · The Book of Job

Definition from research

"we are gathered here in the sight of God" is the marriage rite of the Book of Common Prayer.

"speak now or forever hold his peace" is the old call for objection, once a real legal safeguard against unlawful marriage, now mostly ceremony.

"the end of the world draweth nigh with lightnings and thunderings and voices" pulls apocalyptic imagery from Revelation, joined to Paul's promise that the dead shall be changed "in the twinkling of an eye."

"the sea shall turn to glass" and "the secrets of all hearts shall be revealed" gather the judgment visions of Revelation, the thrones and the sea of glass, with Paul's disclosure of every hidden thing.

"even as ye will answer at the dreadful Day of Judgment" is the marriage charge of the Book of Common Prayer, binding the vow to the final reckoning.

"take this man to be your lawful wedded husband" lets the rite slip its own words, marrying man to man and folding funeral into wedding, so that vow and identity blur, fitting for a man poised between life and death.

"Man that is born of woman hath but a short time to live" is Job 14:1, and the line that follows, "He cometh up, and he is cut down, even like a flower," is Job 14:2, the brevity of a life.

"Spare us, Lord most holy, God most mighty, holy and merciful Savior" is a funeral sentence from the Book of Common Prayer, set to music by Purcell.

"Oh death, where is thy sting? Oh grave, where is thy victory?" is 1 Corinthians 15:55, death undone by resurrection, turned here toward the missing bride.

"Can these bones live?" is Ezekiel 37, the valley of dry bones and the question of whether the dead can rise.

"earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust," closing on "deep calling to deep," is the burial service of the Book of Common Prayer with Psalm 42 folded in.

"As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end" is the Gloria Patri, the doxology of God's unending glory.

See also: Chapter 05 · Guide 05 A Crazy Bus-Driver Losing His Way That He Knew Too Well · Wheel Chapter 05 · Index Chapter 05

Allusions: Deafness and Sign Language

Definition from research

"the lamb had got no fleece, where the little birds had got no feathers" strips the innocent of their protection. In Scripture the lamb carries sacrifice, Christ as the Lamb of God, and the birds carry God's provision, so their bareness reads as vulnerability left uncovered.

"holy Lucifer and Lucifer matches" names the fallen angel. Lucifer means light-bringer, the morning star, a name early Christian writers read into Isaiah's taunt against a proud king and fixed to Satan, the beautiful angel cast out for his pride.

"dead cherry trees blooming with sudden flowers" carries the promise of resurrection, life breaking out of what looked dead.

"Am I not my mother's son?" echoes the moment Jesus redefines family, naming as kin those who do God's will rather than blood alone.

"the setting hens were not setting" recalls Matthew 23:37, Jesus grieving over Jerusalem, longing to gather its people as a hen gathers her chicks and finding them unwilling.

"four angels at four bed-posts, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John" is the old children's bedtime prayer known as the Black Paternoster, angels set to guard a sleeper through the night.

"Conceived on boxwood, born on cedarwood, died on wormwood" is a traditional riddle whose answer is a lute, the instrument's life told through the woods that make and outlast it.

"the angels crying, crying like loons upon the breasts of the waves" sets the sorrow of angels over a fallen world against a human head too empty to hear it. The image gives divine grief a plain earthly voice, the loon's cry over water, and lets it break on deaf ears.

"in the midst of his long hair? Jezebel!" throws out the name of the painted queen of 2 Kings, cast from her window and eaten by dogs, a byword for the harlot and for adornment that ends in ruin.

Time in the novel does not recede. It accumulates, layer on layer, pressing on the present the way radical immanence describes history as a geological fact rather than a closed event. Vera is made to memorize the genealogies, the long biblical descent of names, so that the dead of scripture become sediment underfoot. Miss MacIntosh will not forgive Emperor Constantine for "wrecking the old creation," for confusing the calendar and moving the day of rest, an ancient administrative act she treats as a wound still open in the present week. religion-get-behind-me:
Get Behind Me

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Miss MacIntosh

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Definition from research

The child who whirled around expected Satan to be immediately behind her, and that expectation turns out to be the theology of the whole novel. Nothing in Young's cosmos is safely elsewhere. The devil is at close range, the dead are underfoot, the sacred is in the wind and the empty places, and God, when he appears, is a tired carpenter who left the work unfinished. "God loves the wind, the empty places," Miss MacIntosh says, and the line could stand as the book's creed. There is no ladder here, no beyond that will arrive to explain the room. There is only the room, attended to with full and honest attention, which is where, for Marguerite Young, the sacred has always lived. The whirling child was right. She only had to look behind her.

Homer Capehorn

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Homer Capehorn

Characters: Homer Capehorn · Madge Capehorn

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology

Definition from research

Homer's faith is gentle and worn smooth by common sense. He believes in an afterlife and takes death as a continuation rather than an ending. Speaking of Old Josh, he imagines the next world as "better by far," the lights only dimmed, the old man "still handing out the drinks, only more of them," hospitality carried on past the grave.

He is no dogmatist. He shrugs off grand religious display and prefers plain understanding, and where Madge turns bitter he trusts that goodness and grace are still possible even among human failures. He values real experience over theology, and his reflections on lost love and old friendship show a man who knows how flawed people are and hopes for them anyway. His faith is lived rather than argued, warm and practical and quietly hopeful.

religion-reality-is-constructed:
Reality Is Constructed

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh

Themes: Illusion and Reality

Allusions: The History of Opium

Definition from research

Catherine's opium paradise is the novel's great study of a made world. She "placed her faith only in the unreal," dwelt where forms change their shapes and death is only more dreaming, and the house filled with her constructions until the servants ran in all directions after phantoms. Set against her is Miss MacIntosh, who insists on a shared, sober reality of hard facts and common sense. The book does not simply take Miss MacIntosh's side. It lets the two women stand as the argument itself, over who builds the world and by what right one construction gets to call itself the truth. The most vertiginous lines belong to neither pole and to both. There is, one voice says, "no God but what we dreamed." Another concludes that it was all a dream, and that in another dream we die. Reality here is an agreement, powerful and binding, and the novel keeps asking who authored the version everyone has agreed to inhabit.

religion-chapter-65:
Chapter 65

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Chapter 65 · Guide 65 Mr. Bonebreaker's Umbrella · Wheel Chapter 65 · Index Chapter 65

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Genesis · Judaism · Revelation and the Apocalypse · The Book of Job

Definition from research

Mr. Bonebreaker's long sermon is a tissue of scripture. He gathers "the stray lamb to the fold" (Isaiah 40, Luke 15), calls God's discipline love, "for whom the Lord loveth, the Lord chasteneth" (Hebrews 12), and promises a man will be "as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land" (Isaiah 32).

His apocalypse is Revelation's: the Last Day "with trumpets blowing and angels shouting," the good divided from the evil "as the sheep from the goats, as the wheat from the tares" (Matthew 25 and 13), the saved riding "into heaven on cherubim" through the ivory gates, the lake turned to blood and to "sea of crystal," the unsaved cast out like "whited sepulchres" (Matthew 23).

He warns that God "is tired of man" and "will wipe old Chicago clean as a plate, just as He did the old Jerusalem, the old Nineveh," cities judged and destroyed, and that "men shall be crushed before the moth" (Job 4), for "the wrath of God is revealed from heaven" (Romans 1).

His figures run through the whole of Scripture: Hagar and her son the "wild ass among men" (Genesis 16), Eve's fig leaf and Cain's murder of Abel, a God who "has reproved kings," the promise "to hoar hairs will I carry you" (Isaiah 46), and "God speaking out of the whirlwind" (Job 38).

He turns even Miss MacIntosh's body into text, quoting the Song of Solomon over her mastectomy, "we have a little sister and she hath no breasts," bidding the barren rejoice and "enlarge their baldness like the eagle" (Micah 1), for "God loves the shorn lamb."

Between prophecies he drops into the language of baseball, urging the crowd to "pitch for God's sake at the eleventh inning," and claims to have "put away childish things" and "triumphed over death," his reward a "heavenly pavilion." His creed is that "the perishing meat of this world" is "nought," and only "love will take away an aspect of death."

His apocalypse keeps its images to the end, "the end of the world... like a shadow running backward," the sun going out and the stars falling and "the serpent bite without enchantment."

religion-not-one-self:
Not One Self

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Pillar 1 Not One Self

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Identity and the Self

Definition from research

The novel refuses the single, stable self on nearly every page, and it does so most sharply through Mr. Spitzer. He is a twin who survived his brother Peron, and his survival is a kind of partial nullification. He is mistaken for the dead man, mistakes himself for him, and cannot always say which brother he is. Catherine, Vera's mother, is many selves at once, crying out to know "which self of selves was true," setting her own identity against a rival she names Belshazzar, the last king of a falling kingdom. Radical immanence holds that multiplicity is not a fault to be corrected but the actual texture of being alive, and Young stages that truth in the idiom of resurrection and doubled souls. Mr. Spitzer's confusion is not a failure of self-knowledge. It is self-knowledge, honestly rendered.

Catherine Cartwheel

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · The History of Opium

Definition from research

Catherine, Vera's mother, lives in what the book calls an "opium paradise," and her faith, such as it is, belongs to that world of dreams. She trusts nothing fixed. She assumes "things were not what they seemed" and that "all forms must change their shapes," and religious certainty is just one more solid thing she cannot believe in. She has "placed her faith only in the unreal."

Angels, saints, cherubim, and phantoms drift through her rooms, but she meets them with confusion rather than devotion. Her world is one of "ghostly tides" and fog, of spiritual barrenness rather than hope, and she often plays at death or withdrawal. Cousin Hannah's hard moral certainty only bewilders her further. Where Miss MacIntosh stands on "truth to nature," Catherine stands on nothing at all, expecting no ground firmer than the shifting surface of the evening tide. She belongs to no church and follows no doctrine. Her faith is really faith in unreality, and it leaves her wandering.

Definition from research

Esther's faith is bound up with grief. She has had her share of religious teaching, but her repeated pregnancies and stillborn children have worn her belief down to doubt and fear. Her own mother was devout and cold, and that distance left its mark. Esther's faith is called "bigger than herself," yet she keeps running up against God's silence, the sense that no help is coming.

Biblical images crowd her story, the womb, the veil, the stillborn, birth, but they bring her little comfort. She is lonely in her faith as in everything else, a figure set among empty churches and bleak shorelines, wrestling alone. And yet she is practical about it. She takes the harshness of life and the certainty of death as given, folding even her losses into the natural order. Her belief mixes Christian teaching with folk feeling and something older, a personal faith that never hardens into doctrine. She is tragic but not broken, still holding on at the edge of what she can bear.

Definition from research

Mr. Bonebreaker is the book's apocalyptic preacher, and he believes every word he shouts. He warns of the coming end, the wrath of God, the day when the wicked fall and the righteous are carried up, and he salts his sermons with Cain and Abel, with death, with the promise of eternal life. He casts himself as God's servant, ready to give up comfort and standing to call others to repent.

The zeal does not spare him. He is worn thin, ragged, half broken by his own labors, often mocked, often alone. Still he holds to salvation and to the kingdom he believes is coming. His theology is literal and severe, hard on sin and worldly pleasure, and narrow about who will be saved. In the novel he stands for conviction itself, the hope and the harshness of it both, a man clinging to certainty in a world that offers him almost nothing.

religion-judaism:
Judaism

← Previous · Religion in MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Judaism

Characters: Esther Longtree · Joe Goldberg · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker · Vera Cartwheel

Allusions: Judaism · The Bible

Definition from research

The novel holds no single view of Jews or Judaism. It gives instead a spread of voices, from raw antisemitism to detached political opinion to genuine, complicated sympathy, and it is careful about whose mouth each view comes from.

The ugliest sentiments belong to characters the book has already marked as broken. Mr. Bonebreaker, the ranting Gospel salesman, slurs Jews and builds a heaven where a saved Christian's star outshines a Jew's, and Miss MacIntosh says plainly that this is unfair, even as the lake wind drowns her out. A widow in the Tavern Hotel spits a tirade that blames Jews for everything, praises Hitler, and turns just as viciously on Black people, a slur-laden outburst that indicts only herself. A rubber salesman is sure his failures are a "Jewish conspiracy." In each case the hatred sits in a mouth the reader cannot trust, which is the book's quiet way of judging it.

The most disturbing figure is the Little Toy Salesman, a grotesque who reads as a shrunken Hitler. Small, pot-bellied, bandy-legged, sucking milk from a baby bottle, he blames a "Jewish conspiracy" for his ruin and mutters about the "fleshly Jews" who bred and built the world he despises. He calls himself a murderer of women and children, the lone survivor of a storm that drowned everyone stronger, and he whispers to Esther of a coming war in which "bad men would blow up the world" for fun. The horror and the absurdity together, world-ending hatred packed into a diapered little body, are the point.

Miss MacIntosh's own view is political rather than personal. She hopes the Jews will "all go back to Palestine," asking simply "where would they go," a blunt, dated answer shaped by her anti-colonial cast of mind more than by any malice. Her scorn for money and the Stock Exchange as a "palace of evil" is general anti-capitalism, not a coded slur. Her wish belongs to its moment: the book's mid-century world was one in which the Holocaust had just made the case for a Jewish homeland impossible to ignore, and the state of Israel had newly and contentiously come into being on contested ground.

Against all this stands Joe Goldberg, the one fully drawn Jewish character, and the book's sympathy runs with him. A featherweight champion, "hard as rock," who "knocked out all his enemies," he is brought down by tuberculosis, which the novel calls "God's hand." Dying in the Colorado mountains, wasted and light as clouds, he imagines himself boxing God on a peak, a professional matched against amateurs in a fight with "no rules." His Jewishness is bound up with the fight itself: he traces his strength to a family of "fighters and rabbis," back to those who "fought the angels." He writes Esther long, aching letters, calls her the "peak of his existence," and begs to be remembered before he is "knocked out, forgotten, wrapped in a sheet." It is the most tender portrait in the section, a man who wants only to leave something of himself behind.

Vera, as ever, mostly watches. She records the hatreds and the tenderness alike without stepping in to judge, and the arrangement does the judging for her: the bigots are the deluded, and the Jewish life the book draws in full is the one it grieves for.

"the brightest that ever fell with burning hair" is the fall of Lucifer and the rebel angels, the most radiant of the host cast down for pride, a third of heaven swept out with him in Revelation's account. The burning hair is Young's own fiery image, not scripture.

The bus driver's names come out in a "broken jeremiad," a lament named for Jeremiah, the weeping prophet who mourned a doomed Jerusalem.

His litany of names, "Reuben, Gad, Manasseh," on through Dan and Saul, gathers the tribes of Israel and other scriptural figures. The twelve sons of Jacob founded the twelve tribes, and the number itself carries completeness, a whole people named in a breath.

"the children of Ham" are the descendants of Noah's son Ham, from whom the Bible's Table of Nations traces many peoples.

"a stone without hands," "a stone of stumbling," "a living stone," and the rest chain together biblical stone images that all point to Christ: the stone cut without hands that shatters kingdoms (Daniel 2), the rejected cornerstone (Psalm 118:22), the stone that trips the faithless (Isaiah 8:14), the living and tried stone of 1 Peter and Isaiah 28. The closing line, "He searcheth out stones in the darkness," borrows Job 28's miner digging for hidden ore.

"The stork knoweth her times" opens a long litany of biblical roles and objects, most of them names for Christ or his mediators: the daysman who stands between God and man (Job 9:33), the forerunner (Hebrews 6:20), the advocate (1 John 2:1), the strayed sheep and the unjust steward from Jesus's parables, the wedding garment, the candlestick of God's presence. The stork itself comes from Jeremiah 8:7, its migratory instinct shaming a people who will not know God's law.

"Solomon, Bathsheba!" names King Solomon and his mother Bathsheba, once David's wife.

The claim that "twelve is the age when Christ went out to preach to the wise men" garbles the record: the Magi came to the child, the boy of twelve astonished the temple teachers, and the ministry began nearer thirty. Characters: Joachim Spitzer

Definition from research

Mr. Spitzer keeps an orthodoxy of his own making. He lives by strict private ritual, punctual and exact, his manner and his rooms carrying a churchlike solemnity, and he sets his table with salt shakers, crystal, and gold plate as if expecting the divine to arrive for dinner. The discipline is real, but the belief underneath it is anything but settled.

He is a skeptic who cannot quite let go of hope. He holds faith and doubt at once, sits easily with paradox, and is always aware of how little the human mind can grasp of God. A musician, he thinks of the divine as a silent, perfect harmony beyond all earthly discord, and his unplayed compositions stand for a peace he reaches for and never quite hears. He is unsure of the afterlife, unsure at times of his own identity, forever shadowed by his dead brother and the question of which of them he is.

For all his doubt, he serves. He acts as executor for the dead, companion to the dying, and searcher after lost souls and lost heirs, and that steady care amounts to a kind of faith even when he can promise no cosmic reward for it. He neither embraces doctrine nor rejects the possibility of the sacred. He simply keeps watch at the border between them.
