Chapter 8: What Reality and Illusion Finally Mean

← Chapter 7: Narrative, Time, and Memory · Exploring Reality and Illusion in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling · A Note on the Text →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · The Stone Deaf Man · Vera Cartwheel

This book began with a claim: illusion is primary. Most of what passes for solid ground is built, not found, and kept standing by repetition. Seeing the construction is the first step out from under its spell. Each chapter has tested that claim against a different part of Young’s novel. This last chapter asks what the tests add up to, and what the novel’s ending finally says about reality and illusion.

What the Chapters Found

In perception, Chapter 3 found no character who sees without a lens. What separates Young’s dreamers from her realists is not contact with the real but candor about the lens. In identity, Chapter 4 found selves that are crowds, split and substituted and assembled from other people. The characters who suffer most are the ones who insist on being one. In mortality, Chapter 5 found deaths no one sees, reaching the living only through what the dead leave behind, and an afterlife the living carry themselves. In ethics, Chapter 6 found goodness built by habit and held provisionally, like a basting stitch. In form, Chapter 7 found a style that makes the reader live through the thesis rather than merely hear it.

Together these findings describe a world in which everything is made: sight, selves, deaths, virtues, and time itself. The question the novel leaves is not whether to accept this, since no one in the book gets to refuse it. The question is how to live once it is known.

Fleeing Illusion into Illusion

Vera states the problem at the moment of the unmasking: “What shall we do when, fleeing from illusion, we are confronted by illusion? When falling from illusion, we fall into illusion?” This is the book’s hardest sentence, because it closes the obvious exit. There is no floor of plain fact under the dreaming. Every step out of one illusion lands in another.

Young’s answer is not despair, and it is not Catherine’s surrender either. It unfolds slowly, through the ending, and it has three parts.

The House Goes into the Sea

The first part is that the constructions fall. In the final chapter Vera tells what she could not say aloud: “that my mother was dead, that the opium paradise had crumbled, that the sea had swept over the dark house with its golden turrets and towers.” Catherine, “after many years of sleeping, arose from her bed and walked, not quite sleeping, awake when she died.” Mr. Spitzer learned at last “which brother he truly was the dead.” Miss MacIntosh’s “bald head” lies “upon the waves.” Vera is “in mourning for three deaths.”

The great edifice of illusion that Vera spent her life fleeing is simply gone, swept away “after the storm,” leaving “the chandeliers strewn for miles at the sea’s edge.” Yet its collapse does not reveal a plain reality beneath. Vera finds herself “facing that reality which had been a dream and which had crumbled, perhaps into reality, perhaps into a dream if nothing was real.” The ending refuses to say which. What it insists on is that the old construction is over and a new life must be built.

A Sense Missing

The second part is an admission. Brooding on the deaf, whose world lacks one whole channel of the real, Vera thinks: “Perhaps there is always a sense missing, that sense which would make the world real.” This is the closest the novel comes to a theory of its own. The world never becomes fully real to anyone, because every perceiver lacks something, a sense, an angle, or a light. Catherine lacked the waking world. Miss MacIntosh lacked the dream. Mr. Spitzer lacked the present. The missing sense is not a defect to be cured. It is the condition of seeing at all.

The man Vera finally loves embodies this. He is a stone deaf man who “heard with his eyes,” whose “ears were in his finger-tips,” and who became “the artist of his life.” He lives openly with a sense missing. He does not pretend to hear, and he does not treat his silence as a tragedy that cancels everything else. When Vera spells her name on his hand in the dark, she has found a way of meeting the world that works through the gap rather than denying it.

Dream On

The third part is a blessing, and Young gives it to a minor figure. When the deaf man was a boy and white girls turned away from him, an old Black woman down the road told him: “Dream on dream on for life is imaginary, and this be an imaginary world. And the silence had its tongues, and love came before words were or ever will be.”

That is the thesis of this book, spoken plainly by someone on the edge of the novel’s world. Life is imaginary, not in the sense that nothing matters, but in the sense that everything is made, and the making is where love lives. It is fitting that the sentence comes from a figure the novel’s own detective would have overlooked, someone at the margins who sees the categories most clearly. The framework calls this The Margins Reveal the Truth. Young puts her deepest line in exactly that place.

The Pearls

The novel ends in a field at night. Vera and the deaf man lie under the trees, and a child is conceived: “our child will be our ear,” he whispers. Vera does “not know the night in which I conceived as I do not know the night in which I was conceived.” The string of pearls she wore, “the only property which was left to me” from her mother’s house, is lost in the grass: “never would I find my pearls in the morning light, never even look for them.” They plan a wedding and invite “all the wild flowers and all the birds,” “the old mule that climbed over the fence,” and Esther Longtree, “the mother of the stillborn,” who “loved us all and all things hurt or silent or broken or dead or living.”

The pearls matter. They are the last piece of Catherine’s inheritance and the novel’s recurring image of beauty grown around an injury, like the pearl in Mr. Spitzer’s eye. Vera lets them go and does not search. After a lifetime spent searching for Miss MacIntosh, for truth, and for harmony, her last act in the novel is to stop looking for what she has lost, and to build something new in the dark with a man who cannot hear her, for a child who will be their ear.

What Reality and Illusion Mean

Here, finally, is what the novel teaches, set against the pillar with which this book began.

Illusion is primary. There is no bedrock beneath the constructions, and anyone who goes looking for it comes back holding another construction. Young accepts this without flinching, and she makes the reader accept it too, sentence by sentence.

But the fact that everything is made does not make everything equal. The novel draws its moral lines inside the made world, not between the made and the real. Some constructions admit they are constructions and some do not. Some are held lightly and revised, and some are defended at any cost. Some shelter others, and some, like the detective’s categories, crush whoever falls between their lines. Catherine’s dream and Miss MacIntosh’s common sense are both illusions. The difference that matters is how each is held.

Seeing the construction does not free anyone from it. Vera never reaches a world without masks. What seeing does is loosen the grip, so that an illusion can be worn like a basting stitch, firmly enough to hold for now and loosely enough to come out when the true seam is found. That is the freedom the novel offers, and it is small, honest, and enough to live on.

The rest is love, which in this novel is itself a construction: “a system of mutual deception,” Miss MacIntosh called it, and she was not wrong. Yet it is the construction Young honors most. Vera loved a bald woman for her baldness, “their lack would be my love.” She loves a deaf man through the silence. At the end she will raise a child in “an imaginary world,” which is the only kind of world there has ever been. The novel does not ask readers to wake from the dream. It asks them to dream honestly, with others, and to keep building.

Reflection Questions

  1. Vera asks, “What shall we do when, fleeing from illusion, we are confronted by illusion?” After the whole novel, what is the answer?

  2. “Perhaps there is always a sense missing, that sense which would make the world real.” What sense might be missing from one’s own way of seeing?

  3. The novel places its deepest line, “life is imaginary, and this be an imaginary world,” in the mouth of a figure at its edges. Why might wisdom come from the margins?

  4. Vera loses her pearls and never looks for them. What does it take to stop searching for what is lost?

  5. If everything is made, what makes one construction better than another?

  6. Having followed Vera to the end, what illusion would be worth keeping, knowing it is one?

Chapter 5: Mortality, Death, and the Afterlife

← Chapter 4: Identity, Selfhood, and Otherness · Exploring Reality and Illusion in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling · Chapter 6: The Search for Meaning and the Ethical Life →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker · Mrs. Hogden · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

If illusion is primary, as this book has argued from the start, then death looks like the one exception. Money can be an agreement and a self can be a crowd, but a stopped heart is not held in place by repetition. Death seems to be the bedrock the framework says is missing, the one fact that no dream can soften.

Young’s answer is strange and precise. Death is real in her novel, but no one in it ever sees one directly. Vera’s father is lost on a face of the Jungfrau and never found. Peron falls through a window on the fourteenth floor, and no one knows whether he jumped. Of Cousin Hannah, “it was difficult to know on what date of the calendar her death should be marked.” The canary dies again and again behind Catherine’s back. And the death at the center of the book, Miss MacIntosh’s, has no body and “no eye witnesses.” Death is certain, but it always reaches the living secondhand, as an absence, a rumor, or a pile of things left behind. Absence is exactly where illusion does its work. This chapter follows what Young’s characters build in the places where the dead used to be.

A Death No One Saw

Vera tells of Miss MacIntosh’s end twice. The first account, near the beginning of the novel, is a question: “It seemed that she had walked into the sea. The waves had carried her away. What proof was there?” There were her clothes on the beach, her Pilgrim’s Progress soaked and marked by shells, “her broken black umbrella beating like a bird’s wounded wing at the edge of the sea,” and “all her old properties left behind her, nothing taken, nothing missing, nothing claimed.”

The second account, near the end, comes after Vera knows about the wig and the corset, and it tells what those properties were. On the lonely beach, “her black umbrella, Mr. Bonebreaker’s umbrella, was turned inside out like a trumpet,” “her red wig was found on the back of a shriveled horseshoe crab,” and “her old Admiral Dewey corset was found draped over a rock with its fasteners gleaming like eyes.” Miss MacIntosh walked into the ocean “with her head shining, bald as a lost planet, with her hands crossed over two major wounds, the breast, the side.”

Read beside the earlier chapters, the scene is almost unbearably exact. Everything that made Miss MacIntosh the Rock of Ages is left on the sand: the hair, the corset, the umbrella. What walks into the water is the woman those things had held together, bare-headed and wounded. Her constructed self outlives her. It lies on the beach to be found, catalogued, and remembered, while the person beneath it goes where no one can follow. The one thing she carries with her is a pair of black gloves she had mended long ago “for a sad occasion which she could not foresee.”

Then Vera adds the line that gives the novel its title: “At last, however, she was given to something. My poor darling.” The woman who had given herself to nothing but duty and common sense is finally given over to the sea. With no witness and no body, the death stays open, and Vera keeps it open. “She had only disappeared, I had always said.” Chapter 2 follows the search that grows out of that refusal. What matters here is that the refusal is not simple denial. The evidence itself is a costume. Vera has proof that the made Miss MacIntosh died on the beach. She has no proof about the real one.

The Deathless Bedroom

Catherine has solved death in the simplest way possible, by refusing the line between the living and the dead. She believes herself “both living and dead, this animated and bejeweled corpse.” For her, “death was this dream’s immeasurable extension.” No one in her room is dead, because no one there is alive in the ordinary sense. Her lost husband, her dead cousins, and the kings and drowned sailors all arrive as guests and all stay.

Vera inherited this logic before she learned to question it. As a child she concluded that if a dreamer’s dream “existed and continued and merged with the dreams of others,” then death “might be proved... to be nothing but an old humbug, an imposture, an imposition bearing no grain of truth. The truth was only in the erroneous dream, the bridge between life and death.”

Miss MacIntosh answered with the most humane lesson she ever gave. “When nothing had happened, I was supposed to admit, quite simply, that nothing had happened, that not a leaf had fallen,” for “neither I nor any other mortal was God, and omniscience had not been given to us, fortunately, so that we could not see everything or we should all most certainly lose our minds.” This is not the flat denial it first sounds like. It is a teaching about the limits of sight, and she calls those limits a mercy. Catherine wants eyes that could see everywhere, as Chapter 3 showed. Miss MacIntosh gives thanks that people cannot. What lies beyond death is “God’s murky business and not ours.” If there was any heaven at all, “it should be bare and plain and unfurnished.”

The two women offer two afterlives, one crowded and one empty. Neither can be checked. Both are built. The difference, again, is candor: Catherine furnishes the beyond to escape the present, while Miss MacIntosh leaves it bare so that she can keep her attention here.

The Canary’s Funeral

Between these two positions sits the novel’s smallest and most telling object. Catherine’s canary “was all that had ever stood between her and tides of death, as she would used to say, and so long as this bird lived, she could not die. If ever this little bird went, then she must go, too, searching through all the realms of death with an empty bird cage and a package of bird seed in her hands.”

The bird dies many times. Each time Mr. Spitzer replaces it, warning the servants that Catherine “must not see the dreadful transaction, the plain deceit, the canary’s funeral in the wave-washed garden under the dripping trees, or something worse might happen.” The life she trusts as single and continuous is a line of substitutes, and her own life depends on the deception staying hidden.

This is Pillar Two at its most tender. The canary is not a fact but an agreement, kept up by repetition exactly as the framework describes. Mr. Spitzer holds a private theory that makes the arrangement almost natural to him: “anything which was worth happening at all was worth happening twice,” because “nothing which happened once was real.” The canary is real because it keeps happening. Whether the deception is love or a trap, the novel refuses to decide, and the refusal is honest. It is both. Mr. Spitzer keeps Catherine alive, and he keeps her from ever grieving.

There is a quiet echo that Chapter 4 set up. When Mrs. Hogden arrives at the door years later, she carries “an empty bird cage” and “a package of bird seed.” The image Catherine once imagined for her own journey into death, the searcher with the empty cage, walks into her house on a stranger. Young does not comment on it. She lets the prop reappear, as though the house itself were rehearsing the ending Catherine has put off for so long.

Never Born and Yet Died

Esther Longtree works as a waitress at the small-town hotel where Vera’s bus journey ends. She has been pregnant, or says she has, for years, due, as the hotel’s own account puts it, “every moon.” She claims to have “already given birth to as many as the autumn leaves,” and she “could never sleep at night without hearing the little voices of the little stillborn.” The town mocks her. People say “that she was never pregnant or everlastingly pregnant which was the same thing.”

The novel never settles whether her children existed. Esther herself admits that “nothing ever happened here, nothing much that other eyes could see.” She says she gave birth “as easily as the snow falls from the sky, and it had melted.” Her pregnancies may be real losses, or imagined ones, or grief that has taken the shape of a body. Young leaves every possibility open.

What is not in doubt is the grief. Whether or not the children lived, Esther hears their voices every night. Her body swells and aches with a loss that nobody else can see or count. The line Miss MacIntosh reads aloud from the obituary columns fits her exactly: “Here’s one who was never born and yet has died.” So does the bus driver’s boast in the book’s opening chapters: “I never saw life come, but I have seen life go.” Esther is his reverse. She claims to see life come constantly, and no one else ever sees it.

The framework has a principle for Esther, Grief Doesn't End: grief is not a stage to pass through on the way to recovery but permanent weather, and refusing to perform a tidy healing is a way of staying truthful about what was lost. By any ordinary measure Esther is deluded. By this measure she may be the most honest mourner in the book. She will not let her losses be erased simply because no one else can see them.

The Brother Who Died

Chapter 2 portrays Mr. Spitzer and Chapter 7 gives him a full meditation. His place in this chapter is as the man for whom death will not stay on one side of the grave. He is not sure which twin died. “Had he not always lamented that it was he who had died so suddenly he had not known what had happened? For death was the heart of life. But was life, by extension, the heart of death, he asked?”

His uncertainty makes him the novel’s great attendant at deathbeds. At Cousin Hannah’s bedside the narrator notes that “there was no one so expert as he in conducting a dying soul on its last journey,” and there he arrives at the thought that “each who dies must die twice”: once in the body, and once in the life that was never lived. In the framework’s terms, Mr. Spitzer is the Witness, the one who stays in the room with what is painful and complicated without rushing to fix it or wrap it up. He cannot save anyone. He cannot even be sure he is alive. But he stays.

“One Dies”: Heidegger and the Novel’s Quarrel with Him

Martin Heidegger’s account of mortality in Being and Time helps name what these characters are doing. He argued that everyday life hides death behind the impersonal phrase “one dies,” so that death becomes something that happens to people in general and never quite to oneself. He called that anonymous public self das Man, “the they,” and said it offers a steady tranquilization about death. Against this he set an authentic relation to one’s own death: anticipating it as one’s “ownmost” possibility, which no one else can take on, and which cuts a person off from all relations to others.

Miss MacIntosh’s morning ritual fits the first half of this almost too well. She scans the obituaries “brightly” and says, “There is nothing to grieve over. Here’s a man who has died far from home. Here’s one who has died intestate.” Death arrives as a list of strangers, which is the voice of “one dies.” Her own death, however, fits the second half. She walks into the sea alone, with no witnesses, taking only her gloves. In the end she did not flee the one death that was hers.

Where the novel quarrels with Heidegger is on solitude. For him death is non-relational: each person dies alone and faces it alone. Young’s deaths are relational through and through. Mr. Spitzer cannot tell his own death from Peron’s. Catherine’s life is tied to a bird. Esther’s losses live on in her body. Vera’s grief is the shape of her whole life. In Young no one dies only their own death. Every death is carried by someone else, and often distorted, prolonged, or kept alive by the carrying. Heidegger’s authentic individual facing death alone is exactly the figure Vera’s line calls “the one illusion.”

A brief word about Buddhism belongs here too, because the novel so often seems to echo it. Buddhist teaching holds that all things are impermanent (anicca) and that there is no fixed self (anatta), and much in Young agrees with both. The difference is where the two lead. Buddhism names these truths so that a person can be freed from suffering. Young names them and offers no release. Her characters do not wake from the dream. They keep living inside it, grieving, substituting, and searching.

Grief as Weather

The novel’s final position on death is neither Catherine’s deathless room nor Miss MacIntosh’s bare heaven. It is closer to the framework’s principle of The Sacred Is Here: meaning is here, in the actual world underfoot, not in a promised beyond. The afterlife that Young can vouch for is the one the living carry. It lies in Vera’s search, in Mr. Spitzer’s replacement canaries, in Esther’s sleepless nights, and in the corset on the rock that someone has to find and remember.

That afterlife is made, like everything else in the book. It is kept up by repetition, sustained by illusion, and vulnerable to being seen through. It is also the only one anyone in the novel actually meets. Vera never receives a body to bury, so she never receives the ending that burial promises. The novel does not treat this as a failure she must get over. It treats it as the truth about loss. The dead do not stay on their side of the line, because the line was always drawn by the living, and it is the living who keep crossing it.

Reflection Questions

  1. Miss MacIntosh leaves her wig, corset, and umbrella on the beach and walks into the sea without them. What does it mean that her constructed self is what survives her?

  2. Mr. Spitzer keeps replacing the canary so that Catherine will not die. Is a deception that keeps someone alive an act of love, a trap, or both?

  3. Miss MacIntosh calls it fortunate that “omniscience had not been given to us.” Is there mercy in not being able to see everything, especially about death?

  4. Esther Longtree grieves children no one else can confirm existed. Does grief need proof to be real?

  5. Heidegger says each person dies their own death alone. Young’s characters carry each other’s deaths. Which picture of mortality feels closer to lived experience?

  6. If the only afterlife the novel can vouch for is the one the living carry, what responsibilities come with carrying it?
reality-06-chapter-6-the-search-for-mean:
Chapter 6: The Search for Meaning and the Ethical Life

← Chapter 5: Mortality, Death, and the Afterlife · Exploring Reality and Illusion in Miss MacIntosh, My Darling · Chapter 7: Narrative, Time, and Memory →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Lorena · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker · Vera Cartwheel

If illusion is primary, the obvious next question is how to live. A world built from agreements and kept standing by repetition could seem to excuse anything. If nothing is bedrock, why be good? Miss MacIntosh, My Darling never asks the question in those words, but every character in it answers it. Catherine answers with the dream, Miss MacIntosh with work, and Mr. Bonebreaker with the promise of heaven. Vera answers with a search she cannot finish. This chapter reads those answers as ethical positions and asks what kind of goodness is possible in a world that is made rather than given.

The Basting Stitch

Miss MacIntosh’s ethic fits into one sewing lesson. “A rich girl should be taught to sew like a poor one, to make her basting stitches straight and even.” Then comes the reason, which is the most revealing sentence she ever speaks about how to live: “Large, straight basting stitches were more easily pulled out than small or crooked ones.”

A basting stitch is temporary by design. It holds a garment together while the real seam is decided, and it is meant to come out. Miss MacIntosh does not teach Vera to sew permanent things. She teaches her to sew in a way that can be undone cleanly. The whole of her morality has this shape: plain, orderly, useful, and built for revision. Her creed is “Common sense is the finest sense,” and her road through life is “a granite road and not the sea road.” Yet the stitch she values most is the one that comes out.

The framework this book follows has a principle for this, Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary: since nothing is ever truly final, the honest move is to build anyway, provisionally, and keep revising, and to distrust the frozen, finished blueprint. Miss MacIntosh would never have put it that way. She believed her rules were granite. But her hands knew better than her proverbs. She built a life for Vera the way she basted a sleeve, firmly enough to hold, loosely enough to be pulled out and redone.

The Rules and Their Edges

Her ethic has hard edges, and some of them cut. She teaches that “Life was hard, and it was intended to be hard.” She holds that “God had doubtless put us where He had intended,” so that everyone should keep to their place. She calls marriage “the only normal state for a woman” and advises Vera to marry a little shoemaker and expect little. She trains Vera in basting and bookkeeping for a domestic life that Miss MacIntosh herself never had.

The irony is plain once the rest of the novel is known. The woman teaching the center’s rules lived at the edges of every one of them. She was unmarried and bald. She had loved a dancing girl named Lorena. Late in life she says she “should have been an honest woman or an honest man.” The framework calls this The Margins Reveal the Truth: the people who do not fit the categories see the categories most clearly. Miss MacIntosh saw them clearly enough to teach them perfectly, and she lived outside them in secret. Her lessons were not hypocrisy so much as protection. She handed Vera the ordinary life as a shelter she could not have herself.

The Umbrella Was Mr. Bonebreaker’s

One detail on the beach where Miss MacIntosh disappeared changes the meaning of her most famous possession. Her black umbrella, the sword and shield she carried against weather and illusion alike, is named in that final scene as “Mr. Bonebreaker’s umbrella.”

Mr. Bonebreaker was the “Gospel salesman” from Chicago to whom she was once engaged. He preached that “the end of the world is at hand, like a shadow running backward,” and dreamed always “of that heavenly crown, that golden raiment.” In Miss MacIntosh’s own judgment, “he could not bear to face the truth that he was poor.” He broke with her. Looking back, she “could see how she had been taken in,” though in the end she blamed life rather than him: she “had been betrayed without forewarning betrayed by life.”

So the most practical woman in the novel carried, for the rest of her life, a relic of its most extravagant dreamer. The instrument she held up against illusion was a gift from the man who deceived her with promises of a world to come. The novel does not explain this. It simply sets the umbrella on the sand, turned inside out “like a trumpet.” Even Miss MacIntosh’s realism was sheltered under something left over from a dream, which fits the pillar at the heart of this book: the solid thing turns out to be made, and made partly from what it opposes.

Mr. Bonebreaker also clarifies the ethical difference between the two kinds of faith. His looks to a golden beyond. Hers looks to the next task. The framework calls the second The Sacred Is Here: meaning is here, in the actual world underfoot, and the appeal to a distant beyond is the oldest way to justify sacrifice in the present. Miss MacIntosh learned that lesson by being on the wrong end of it.

Bad Faith and Ambiguity: Sartre and de Beauvoir

Jean-Paul Sartre gave the name bad faith to a particular kind of self-deception: the lie a person tells to escape their own freedom, usually by pretending that their situation, their role, or their nature leaves them no choice. Catherine looks like the textbook case. She withdraws into opium and lets the dream decide everything.

Yet the novel complicates the diagnosis. Chapter 3 noted that Catherine “pretended that the real was the dream.” She knows what she is doing. Bad faith in Sartre’s sense requires hiding the choice from oneself, and Catherine hides nothing. Her coma is a chosen sovereignty, openly held. Miss MacIntosh comes closer to Sartre’s model, because she denied for decades that her own solidity was a performance.

Simone de Beauvoir offers the more useful frame. In The Ethics of Ambiguity she argued that human beings are irreducibly ambiguous, free and bound, subject and object at once, and that the ethical task is to live inside that ambiguity rather than escape it. Every serious flight from ambiguity is a moral failure, whether it runs toward total freedom or toward total rule. By that measure Catherine and Miss MacIntosh fail in mirror image. Catherine resolves the ambiguity by dreaming it away. Miss MacIntosh resolves it by legislating it away. Vera is left with the ambiguity itself, which is the only place, de Beauvoir would say, where an ethical life can start.

Virtue as a Made Thing

Aristotle held that virtue is not born but built. A person becomes brave by doing brave things and just by doing just things, until repeated action hardens into a stable disposition. Character, in his account, is habit that has become second nature.

Read beside Young, the idea has a striking consequence. Virtue is exactly the kind of construction Pillar Two describes, a reality kept up by repetition. Miss MacIntosh’s steadiness was not a natural fact about her. She made it every morning with her tasks, her corset, her exercise, her proverbs, and her umbrella, just as she made her red hair every morning with a wig. The novel does not treat this as an exposure that cancels her goodness. It treats it as the way goodness always works. A virtue can be constructed and still be real. It is real in the way a basted seam is real: holding for now, because someone keeps holding it.

The Detective and the Quiet Mystery

The novel’s sharpest ethical scene has nothing to do with Vera’s household. It belongs to Esther Longtree, the waitress whose uncounted pregnancies were followed in Chapter 5, and to the detective who torments her.

He sends her “old newspaper clippings of old murders” by mail, as warnings, and threatens “her with exposure for having hidden away his little children.” Esther cannot tell the investigator from the crime: “Maybe, she guessed, he being the murderer he, the detective!” Her question to him is the question of the whole novel: “The truth that she was always pregnant? The truth that she was never pregnant?”

The detective is the novel’s portrait of a certain kind of knowing, the kind that can only see what its categories allow. “Things were either white or black to him.” He spends his life on “all the white mysteries,” but “the black mysteries were too quiet even for him and scared him away.” Esther’s sorrow is one of those quiet mysteries. His method has no place for a grief without evidence, so he treats it as a crime.

Here the argument of this book turns ethical. A person who mistakes a construction for bedrock, in this case the investigator’s sorting of the world into white and black, solvable and unsolvable, does real harm to the people who fall between its lines. Esther is the novel’s clearest case of what the framework calls The Margins Reveal the Truth, and the detective is its clearest case of what happens when a system refuses to look there.

The Ethics of Attention

What does the novel offer in place of the detective’s method? It offers listening. In the last chapter Vera could have told Esther everything: that her mother is dead, that the house has gone into the sea, that she is “in mourning for three deaths.” “But I spoke not,” she says, “for I listened as one might listen for one lonely heartbeat in the midst of the great silence.”

Simone Weil, whose account of perception Chapter 3 drew on, put attention at the center of ethics. For her, attention meant holding one’s own mind open and empty enough to receive another person as they actually are, without filling the gap with one’s own imaginings or judgments. The framework names the same stance the Witness: staying in the room with what is painful and complicated without rushing to fix it or wrap it up. Mr. Spitzer at every deathbed, Vera at Esther’s table, and Miss MacIntosh at the edge of Vera’s dreaming all practice some version of it.

None of them finishes the work. Mr. Spitzer never settles his brother’s case. Miss MacIntosh never completes Vera’s education. Vera never finds the woman she is looking for. The framework has a principle for this too, Unfinished Is Honest: the unfinished is not failure but honesty, and anyone who claims to hold the complete and final answer is usually selling something. In this novel that someone is Mr. Bonebreaker with his golden crown. Everyone else keeps basting.

Reflection Questions

  1. Miss MacIntosh prefers “large, straight basting stitches” because they “were more easily pulled out.” What would it mean to hold one’s own principles that way?

  2. Miss MacIntosh taught Vera an ordinary life she did not live herself. Is it hypocrisy to teach a rule one cannot follow, or can it be a form of protection?

  3. The realist’s umbrella was a gift from a dreamer who deceived her. What in ordinary life shelters people that came from something they have since rejected?

  4. Catherine knows she is pretending. Does knowing make a retreat from reality more honest, or only more deliberate?

  5. The detective sees “things” as “either white or black.” Where do systems of judgment fail the people who fall between their categories?

  6. Vera “spoke not” and listened to Esther instead. When is listening a stronger ethical act than speaking?

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

Definition from research

The comedy of mistaken identity clings to Mr. Spitzer, who keeps being greeted as his own dead brother and has to explain, with mounting embarrassment, that he is "not his dead brother" but a perfect stranger who happens to share the face. His fumbling, over-careful protests, delivered to callers who will not believe he is himself, make him a figure of gentle absurdity, a man forever proving his own existence and losing the argument. His pose as a kind of cartographer of dreams, charting the mother's visions on a mariner's chart of waters no one has sailed, adds to the picture of a lawyer permanently lost in someone else's map.

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Definition from research

Vera's discovery of Miss MacIntosh's baldness is the book's sharpest turn of tragicomedy, humor and horror in the same image. Stripped of her red wig at midnight, the plain nursemaid becomes to the child "this fearful man," a "bald, furrowed head" looming "like a skull," so that Vera decides "my lover had been a man." Later the same figure is recast in circus terms, Miss MacIntosh reimagined as the ring-master in a high silk hat with "a red, curling mustache like a waterfall." Definition from research

This chapter delivers the most sustained piece of absurdist invention: Esther's conception by silver spoon. Because her parents never touched, a third woman was hired to carry "the little spoon with the elixir of life" back and forth between them across the kitchen for seven years. The whole elaborate machinery is described with a straight face, which is what makes it funny. Her uncle, "laughing until his face turned purple," tells her she "came out of a little silver spoon," and explains the choice of silver as "the greatest conductor of heat and cold," mock-scientific reasoning applied to nonsense.

The go-between herself is a comic-grotesque figure in men's shoes, hat, and coat, smoking a cigar, walking a line that was "oblique," a farmer "plowing no furrow." Young repeatedly deflates the cosmic strangeness by insisting it is ordinary, "nothing to talk of," something that happens "in the barns and stables" all the time. That refusal to be impressed by the impossible is itself the joke.

Definition from research

The comedy here is gallows humor built around Esther Longtree, the "stillborn mother," and it works by taking her private guilt and staging it as a courtroom farce. She imagines her own trial and produces an alphabet of evidence, exhibit A the agony, exhibit B the birthday, exhibit C the candle on the cake, all the way down to U for "an umbrella or her uterus." The mock-legal inventory turns anguish into a deadpan catalog, which is one of Young's steadiest comic devices.

The running joke of the chapter is the white detective who will only solve "white" mysteries and bolts the moment anything black enters the case. He drops a double murder because blackbirds ate the same bread crumbs. The absurd literalism of a man who "drew the line between the whiteness and the blackness" is played for grim comedy even as it carries the chapter's real subject, which is racial murder and denial. Two macabre set pieces round it out: the three-hundred-pound abortionist whose whole scheme unravels because she kills a woman who was only pregnant in a dream, and the mother who lets her children play with a skull, sets their father's hat on it, and cheerfully confirms "that their father had come home" when the headless body is finally found. The humor is entirely in the flat, untroubled delivery of horror.

Here the comedy is loud and physical, then goes suddenly cold. Esther's braying laugh, "Hee, haw, my darling," rattles the silverware and shakes the coffee cups. Her humor is called "convulsive," her face turning black as she laughs. Old Doctor supplies the chapter's best absurd flourish, warning that if she does not hurry she will give birth to a full-grown little man "wearing a bowler hat and smoking a black cigar," walking out of her womb "swinging a bright cane," the cigar lit from the coal burning inside her.

The comic bravado is a mask. This is the chapter that reveals Walter, the living, accusing first child, and the mule laughter keeps breaking against real horror. Young lets the two coexist rather than resolve, so the reader is never allowed to settle into either. The verbal comedy of inversion runs through it too, her habit of asking "where is black white, where is white black, where is the dead child living, where is the live child dead," which reads as riddling nonsense and as a genuine map of her broken mind at once.

Definition from research

The landlord and the hangman resume their macabre comedy, and the chapter runs on their exchange of grim confidences. The hangman, Mr. Weed, tells his life story in a "stifled voice as if there were a rope being drawn around his neck," a respectable family man who dances at the edge of the lamplight and wipes his forehead with the black flag he waves when a knot has done its work. The landlord grumbles, plays up his deafness, and swaps prophecies of drowning against the hangman's prophecies of hanging. The relief is entirely in tone, two men treating the gallows and the grave as ordinary trades to be complained about over a counter.

Doctor O'Leary, the mad country physician, is a comic-grotesque figure who recurs through the late chapters and earns an entry of his own. His method is to diagnose the living as dead and the dead as merely sleeping. He tells Vera she has "carried a marble statue in your womb," a child turned to stone "except for its pink heel," and delivers the verdict with cheerful finality, "you are in your grave, my dear, and it is a cherub sleeping in this pool." The same logic surfaces when he delivers a real baby while convinced he is dreaming, refuses the father's offered cigar, and renounces medicine on the spot: "Life is a dream, and I have been wrong and much wronged, and I must give up this practice." Like the Egyptian scene, the comedy comes from a literal, professional man forever mistaking the dream for the diagnosis.

comedy-introduction:
Introduction

Comedy in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh

Allusions: Deafness and Sign Language · Exploration and the Poles

Definition from research

Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is usually described in terms that leave no room for laughter. It is long, dense, and incantatory, an oceanic prose poem about grief, memory, and the failure of dreams. What that description misses is that the book is also, page by page, one of the funniest American novels of its century. The comedy is not a coat of relief laid over the sorrow. It is built into the same sentences, and it does much of the novel's real work.

Young's humor almost never arrives as pure relief. It arrives braided into loss, so that a joke and a wound are usually the same object seen from two sides. The bus driver whistling through near-fatal crashes, the waitress laughing "Hee, haw, my darling" over the children she has buried, the deaf man singing love to a woman who has already left him: in each case the laugh and the ache are struck at once, and the reader is never allowed to settle into one and be done with the other.

Several comic engines run through the whole book. The first is the collision of a literal mind with a world that obeys dream logic. Miss MacIntosh with her creed that "common sense is the finest sense," Mr. Spitzer with his almost perfect jeweled watch, Doctor O'Leary with his diagnoses, all are practical people set loose in a house or a city where the furniture has names and the dead keep calling. The literalist is the joke as much as the dream is, and the harder each one insists on the plain facts, the more lost and the more comic he becomes.

The second engine is the grotesque body. Young fills the novel with bodies that are wrong in some fundamental way, the toy salesman who is a grown man behaving as an infant, the horn-blower who plays until he coughs blood, Esther Longtree forever pregnant with nothing, the giant daughter born to a doll-sized mother. These figures are ridiculous and pitiable at the same instant, and the comedy is what keeps the pity from curdling into sentiment.

The third is the deadpan catalog. When feeling threatens to swamp a scene, Young reaches for a list, and the list turns anguish into inventory: the alphabet of courtroom evidence that runs down to "an umbrella or her uterus," the roll of drowned passengers, the string of explorer and poet names the invalid gives her one substituted canary. The orderly form of the list is set against the disorder of what it holds, and the gap between them is the laugh. Beneath all of it runs the book's habit of treating the impossible as ordinary, conception by spoon, an invisible elephant in the corridor, a household staffed by phantoms who must be offered refreshments. Nobody in the novel is surprised by anything, and that refusal to be surprised is the steadiest joke Young tells.

The other chapters

These pages cover the 29 chapters where comedy carries the most weight. The other chapters are not without it. Young’s humor runs through almost the whole novel, often in the same sentence as grief. Here are the comic moments in the chapters without their own page.

  • Chapter 4: A fat, soft-faced lady on the train warns Vera that Midwesterners are deaf because they do not wish to hear.
  • Chapter 5: Moses rails against the New Deal though he never has time to vote, and swears he will never cut his hair.
  • Chapter 7: Moses mocks old Doc, who drives a Model T with no wheels to patients who are ghosts. After Madge’s darkest gossip, Homer announces that he is hungry.
  • Chapter 8: Madge and Homer quarrel over Beatrice Fitzgerald: common prostitute, or hard worker who lost an eye to a boy’s arrow.
  • Chapter 9: Vera declares she is dancing with Death and is sternly corrected. Solomon the turtle drags a geranium pot across the schoolroom.
  • Chapter 10: A dream wedding with Mr. Spitzer as the veiled bride and Miss MacIntosh as the bridegroom.
  • Chapter 11: Sir Walter Raleigh removes his head along with his plumed hat, and Mr. Spitzer, as always, misses it all.
  • Chapter 12: Catherine suspects Mr. Spitzer of betting on phantom horses as his dead brother.
  • Chapter 15: Vera’s first critical look at Miss MacIntosh: the umbrella carried indoors, the windows thrown open in winter, the day-long lecture of proverbs.
  • Chapter 16: Vera rides her pony up the grand staircase, past mosaic emperors and a funeral gondola.
  • Chapter 21: Miss MacIntosh, wig shining, scolds Vera for dancing without a partner and sends the birthday dress to the ash bin.
  • Chapter 23: Miss MacIntosh’s breakfast tirade against Benjamin Franklin, whose lightning experiments put an end to privacy.
  • Chapter 25: Mr. Spitzer walks through a glass wall without noticing, pays for the wall, and is told when he sues that Mr. Spitzer died years ago.
  • Chapter 26: Two Boston spinsters who each believe they are Cleopatra, and Siamese cats who may live forever on an inheritance.
  • Chapter 27: Calling cards and a passport so the dead man will be identified as himself, and a man who says no while nodding yes when asked if he wants to die.
  • Chapter 30: Cousin Hannah crosses deserts disguised as an Arab king, and Eustace, the invisible visitor, takes many shapes.
  • Chapter 32: Hannah beats the bridegroom with her white umbrella, and Catherine remembers marrying a sailboat, a porpoise, and a star.
  • Chapter 34: A dog recites the wedding ceremony in Latin and a St. Bernard gives the last sacrament.
  • Chapter 39: The perpendicular pronoun I comes to visit the horizontal mother.
  • Chapter 40: A ship’s figurehead knows more than its captain, because it always goes first.
  • Chapter 43: Hannah, champion of bloomers, longs on her deathbed for silk skirts and parasols.
  • Chapter 46: Mr. Spitzer asks strangers in the fog whether they have seen Hannah, and a steeplejack answers him in paradoxes.
  • Chapter 51: A mouse eats Mr. Spitzer’s chords, he lists himself as a lawyer to starfish, and he meets a woman who believes she is a birdcage.
  • Chapter 53: The timid twin finds he knows boxing records and speakeasies that only his brother knew.
  • Chapter 54: Accused of stealing a rajah’s jewel, Mr. Spitzer turns out to prefer glass jewels to real ones.
  • Chapter 55: Peron forges his brother’s checks and leaves him the debts, and Joachim ends up in a beachcomber’s shack wondering whose funeral it was.
  • Chapter 56: Peron goes to his grave with poker chips and dice while a racetrack bugler plays.
  • Chapter 57: A bill keeps arriving from a tailor who cannot be found, and a Confederate soldier in the library believes the South won.
  • Chapter 58: A violinist plays an imaginary violin, and Mr. Spitzer recognizes the silent piece at once.
  • Chapter 59: Mr. Spitzer tosses coins to beggars and musicians without knowing who is rich or poor, living or dead.
  • Chapter 60: Moose calls practiced in the city are answered by a moose in the fog, and wild ducks follow him for days.
  • Chapter 61: A mute’s trained frog recites the Lord’s Prayer.
  • Chapter 62: Mr. Spitzer is startled to learn that he is in Boston and not Philadelphia.
  • Chapter 64: Boys fish for Miss MacIntosh’s wig with hooks, and a phrenologist admires her skull.
  • Chapter 65: Mr. Bonebreaker, prophet of the end of the world, flees and leaves his umbrella behind.
  • Chapter 66: Miss MacIntosh describes her imaginary raids on the Stock Exchange, her palace of evil.
  • Chapter 67: The bus cannot park between a leaking milk truck and a hearse, and Moses curses old Doc’s ghost car.
  • Chapter 69: Vera’s room is marked Fire Escape, and Dr. O’Leary rages all night at his dead sister until Vera screams at her to go.
  • Chapter 72: Esther, the immortal medical case, is pregnant with the little shadow boxer by traveling salesmen.
  • Chapter 73: The undertaker complains that Esther brings him no business.
  • Chapter 76: The detective solves every mystery except his own.

In a few chapters comedy steps back almost entirely: 13, 17, 19, 20, 28, 37, 41, 45, 47, 49, 63, 74. These include the morning Vera discovers what Miss MacIntosh has hidden (Chapters 17, 19, and 20), Mr. Spitzer’s quietest meditations, and Esther’s account of the detective in Chapter 74.

Chapter 2

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Dante · Exploration and the Poles

Definition from research

The comedy of the pregnant girl on the bus is satire by accumulation. Young dresses her in the entire world of athletics at once, a silk print of "black sail-boats sailing over purple trees and red football players playing over steeples and white skiers skiing over sail-boats," with tennis players on her scarf, footballs and golf clubs on her charm bracelets, and, crowning it all, a hat holding "one stuffed yellow canary with a moth-eaten wing." The effect is a portrait of identity assembled entirely from cheap sporting motifs, a person who is all surface trophy and no interior. The bus driver's gruff running commentary belongs here too, his self-satisfied rant delivered as "a drunken bus-driver, rolling along here in my own feather bed," a man who narrates his own bravado to an audience of no one.

The mother's dead chauffeur, James, is one of the chapter's steadiest comic runners. An ex-convict who long ago absconded with her automobile, he lives on in her mind as a driver perpetually en route to the Arctic, "still driving to Alaska, still evading, of course, the stupid police." She rides beside this absence for years, issuing orders through an imaginary speaking tube, "Home, James, she would say, helplessly, for where is home?" and then, indifferent to every signal, "Go through the red light. Pay no attention to the other drivers with cars and horses." The dark comic turn is that she knows he means to kill her once they reach that frozen country and still cannot stop giving directions, a passenger commanding her own murderer down streets that never end.

The canary is comedy built on a con the invalid never sees. Because her life depends on the little yellow bird outliving her, Mr. Spitzer keeps a supply of spares and quietly swaps a living one for each that dies, so that she believes a single bird has lived through all the years. She renames this immortal creature as the mood takes her, a rotating roll call of explorers and poets, "Juniper, Tulip, Cellini, Solomon, Methuselah, Marco Polo, Admiral Peary, Shackleton, Dante," imagining she may yet keep an "octogenarian canary." The joke lands when she watches Marco Polo escape through an open transom and, rather than grieve, concludes with perfect calm that she must now live forever, since no one could find one lost canary in a hurricane.

The gold-turbaned Egyptian is the chapter's best single scene of mistaken identity. Announced as a spirit from the underworld and received as one, he proves to be an old horse-racing acquaintance whose sacred document, a "papyrus which might have come from the tomb of a pharaoh," turns out under candlelight to be "a race dope sheet listing those Arabian horses no longer running." The comedy is Mr. Spitzer's laborious, lawyerly effort to convince the dancing visitor that he is dead and has come to the wrong man, an argument he nearly has to settle by "lifting him by his shirt-tail." It is the purest instance of the book's running gag, a literal man trying to reason a dream back out the door.

The dead grandfather supplies a strain of religious absurdity. A self-made manufacturer, he ran his household "like a church although perhaps he was its only member," kept "a place set at his table for the wanderer angel," and turned no beggar from his door "for fear it might be an angel in disguise." The comedy sharpens in his blindness, when he is led on his garden rounds by a Seeing Eye dog that is itself blind "yet never lost his path," the two of them pacing the dark walks together, each trusting the other to see. The joke and the pathos arrive in the same image, which is the chapter's whole method in miniature.

A smaller recurring gag attaches to Mr. Spitzer's cane. The suspicion follows him that he carries "a small whiskey flask inside the sphere of his ivory-headed cane," stopping on the long sea road to take "a nip like some old Pan among the silver reeds." He denies it with wounded dignity, insisting the cane holds only a slip of parchment with instructions to be opened at his death, a solemn cover story for what may be nothing grander than a hidden drink.

One tiny bookend joke is worth catching. Among the mother's furnishings are "twelve grand pianos in the house, and no one ever played them," and the number refuses to hold still, for by the book's end the flood has carried off the twelve pianos and "the thirteen pianos, one of which never was." The inventory of her dreams keeps gaining an instrument that never existed, a small running comic accounting of things that were never there.

comedy-conclusion:
Conclusion

← Previous · Comedy in MMMD Home

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

Allusions: Deafness and Sign Language

Definition from research

Taken together, the comic passages are not a series of interruptions in a sad book. They are how the book thinks.

The most consistent thing the comedy does is refuse comfort. Young's jokes tend to implicate rather than soothe. The white detective who abandons a murder the moment blackbirds enter it, the toy salesman whose grotesque babble curdles into paranoid, hateful raving, these are figures the reader laughs at and then recoils from, and the recoil is part of the design. The humor keeps pointing at the thing a gentler book would look away from, and it will not let the reader off with a chuckle.

It also protects the novel from its own lushness. Young's prose runs toward incantation, toward the beautiful and the elegiac, and left unchecked it could tip into unbroken lament. The comedy is the counterweight. A misspelled sign, a mule's bray, a man tipping his hat to the drowning, these keep the grief honest by keeping it in company with the ridiculous, so that no sorrow in the book is ever quite allowed to admire itself.

There is a deeper reason the comedy belongs. The novel's whole argument is that reality is a shared fiction, that the self is not one stable thing, that dream and fact bleed into each other, that nothing stays. Comedy is the natural language of exactly those ideas. Mistaken identity, impersonation, the person who cannot tell the living from the dead, the impossible administered as routine, these are jokes, and they are also the book's philosophy acted out in front of the reader. When Mr. Spitzer confesses that his whole life has been "this joke, almost a celestial joke," he is describing the mechanism of the entire novel.

The comedy is also where the meaning lives, and it lives at the margins rather than the center. The figures who carry the book's deepest feeling are its grotesques and outsiders, the cross-eyed waitress, the hangman, the deaf man, the toy salesman, the bald nursemaid. Young plants her truth in precisely the people a tidier novel would use as comic relief, and by making them absurd and sacred at once she refuses to let the reader choose between the two responses.

That refusal is finally what the whole comic method insists on. The book closes not on a drowned world or a dead child but on a spelling error, "Owt to luntsch, bee bak in a whale," and on the flat aside "For she could not spell either." After more than a thousand pages of loss, Young signs off with a pun, and the choice is not a retreat from seriousness. It is the last line of the argument. In this novel the comic and the elegiac were never two separate things holding each other at bay. They were always the same attention, turned with equal steadiness on a world that is at once ridiculous and beloved.

Definition from research

This is the great grotesque comic set piece of the closing stretch, the little toy salesman. He is a fully grown man who behaves as an infant. He drinks milk "from a baby bottle" warmed to skin temperature, needs his chin wiped, "could not tie his own shoe-laces," bawls, waddles "like an old diapered baby," waves a toy popgun, and has only three teeth "like tiny snowdrops." Esther, ever maternal, plans to marry him and correct his habits, teaching him "by light blows" to sit still, tie his laces, and above all "to shed tears," since he has no tear ducts. The romance between a woman perpetually pregnant with nothing and a man who is essentially a baby is pure grotesque comedy.

His shipwreck monologue extends it into a grand comic catastrophe. He sits safe in a rubber life boat "tipping his straw hat to women and children whose faces and hands crowded the sea," politely bidding each drowning passenger goodbye. The doomed ship is stocked with absurd figures: four cardsharps who cheat with mirrors and discover "there was a way for all to win," each holding "the perfect flush" as they go down; "a woman who thought that she was two women"; a glass-eyed oculist who insists he sees better with his glass eyes; and a mad German captain who, sinking, keeps conducting, his withered arm lifting to produce "more beautiful music than ever was heard by the living." The whole drowning becomes a stately, ridiculous funeral. It should be said that the salesman's monologue also curdles into paranoid, hateful raving about the sea and sky as a conspiracy against him, a delusion Young presents as the ugly, monstrous underside of the comic figure rather than as anything to laugh with. The grotesquerie and the menace are deliberately inseparable.

Definition from research

The final chapter distributes its comedy across three revelations and lets the tone soften toward tenderness at the end. First is the "celestial joke" of Mr. Spitzer, who confesses he is really Peron, a man who "knew not one note of music from another note" and "scarcely the difference between the plaintiff and the accused," yet has spent years impersonating a musician and a lawyer, preaching funerals and closing an estate. His whole life, he admits, has been "this joke, almost a celestial joke."

Second, and funniest, is the old clam-digger who compulsively buries himself in the sand, leaving only "an opening for his mouth and nose," so that migratory birds mistake him for the landscape and land on him, gulls descending on him with "loud mewings and cryings," a heron perching until "the rock had moved." Spitzer's fussy, fatherly warnings that the man will "dig one hole too many" and forget where it is turn the habit into an ongoing comic bit.

Third is the stone deaf man who ends the book, roaring at a silent lover through the wall. His opening lines, "Little boidies don't have no tits. Little boidies don't have no umbilical cords," and then "I am glad I have tits, ain't you," land as pure absurd non sequitur. His fumbling at the wrong door builds a small comic aria: "It's the wrong door. My God Who art my enchantment, we be in the wrong hotel. I be the wrong man. You be the wrong girl. It's the wrong key. It's the wrong world." The novel then closes on its last joke, Esther Longtree's restaurant sign, misspelled in full: "Owt to luntsch, bee bak in a whale," followed by the deadpan tag, "For she could not spell either." After eighty-two chapters of drowned worlds and dead children, the book signs off on a pun and a spelling error, which is Young's way of insisting that the comic and the elegiac were never separable in the first place.

She is drawn as a battle-scarred general of the vote, "cuirassed by suffrage," girded "like a great Crusader's," the captain of "a lost campaign," her old grey army coat pinned with medals earned in "so many foreign and domestic wars." Attached to her is the chapter's theological-athletic joke, her scorn at the prospect of "Dog races in Heaven as on earth" on the firm ground that "bowling is better," backed by the strong right arm she built up in the bowling alleys. The humor is the collision of the sacred and the sporting, a suffrage Crusader who would sooner bowl her way into heaven than watch the dogs run there.

3. The Drill That Becomes a Lament

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Allusions: Deafness and Sign Language · The Bible

Definition from research

One set of references travels further than any other and changes its meaning at each stop: the genealogies of Israel.

In chapter 9 they are schoolwork. Miss MacIntosh prefers the begats to the Bible's stories because they need no interpretation. Vera must memorize "all the genealogies of the Moody Bible, the sons of Levi, Judah, Er, Onan, Issachar, the sons of Tola, Phuvah, Zebulun." The threat attached is practical: they will memorize "from Abraham to Abraham" and skip the afternoon drive.

In chapter 7 the same names come from the bus-driver, and they are grief. He is speaking of the old doctor and "the poor humanity that was dead before it was ever born." Then comes the roll call: "Reuben, Gad, Manasseh, Jahaziel, Eliezer, Luke, Dan, Saul, blind as a bat." He adds "the children of Ham, deaf as a post, all these people begetting, begetting, begetting shades." The genealogy that should prove continuity has become a list of the dead and the never-born.

In chapter 10 the names return as questions: "Where, my dearest heart, is Issachar? Where is Nepthalin? Where is Reuben who begot a horde?" The questions run into the burial service, "earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust."

Then in chapter 18 the drill turns on its teacher. Miss MacIntosh, stripped of her disguise, cries out the names she once assigned as homework: "Where is Issachar, my dear, my dear of dears? Where is Reuben? Where is Nabal? Where is Mr. Spitzer?" She slips a living man in among the patriarchs. The memorized list has become a roll call of everyone lost, and it has entered her own life.

This is one of Young's most exact strategies. She does not change the text. She changes who says it and when. A list learned for use becomes a lament once the person reciting it has lost something. The same names serve the schoolroom, the barroom, the funeral, and the breakdown. Section 2 describes meaning as passing through everything a reader has read. Young makes that happen inside the novel, four times, with one list.

intertext-s6-falada-and-the-goose-girl:
Falada and "The Goose Girl"

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Esther Longtree · Falada · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Allusions: Fairy Tales and Folklore

Definition from research

Category: optional. The pony's name points to the Grimm tale, and knowing the tale deepens the passages, but they read clearly without it.

In the Brothers Grimm's "The Goose Girl," a princess travels to her wedding with her maid and her talking horse, Falada. On the way the maid forces the princess to change places with her and marries the prince as a false bride. She has Falada killed, but the horse's head is nailed beneath a dark gateway, and each morning it speaks the truth to the real princess as she passes. In the end the truth comes out.

Vera's black pony is named Falada. On her fourteenth birthday she rides him through the night, "Falada, his dish eyes shining like two moons" (chapter 16), and "He wore no saddle, and yet the rider did not part from the horse." At the height of the ride she says, "I was the headless rider." In chapter 18, when Miss MacIntosh's disguise is uncovered, Vera imagines their roles reversed, "as if I myself had become Falada, as if she were now the rider."

The novel is full of false brides and displaced identities: the bus-driver's wife who may not exist, Esther Longtree's imagined pregnancies, Miss MacIntosh's wig. Falada's severed head, which goes on telling the truth after death, is the figure of a witness. Naming the pony for him marks Vera as a girl who will spend her life trying to tell the true bride from the false.

intertext-s1-how-young-uses-other-texts:
Section 1. How Young Uses Other Texts

Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Philosophy: Spinoza

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Don Quixote · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Judaism · Milton · Shakespeare · The Bible · The History of Opium

Definition from research

Miss MacIntosh, My Darling opens on a Grey Goose bus crawling through fog somewhere in the interior of the country. Before the first chapter has gone far, Vera Cartwheel reaches for a book to explain a stranger. The bus-driver whistles, drinks, calls on the angels, and talks about a wife waiting for him at home. Vera has no way of knowing whether that wife exists. She wonders whether he is "perhaps even some mad Don Quixote chasing windmills, a virgin spirit, nobody." Then she catches herself and admits that his whole family life may be "an emanation of my over-active imagination" (chapter 1).

The allusion arrives as a guess, and the guess exposes the person who makes it. Cervantes's knight read too many books and mistook them for the world. Vera is a reader too, and within a sentence she confesses to doing the same thing. The reference explains the bus-driver no better than any other guess would. What it explains is the young woman on the bus who needs him explained.

A page later the windmill turns physical. Vera recalls what the bus has already passed on its way through the fog: "an enormous coffee urn with its lid opened against the sky, a wigwam nightclub," and then "a windmill, a leaning tower, Noah's Ark, the old woman who lived in the shoe" (chapter 1). These are roadside buildings, novelty architecture standing in what she calls "the watery greyness of the Middle West." Quixote's windmill, the tower of Pisa, the ark from Genesis, and a nursery rhyme have all been rebuilt in lumber and paint beside an Iowa road.

There is nothing sneering in the passage. Someone built those things, likely with pride, and travelers drove past them on the way to somewhere else. Young shows the great traditions of the West already arrived in the middle of the country, already rebuilt cheaply and sincerely, long before her narrator came along to notice them. The inheritance is not locked in a library in Boston. It stands in a cornfield, weathered and a little absurd, and still recognizable.

The Thesis

These two moments, placed side by side at the very start, hold the method of the whole novel. Young's allusions arrive worn and secondhand, filtered through a character's need. A reference in this book rarely tells what its source means. It tells what a person needed the source to do.

That turns every allusion into a question about the person holding it, not only the text it points to. Why does Vera reach for Quixote? Why does a nursemaid prefer Bunyan to the Bible? Why does an Iowa bus-driver recite the tribes of Israel? The answers are different each time, and they add up to a portrait of how people in this novel furnish their minds.

The question also fits the scale of the book. An index built for this volume finds about two thousand references across the novel's 82 chapters. They draw on Scripture, Greek myth, Mother Goose, the English poets, European history, American presidents, hymns, almanacs, and the names of stars. No reader can hold all of that at once, and the novel does not ask anyone to. It asks a smaller and more useful question of each reference: who is holding this text, and what did they need it to do?

Before the first chapter ends, Young names the myth that governs the rest. Vera says, "All my life I had been reaching for the tangible, and it had evaded me, much like the myth of Tantalus" (chapter 1). Tantalus stood in water that drained away whenever he bent to drink, under fruit that rose out of reach whenever he stretched for it. Vera's long search for Miss MacIntosh, the plain nursemaid who seemed the one solid thing in a house of dreams, follows that pattern exactly. Every time the real seems close enough to hold, it recedes. The allusion is not ornament. It is the plot, stated in one sentence.

What the Index Shows

Sorting the references by the character who carries them brings three findings into view.

First, each character holds the inheritance in a different way.

  • Miss MacIntosh carries reference books, not stories: Pilgrim's Progress, Franklin's almanac maxims, the genealogies of the Bible, the Hebrew calendar. She prefers Bunyan to Scripture because "old Bunyan was fairly safe even though not altogether trustworthy" (chapter 3). She treats the great men of history as personal opponents. Every reference to Benjamin Franklin in the novel belongs to her, and she never forgives him: "it was he who had written that early to bed makes us wise" (chapter 23), and then he brought the electric light.

  • Catherine Cartwheel, Vera's mother, holds history as a crowd of houseguests. In her opium dreams she is "entertaining the P's, the Q's, the R's" (chapter 11), and her rooms fill until "Spinoza and Shakespeare and Mrs. Sydington were already in the green" (chapter 24).

  • Cousin Hannah takes the parts of conquerors and questers and fails at the quest. She is "that Jason who had not found the golden fleece" (chapter 42).

  • Mr. Spitzer keeps his references in pairs and in the geography of the afterlife. He is the one who concludes, after listing the names of God, that "God was many things to many people" (chapter 29).

  • The bus-driver turns Scripture into oaths and barroom litany.

  • Esther Longtree builds an imagined motherhood out of sacred and fairy-tale material, down to "the Song of Songs of the sterility" (chapter 77).

  • Vera, who narrates nearly all of it, owns surprisingly few references herself. The ones she owns, like Quixote and Tantalus, are about seeing without grasping.

Second, Young's handling of her sources repeats in a small set of strategies that cut across the whole cast.

  • She flattens the canon into roadside buildings and pet names.

  • She stores it in catalogs and alphabets that cannot rank what they hold.

  • She lets one text change its meaning by changing who recites it. The genealogies of Israel begin as Miss MacIntosh's schoolroom drill. The bus-driver recites them as a lament for "the poor humanity that was dead before it was ever born" (chapter 7). They end as Miss MacIntosh's own cry of loss, "Where is Issachar, my dear, my dear of dears?", and among the patriarchs she slips a living man: "Where is Mr. Spitzer?" (chapter 18).

  • She hands famous roles to the wrong people. The bus-driver, guarding his uncut hair, becomes "Penelope weaving this web, not Ulysses" (chapter 5), and two Boston spinsters each claim to be Cleopatra (chapter 26).

  • She lets the great enter through their injuries: "crippled Mr. Alexander Pope" and "blind Milton dictating Paradise Lost to those indifferent daughters" (chapter 2).

  • She treats the calendar as something people built. Miss MacIntosh returns again and again to the Emperor Constantine for changing the day of rest, and 10 of the novel's 11 references to Constantine are hers.

  • She gives borrowed crowns to people with little else.

  • She lets one shared picture of death, Charon's ferry and Gabriel's horn, pass across every class, from a Boston lawyer to an Iowa bus-driver.

Third, these strategies all do the same underlying work: they keep the inheritance while refusing it final authority. Nothing is thrown away. Nothing keeps its original rank for long.

  • The Bible is doubted by its most devoted reader, who admits in the end that "The Bible exaggerates" (chapter 63).

  • Pilgrim's Progress, Miss MacIntosh's chosen guide, turns up on the beach as "her Pilgrim's Progress water-logged with marks of sea shells on its pages" (chapter 3). Near her own end she names the journey for what it has become: "ours is a Pilgrim's Progress from nowhere to nowhere" (chapter 63).

  • Calderón's famous line that life is a dream is spoken not by a sage but by Miss MacIntosh in her collapse (chapter 18) and by a drunken country doctor. He delivered a real baby while believing he was dreaming, and afterward he announces, "Life is a dream, and I have been wrong" (chapter 77).

  • Even Miss MacIntosh's scorn softens into pity for the great men who failed as she has: "Oh, my poor Canute who could not stay the tide although he bid the tide stand still!" (chapter 63).

The inheritance survives, soaked through, relabeled, and spoken by unlikely mouths.

Why Young Called Her Work Classic

Critics often called Miss MacIntosh, My Darling experimental. Young insisted that it was classic, and her use of other texts supports her. Her sources are the common stock of Western reading: the Bible, Homer, Virgil, Cervantes, Bunyan, Milton, Calderón, Grimm, and Mother Goose. A reader in 1965 would have met most of them in school, in church, or at bedtime. Nothing in her borrowing is obscure for its own sake.

What makes the novel feel strange is not the sources but the way they are kept. Young treats the Western inheritance the way a family treats an attic, not the way a museum treats a collection. Things are stored there because someone once needed them. They come down worn and relabeled, and they are put to uses their makers never pictured. A nursery rhyme becomes a roadside building. A royal genealogy becomes a grandmother's promise to an illegitimate boy in the Ozarks that he could win any throne "if he believed in America" (chapter 65). A town remembers its prettiest girl as Lincoln's sweetheart and explains, without irony, "We elected her to be immortal" (chapter 6).

This is what Young meant by classic. She took the tradition whole and set it down in the American interior among ordinary people. There it is used, misremembered, loved, and argued with. It is classic in the sense of being common property.

How This Section Proceeds

The sections that follow lay out the evidence for this reading, one step at a time.

Section 2 gives a short guide to intertextuality. It explains the few terms the volume uses and the three kinds of reference readers will meet: obligatory, optional, and accidental.

Section 3 describes how the references were found, checked, and assigned to the characters who carry them.

Section 4 gathers the references by character, showing what each person holds and why.

Section 5 names the strategies that recur across the whole cast.

Section 6 turns to the major source texts one at a time, beginning with Pilgrim's Progress, and says how firmly each is anchored in the novel.

Section 7 reads these patterns against the principles of radical immanence.

The last three sections provide a reference index for readers who want to follow a single name through the book and a bibliography of every source cited.

Throughout, the question from the first chapter stays in view: who is holding this text, and what did they need it to do?

Category: obligatory. Penelope is named three times, and her story is needed to see what Young does with it.

In Homer's Odyssey, Penelope waits twenty years for her husband Ulysses to return from Troy. To hold off her suitors, she weaves a shroud by day and unravels it by night. She is the faithful one who stays at home while the hero wanders.

Young gives her part to a man. The bus-driver, guarding his uncut hair, "was Penelope weaving this web, not Ulysses who wandered over the wide seas" (chapter 5). In Catherine's alphabet, "Penelope's web" sits between Admiral Peary and the Pleiades (chapter 11). Miss MacIntosh uses the story to argue against electric light: "Ulysses, if ever he had seen Penelope under electric lights, would never have come home, would have wandered the wide seas forever, and she would always have woven her web" (chapter 23).

Each carrier bends the myth to a need. The bus-driver needs to be the one who waits. Catherine needs a word that begins with P. Miss MacIntosh needs a reason to hate the light bulb. The web that is never finished suits a novel that is never finished either.

intertext-s5-1-the-roadside-canon:
1. The Roadside Canon

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Madge Capehorn · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Allusions: Dante · Don Quixote · Genesis · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest

Definition from research

The first strategy appears on the novel's first pages and governs everything after. Vera recalls what the bus has passed on its way through fog: "an enormous coffee urn with its lid opened against the sky, a wigwam nightclub," then "a windmill, a leaning tower, Noah's Ark, the old woman who lived in the shoe" (chapter 1). Scripture, a Tuscan landmark, a nursery rhyme, and the windmill Don Quixote charged have all become novelty architecture on an Iowa road.

Young repeats the move throughout. In chapter 10 a litany of Israel's tribes runs straight into American states without a pause: "Where is Manasses? Where is Kansas? Where is Iowa?" The names of Genesis and the names on a road map share one breath and one grammar. Miss MacIntosh's hometown is called What Cheer, a real Iowa town, and she remembers it as a place "where there were no graven images" (chapter 3). The Second Commandment has been settled there, in a town named for a cheerful greeting.

The inherited names keep turning up on small things. Esther Longtree names her lovebirds "Sweetie Petie, Mr. Bubbles, Martin Luther, Beau Geste" (chapter 72). Catherine's one yellow canary answers to "Juniper, Tulip, Cellini, Solomon, Methuselah, Marco Polo, Admiral Peary, Shackleton, Dante" (chapter 2). In chapter 6, the townspeople remember their favorite girl as "Abraham Lincoln's sweetheart and Lincoln's mother afterwards and Jenny Lind." One of them explains the process plainly: "We elected her to be immortal."

That sentence is the strategy in small. In Young's Middle West the great names are not inherited by birth. They are elected, borrowed, painted onto buildings, and given to pets. Sometimes they arrive damaged. Madge insists the girl was "no Venus Adonis, no handsome girl with a broken arm" (chapter 6). She has fused the armless Venus de Milo with Adonis and kept the broken arm. Young does not correct her. The heritage reaches the interior of the country half-remembered and still loved, and the mistake is part of how it lives there.

This strategy is where Young's intertextuality meets the principle the radical immanence notes call "Reality Is Constructed." Culture is shown as something people build and keep putting up. The canon is not a monument behind glass. It is a coffee urn on a roadside, and the people who built it meant it.
