The Protestant Ethic

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Allusions: Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest

Definition from research

Category: accidental. Weber is never cited, and the word "Protestant" appears only twice, in passing. The connection belongs to readers.

Max Weber's The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1905) argued that Protestant faith, with its stress on hard work, thrift, and plain living as signs of grace, helped shape the modern economic world.

Readers reach for Weber because Miss MacIntosh fits his description so closely. She was "always, therefore, very industrious, even in the hottest days, always bustling back and forth, enthusiastic" (chapter 3). For her, "The path of virtue was rugged and hard and girt about by rocks having no foothold" (chapter 3). "If there was any heaven, it should be bare and plain and unfurnished" (chapter 3). In her hometown of What Cheer, "God was worshiped in a building of plain walls such as befitted God or out of doors where there were no walls." She believed that God "had left many things uncreated," and that "We should do very well to take care of each new day as it came" (chapter 3).

Her plain ethic has a social side Weber would not predict. "The mill workers were striking, and she would like to picket for them if only there was time" (chapter 22). The fit with Weber is real, and a reader who brings him to the novel will find much to discuss. But the connection is the reader's, not Young's, and the volume labels it that way.

intertext-s6-benjamin-franklin-and-poor-:

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Definition from research

Category: obligatory. Franklin is named repeatedly, and Miss MacIntosh's quarrel with him cannot be followed without his maxims.

Benjamin Franklin published Poor Richard's Almanack from 1732 to 1758. Its maxims of thrift, industry, and early rising became part of American speech. Franklin was also the scientist who flew a kite in a thunderstorm, the inventor of the Franklin stove, and a founder of the republic.

Miss MacIntosh made Vera learn "everything that old Benjamin Franklin had ever said about early to bed and early to rise" (chapter 15). She honors him as the author of "Poor Richard's Almanack, these simple homilies" (chapter 63). She also cannot forgive him. "Vain man, Benjamin Franklin!" she cries (chapters 23 and 63), because the man who preached early rising also opened the age of electric light and "it was he who had written that early to bed makes us wise" (chapter 23). She dreams of "a lightless night before Benjamin Franklin flew his kite" (chapter 63).

The almanac outlives her. In the old doctor's house, Vera finds "Poor Richard's Almanack, which I knew so well" (chapter 71). Every reference to Franklin by name in the novel belongs to Miss MacIntosh. He is her model and her enemy at once, the practical American who could not stop improving the world.

Category: obligatory for the line, though Calderón is never named. The line is quoted twice, and the novel's argument depends on it.

Pedro Calderón de la Barca's play La vida es sueño, first performed in 1635, tells of a prince, Segismundo, imprisoned in a tower from birth. He is brought to court, then drugged and returned to his tower, and told that his day of power was only a dream. He concludes that all of life may be a dream, and that one must act well within it anyway.

Young quotes the line twice and gives it to unlikely speakers each time. Miss MacIntosh, stripped of her disguise, cries, "We each must die and know that this life was all a dream" (chapter 18). Later, in Esther Longtree's chapter, comes "a crazy old doctor who, when he was called out one night in what he thought was a dream, delivered a real baby." Afterward he says, "Life is a dream, and I have been wrong and much wronged, and I must give up this practice" (chapter 77).

Calderón's line belongs to a prince in a tower. Young hands it to the realist who swore she never dreamed and to a drunken country doctor. The line stays true, becomes a little ridiculous, and keeps both qualities. The essay "Roles Worn by the Wrong People" in Section 5 places this among Young's other transfers of famous words.

intertext-s6-pilgrims-progress:
Pilgrim's Progress

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Pilgrim's Progress

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Allusions: The Bible

Definition from research

Category: obligatory. The novel builds on Bunyan's allegory, and a reader who does not know it misses part of the meaning.

John Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, published in 1678, follows Christian from the City of Destruction along a narrow road to the Celestial City. On the way he passes the Slough of Despond and other trials. It was for centuries one of the most widely read books in the English language, and a child of Miss MacIntosh's generation would have known it almost as well as the Bible.

In the novel it is Miss MacIntosh's chosen guide. She prefers it even to Scripture, because "the Word of God was that which should be taken with a grain of salt," whereas "old Bunyan was fairly safe even though not altogether trustworthy" (chapter 3). She reads life through Bunyan's map. The world is "a guide through this great wilderness, this mortal life which was a path of thorns and very narrow and very uncertain" (chapter 3). She speaks of her own past as "wallowing in a Slough of Despond, almost the gutter itself" (chapter 3). She and Vera are "two grey pilgrims climbing the naked rock" (chapter 18).

Young keeps Bunyan's road and removes its ends. The book itself is found on the beach, "water-logged with marks of sea shells on its pages" (chapter 3). In chapter 63 Vera remembers Miss MacIntosh as "the surefooted Pilgrim, the one person never dreaming where all might dream." In that same chapter Miss MacIntosh names the journey for what it has become: "ours is a Pilgrim's Progress from nowhere to nowhere."

Bunyan promises arrival. Young refuses it, and yet she does not mock the pilgrim. Miss MacIntosh still urges that we walk "as if we knew where we were walking" (chapter 63). The essay "The Drowned Guide" in Section 5 follows the same pattern through her other guidebooks.

intertext-s5-2-the-catalog-and-the-alpha:
2. The Catalog and the Alphabet

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Astronomy · Judaism

Definition from research

Almost every character in the novel makes lists, and the lists are where most of the book's references live. Young uses the catalog to flatten hierarchy and to multiply identity.

Catherine's lists are alphabetical. In chapter 9 "the P's were crowding upon her," and the P's include "Pandora's bottomless box, pyramids, peninsulas, pebbles, prologues, pterodactyls." By chapter 11 she has "passed beyond Pericles, Admiral Peary, Penelope's web, the Pleiades, the formal penguins." Myth, polar exploration, astronomy, and zoology stand in a row, ordered by nothing but their first letter. An alphabet cannot rank. That is its use to her.

Miss MacIntosh's lists run the other way, toward drill and fact: navigation, the deaths of kings, the Jewish calendar, the stations of the Exodus. In chapter 20 Vera is to "learn the Jewish calendar, Nisan which is March, Jyar which is April." She also learns "the itinerary of the children of Israel from Egypt to Canaan, the stations such as Rameses, Succoth, Etham, PiHahiroth, Marah, Elim." Miss MacIntosh's catalog aims at use. Catherine's aims at reverie. The material overlaps anyway.

Mr. Spitzer keeps the naturalist's catalog. His butterflies carry the gods inside their Latin names: "the butterfly Aphrodite, named after that goddess of beauty and love," the "butterfly Apollo," Io written on both wings (chapter 29). In the same chapter he lists the names of God: "the True Vine, the Bread of Life, the Gate, the Door," running through "the Man of Sorrows, the Old Man, the King of Glory." Then he draws the conclusion the list has been building toward: "God was many things to many people."

That sentence explains why Young loves the catalog. A list lets one thing be many things at once. The canary has nine names. God has dozens. Cousin Hannah is imagined as "Clovis or Cuthbert or Crispin or Charles the Mad" (chapter 38). Each catalog refuses the single fixed identity, which is the "Not One Self" of the radical immanence notes put into grammar.

The catalog also shapes the novel itself. Readers often find Young's lists overwhelming. The index suggests the overwhelming is the point. The lists are how characters hold a world too large to hold, and the novel's length is the length of those lists, never finished.

intertext-s6-don-quixote:
Don Quixote

Definition from research

Category: obligatory. Cervantes is named in the first pages, and his knight sets the terms for how the novel's people read the world.

Miguel de Cervantes's Don Quixote, published in two parts in 1605 and 1615, tells of a country gentleman who reads so many romances of chivalry that he mistakes windmills for giants and sets out as a knight-errant. The book laughs at him and loves him at once.

Vera reaches for him on the first page. Watching the bus-driver, she wonders, "Was he, after all, a bachelor, perhaps even some mad Don Quixote chasing windmills, a virgin spirit, nobody" (chapter 1). A page later the bus has passed a real windmill standing beside the road among other roadside buildings. Quixote's error, mistaking what one has read for what is there, becomes the novel's founding question about all its people.

The knight's shape returns in Cousin Hannah, the suffrage captain who rides through storms and mountain passes. She is "a Captain Derring-Do" to Catherine (chapter 30), "a French chevalier" in her own wishes (chapter 38), and "the Black Knight or blackamoor" to the Swiss (chapter 52). Like Quixote, she never finds what she rides for. Vera and her pony Falada form a smaller pair of rider and horse: "we ourselves were the dream, the rider and the horse" (chapter 18). Young shares Cervantes's double view. The dreamer is foolish and the dreamer is also the most human person in the room.

intertext-s7-what-the-lens-shows:
What the Lens Shows

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Definition from research

Held against these principles, Young's intertextuality looks less like ornament and more like a working method. She keeps the whole Western inheritance: Scripture and Greek myth, the English poets and the European kings, the hymns, the almanacs, and the nursery rhymes. She lays it down in the ground of the American interior. She gives it to ordinary people to carry, among them nursemaids, lawyers, salesmen, bus-drivers, and girls in small towns. And she never lets any of it harden into final authority. The guide drowns, the crown is borrowed, the calendar was made by a man, and the lament is spoken in the words of a drill. The novel is classic in that it keeps everything, and it is new in that it lets nothing rule.

"Meaning is here, in the actual world underfoot, not in a promised beyond."

Bunyan's pilgrim walks toward the Celestial City. Young's pilgrim walks into the September sea. The promised beyond belongs in this novel to Mr. Bonebreaker, the Gospel salesman. He warns that "the Last Day is at hand, and hell lies under us," promises that "there would be stink in Chicago on that Last Day" (chapter 65), and dreams of European thrones. The principle names such appeals as the oldest way to justify sacrifice in the present, and Bonebreaker's promises cost Miss MacIntosh dearly.

Against them stands her own creed, which belongs to the plain American line of common sense and pragmatism: "Common sense is the finest sense." She wants Vera to "lead a useful life" and to face "the clear reality of simple things" (chapter 1). The novel lets both her creed and her failure stand, and in the space between them the ordinary world keeps its meaning.

Definition from research

Category: optional. Browning's poem is named once, in a passage whose meaning it deepens.

Robert Browning's "Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came" (1855) takes its title from a line sung by Edgar in King Lear. A knight crosses a blasted landscape toward a dark tower where others have failed. The poem ends as he sets his horn to his lips and blows.

In the novel, Catherine asks Cousin Hannah to search the Alps for her lost husband. The list of places ends: "search for him where Childe Roland had blown his horn before a dark tower and where no other sound had ever been heard" (chapter 30). Browning's quest becomes one more address in a catalog of places to look, a place of silence where the search goes unanswered.

The link to King Lear runs through the novel too. The bus-driver's circle sees the old doctor as "A fool, Lear in the storm" (chapter 7). Browning found his quest in Lear's storm, and Young finds it in an Iowa night where a drunken doctor drives into a ditch.

intertext-s5-8-borrowed-crowns:
8. Borrowed Crowns

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker · Mrs. Hogden · Vera Cartwheel

Definition from research

Several characters claim descent from greatness, and Young treats every claim with the same mixture of comedy and sympathy.

Mr. Bonebreaker's grandmother in the Ozarks told him "he was a true king, the king of almost any European country." Only "the bar sinister" kept him from "almost any throne he chose," and "it was all in the Almanach de Gotha and various other almanacs." He "could take the Hapsburgs by storm, sweep the Stuarts off their feet, achieve almost any miracle if he believed in America" (chapter 65). Mrs. Hogden, hired as a companion for Vera's mother, is "a descendant of Daniel Boone and William the Conquerer and Alexander Graham Bell" (chapter 70). Esther Longtree's mother was a "pallid descendant of George Washington's sister" (chapter 78). The two Cleopatras of Boston claim not descent but identity.

Mr. Spitzer's shelves hold the satire of all this in a single invented title, "Burke's Peerage in the Penguin World" (chapter 55). The reference book of British nobility has been moved to the ice floes, where penguins stand in rows as formal as any peerage.

The pattern shows Young's view of American democracy and its borrowed crowns. A country without titles is full of people quietly claiming them. The claims pass through almanacs and grandmothers, not courts. The phrase in Bonebreaker's passage is exact: he could win any throne "if he believed in America." The crown and the republic are joined in one hopeful, impossible sentence. Young does not sneer at the claimants. Each borrowed crown covers a real deprivation: an illegitimate birth, a sterile marriage, a hired companion's small room. The borrowed grandeur is how poor or overlooked people keep some dignity.

intertext-s6-the-tale-of-the-shipwrecked:
The Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree

Allusions: Ancient Egypt

Definition from research

Category: optional. The Egyptian tale is not named, but its figure, the drowned Egyptian sailor, appears in three chapters, and its pattern returns in the toy salesman.

The Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor survives on a papyrus from Egypt's Middle Kingdom, nearly four thousand years old. A sailor is the only survivor when his ship goes down in a storm. He is washed up on an island, where a great serpent tells him its own story of loss. A star fell and destroyed its whole family. The sailor returns home and lives to tell of it.

Young brings the figure into Catherine's bedroom as "a drowned Egyptian sailor, gold-turbaned" (chapter 2). His "hieroglyphic language" returns in chapter 40, and in chapter 54 "Some dead Egyptian sailors were unwinding their winding sheets."

The tale's pattern returns fully in Esther Longtree's toy salesman. The drowned were "the captain, the crew, the women, the children, the moon, the sun, the stars, the kittens." Of the salesman the novel says, "He had been saved. He had been the lone eye witness, he who had not wanted to live" (chapter 81). "He had sat safe in a rubber life boat, gently rocking in the vasty deep." Esther cannot forgive him for surviving and calls him "a murderer of women and of little children." Where the ancient sailor comes home to tell his tale, Young's survivor carries it as guilt. Even the falling star returns, among the things that drowned.

intertext-s6-platos-symposium:
Plato's Symposium

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel

Philosophy: Plato and Platonism

Definition from research

Category: optional. The dialogue is not named, but Plato and the Platonists are, and one of its leading figures appears in Catherine's house.

Plato's Symposium describes a banquet in Athens where the guests take turns giving speeches in praise of love. Near the end, the drunken general Alcibiades bursts in, uninvited, and gives his own speech.

Catherine's guests include "Platonists of the period of the intellectual flowering of Athens" (chapter 2), and one of her rooms is "already occupied by Plato's boat" (chapter 24). Alcibiades appears too, first as "the bloody head of Alcibiades staring through an upper window" (chapter 2), then as "bawling Alcibiades, that drunken war lord" (chapter 40). Years later his head is "in the drainpipe, literally" (chapter 70).

Catherine's house is a banquet of voices talking through the night about love and longing. Young even includes the drunken latecomer, though she gives him the fate of the historical Alcibiades, who was murdered, and keeps his head in the house long after the party.

intertext-s5-7-invented-time:
7. Invented Time

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Time

Symbols: Clocks and Watches

Allusions: Judaism · The Bible

Definition from research

A surprising number of the novel's references concern calendars, and nearly all of them treat time as something people built.

Miss MacIntosh's longest grudge is against the Emperor Constantine. She blames him because "he went over to the pagan Church of Rome and got us all off on the wrong day of the week, resting on Sunday which was the day God had not rested" (chapter 22). She returns to the grievance again and again (chapters 23, 63, 64, 66). The source seems to be her old suitor, the Gospel salesman Mr. Bonebreaker. He preached that "the old creation which was wrecked by the Emperor Constantine shall not be restored," and that in the new creation "there will be no time as in our present sense, no memory" (chapter 65).

Other calendars surround hers. Vera learns the Hebrew months, "Nisan which is March, Jyar which is April" (chapter 20). Catherine watches for "the groundhogs who emerged on Candlemas Day to see if winter was over" (chapter 41). The mute's frog dies on Maundy Thursday (chapter 61). Each calendar is local, made, and different from the others.

The strategy matters because the novel's own handling of time is so loose. Clocks stop at different hours, and years pass in a sentence. By filling the book with competing calendars and one emperor who changed the week, Young shows time as an agreement people keep, which a single man was once able to alter. Miss MacIntosh's anger at Constantine is comic, but it rests on a real perception: someone built the calendar, and so it could have been built otherwise. That is the "The Past Doesn't Go Away" of the radical immanence notes, which warns against calling any arrangement inevitable and so hiding the people who made it. Miss MacIntosh names the builder.

intertext-s5-9-the-common-underworld:
9. The Common Underworld

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest

Definition from research

Two references pass through more mouths, across more classes, than almost any others: Charon the ferryman and Gabriel's horn.

The bus-driver jokes about the dead with "not a cent with which to pay old Charon when they crossed the river in a leaking boat" (chapter 5). Mr. Spitzer carries a coin "in his purse for old Charon when he should make his last passage" (chapter 53). Catherine's house opens onto "the Stygian river flowing through a bedroom" (chapter 3). Cousin Hannah's travels pass "Charon's empty boat drifting on the midnight tide" (chapter 30). In the final chapter the shore itself is "the coast of Charon" (chapter 82).

Gabriel's horn travels the same way. The bus-driver will not leave his water hole "not even if Gabriel should blow his horn" (chapter 5). The doctor's circle speaks of "old angel Gabriel blowing his tin horn" (chapter 7). A stranger in chapter 68 ties "knots which none shall untie until Gabriel blows his horn." Mr. Spitzer imagines the dead "sleeping like this no doubt when Gabriel blew his horn" (chapter 82).

This is the strategy of the shared vocabulary. A Boston lawyer and an Iowa bus-driver hold almost nothing in common, yet they share one picture of death: the ferry, the fare, the final trumpet. The pagan ferryman and the Christian archangel sit side by side without conflict, because neither is held as doctrine. They are common speech, the way ordinary Americans talk about the end.

The strategy also shapes the novel's frame. The book begins on a bus crossing a river country in fog, driven by a man who jokes about Charon's fare. The reader is on the ferry from the first page. Young never says so. She lets the shared references do the work, which is how intertextuality operates throughout the novel: through what everyone already knows, spoken by people who do not know they are quoting.

intertext-s5-4-the-drowned-guide:
4. The Drowned Guide

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: The Bible

Definition from research

Every guidebook in the novel fails, and Young makes the failure physical.

Miss MacIntosh carries Pilgrim's Progress as her guide, preferring it to the Bible because "old Bunyan was fairly safe even though not altogether trustworthy" (chapter 3). She trusts the Bible less. "The King James version of the Bible was not to be trusted" (chapter 21), and later, "The Bible exaggerates" (chapter 63). Her other guides are almanacs: Franklin's maxims, the Farmer's Almanac, the World Almanac. Vera learns "everything that old Benjamin Franklin had ever said about early to bed and early to rise" (chapter 15).

The guides do not survive contact with the sea. Vera finds the Bunyan "water-logged with marks of sea shells on its pages" (chapter 3). Years later she still argues about it with Mr. Spitzer: "her little Pilgrim's Progress is swollen with salt water" (chapter 68). Franklin's authority collapses through his own inventions. Miss MacIntosh cannot forgive the man who preached early rising and then brought electric light: "it was he who had written that early to bed makes us wise" (chapter 23).

The most striking failure is spoken by the guide herself. In chapter 63, urging Vera forward, Miss MacIntosh says, "ours is a Pilgrim's Progress from nowhere to nowhere." She keeps Bunyan's title and his image of the pilgrim on the road. She removes both ends of the road. There is no City of Destruction to flee and no Celestial City to reach. There is only the walking.

The guides are not mocked. Miss MacIntosh walks on "as if we knew where we were walking," and the novel honors her for it. What fails is the promise of arrival. This strategy carries the principle the notes call "Unfinished Is Honest," and it may be the clearest single sign of what Young wanted her novel to do. The book keeps the old maps, lets the water in, and walks anyway.

intertext-s6-common-sense-and-american-p:
Common Sense and American Pragmatism

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Order, Chaos, and Discipline

Philosophy: William James and Pragmatism

Definition from research

Category: optional. Paine's pamphlet is not named, but "common sense" is Miss MacIntosh's watchword in eighteen chapters, and her creed belongs to the American line of plain reason and practical results.

Thomas Paine's Common Sense (1776) argued for American independence in plain language addressed to ordinary readers. More than a century later, William James's Pragmatism (1907) gave a whole lecture to "Pragmatism and Common Sense," and judged ideas by their practical results in lived experience.

Miss MacIntosh stands in that line. "Common sense is the finest sense, she had always said" (chapter 1). She wants Vera to "lead a useful life" and to face "the clear reality of simple things" (chapter 1). She judges every idea by what it does, and "never would she secede her common sense to the illusion" (chapter 63). Her teaching is practical to the point of comedy. She asks what the best time is to plant corn, in the middle of reading Bunyan (chapter 3).

The novel honors her creed and tests it. The woman of common sense wears a wig, keeps a secret past, and walks into the sea. The creed survives her failure, and the novel lets both stand.

Paradise Lost

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Paradise Lost

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Genesis · Milton

Definition from research

Category: optional. Milton and his poem are named once, and several of Milton's figures appear, but the novel does not rest on the poem's story.

John Milton's Paradise Lost, published in 1667, tells of Satan's rebellion and fall and of Adam and Eve's expulsion from Eden. Milton, blind by then, dictated the poem to helpers, among them his daughters.

Young remembers the poem through its author's injury: "blind Milton dictating Paradise Lost to those indifferent daughters" (chapter 2). Milton's figures scatter through the book. A marriage ceremony calls on "Lucifer who was the brightest and is fallen farthest" (chapter 10). Catherine's mind becomes "the medley, the imbroglio, Pandemonium, Saturnalia of her deranged imagination" (chapter 40), using the name Milton coined for the capital of Hell. Mr. Spitzer pictures a light "falling from the wing of the great archangel Uriel" (chapter 49), Milton's regent of the sun. Miss MacIntosh's lessons recall "Man's Fall which came from Eve's eating an apple of the tree of knowledge, and the apple was no sweet mackintosh" (chapter 9).

The great epic of the Fall enters the novel as a handful of names and one image of a blind man and his bored daughters. The essay "The Canon Through Its Wounds" in Section 5 places this among Young's other injured greats.

intertext-s6-thus-spoke-zarathustra:
Thus Spoke Zarathustra

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Philosophy: Nietzsche

Definition from research

Category: optional. Nietzsche is never named, but his central teaching is, and his great image runs through the book.

Friedrich Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, published between 1883 and 1885, follows a prophet who comes down from the mountains to teach. Two of its ideas matter here. The first is eternal recurrence, the thought that all things return again and again. The second is the image of man as "a rope over an abyss," stretched between what he has been and what he might become.

Mr. Spitzer, grieving his twin brother, asks, "Should not eternal recurrence be the one law of life" (chapter 42). The word "abyss" appears in thirty-three chapters of the novel and gathers around the Spitzer brothers. Mr. Spitzer pictures Peron's last hours as a long hovering at the edge: "not suddenly had he come to the great abyss, the yawning chasm" (chapter 58).

Young's use of Nietzsche is gentle. Eternal recurrence, which Zarathustra offers as a hard test, is for Mr. Spitzer a hope: that the lamp that went out might be lit again. The abyss is not the ground of a new man but the place where a brother was lost. The named teaching and the abyss make it an optional reference.

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Esther Longtree · Homer Capehorn · Joachim Spitzer · Madge Capehorn · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker · Mrs. Hogden · Vera Cartwheel

Allusions: Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest

Definition from research

Every reference in the novel has a carrier, the character whose voice or mind produces it. Read one carrier at a time, the references stop looking like a scattered hoard and start looking like portraits. Each person in the book holds the Western inheritance in a way that belongs to that person alone. What they reach for, and how they hold it, tells as much about them as anything they do. This section takes the carriers one by one, beginning with the three who carry the most.

intertext-s6-dante-and-the-divine-comedy:
Dante and The Divine Comedy

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer

Themes: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

Allusions: Dante

Definition from research

Category: optional. Dante is named in chapters 2 and 40, The Divine Comedy in chapter 29, and Inferno and Paradiso in chapter 54. The links are real, but the novel does not follow Dante's plan.

Dante Alighieri's Divine Comedy, completed around 1321, carries its poet down through the circles of Hell, up the mountain of Purgatory, and into Paradise, guided first by Virgil and then by Beatrice. Its underworld is strictly ordered. Each sin receives a fitting punishment.

In the novel Dante appears as one of the nine names of Catherine's canary (chapter 2) and among her visitors from the realm of the dead, "ageless Dante" (chapter 40). Mr. Spitzer carries him most seriously. He wonders when "he should come to the last infernal circle of this Divine Comedy of life and death" (chapter 29). He imagines an old aunt who "might be an old uncle in Paradiso if this was Paradiso. Yet it might be Inferno, for Mr. Spitzer's was an escalator psychology" (chapter 54). In the doctor's house hangs "an old steel engraving of Dante wooing Beatrice" (chapter 71). Rhadamanthus, the judge of the dead, finds Mr. Spitzer guilty of forgotten crimes in Catherine's imagination (chapters 11 and 14).

Young keeps Dante's geography and loosens its order. Mr. Spitzer rides an escalator where Dante climbed a mountain, and he cannot tell which floor is which. The underworld in this novel is not a place of fitting punishments. It is a crowded, shifting region where the living keep visiting the dead.

intertext-s3-how-the-references-were-fou:
Section 3. How the References Were Found and Checked

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker · Vera Cartwheel

Philosophy: Nietzsche · Plato and Platonism · William James and Pragmatism

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Edgar Allan Poe · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · The Bible

Chapters discussed: 65

Definition from research

The text. The novel was first published by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1965 and reissued in two volumes by Dalkey Archive Press in 1993. So every citation here gives a chapter number instead of a page. A reader holding any edition can find a passage by its chapter and a phrase from it.

Named references. Every capitalized name in the novel was reviewed by hand, about two thousand distinct forms in all. Each was sorted into one of three groups:

  • a reference to something outside the novel, such as a person, book, myth, song, place, or event;

  • an invented character or place;

  • an ordinary word that happened to begin a sentence.

Each reference was then searched through the full text, and every place it appears was recorded with its chapter and a line of surrounding text.

Unnamed allusions. Many of Young's borrowings do not name their source, so a second search looked for the wording of known sources: Bible verses, Shakespeare, Virgil, Coleridge, Poe, Franklin's maxims, hymns, and nursery rhymes. Each possible match was read in context before it was kept.

A reading pass then found allusions that no search would have caught. Two examples show the range:

  • At the old doctor's bedside, the novel slips in Othello's "men whose heads do grow beneath their shoulders" without naming the play (chapter 8).

  • When the Gospel salesman Mr. Bonebreaker warns that "there would be stink in Chicago on that Last Day" (chapter 65), he is borrowing the prophet Isaiah's promise that "instead of sweet smell there shall be stink."

Categories. After the essays were drafted, the categories were reviewed a second time. That review moved several texts into the optional category, once their anchors were found. These were Nietzsche, the Egyptian Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor, Paine and American pragmatism, the pastoral poems, and Plato's Symposium. For example, the novel names eternal recurrence outright: "Should not eternal recurrence be the one law of life" (chapter 42).

Carriers. Each reference was assigned to its carrier, the character whose voice or mind produces it. When one character reports another's visions, the one who imagines or speaks is the carrier. For example, Mr. Spitzer watches Catherine's imaginary guests, and those guests are counted as Catherine's references. Every literary, biblical, mythic, folk, musical, religious, and historical reference was read in context to settle its carrier, about 860 entries in all.

Quotations. Every quotation in this volume was checked word for word against the novel's text, and its chapter was confirmed. The results appear in Section 9.

Who carries the most. The finished index holds about two thousand entries, and the counts say something about the novel.

  • Mr. Spitzer carries the most references by far, about 735. His chapters hold the book's longest catalogs: butterflies with the names of gods, the names of God himself, and twin portraits in his brother's house.

  • Catherine Cartwheel carries about 360, most of them imaginary guests and dreamed travels.

  • Miss MacIntosh carries about 310.

  • Vera's own narration carries about 230.

The mix matters as much as the totals. Miss MacIntosh holds more biblical references than any other character, which fits a woman who drills genealogies and distrusts the Bible's stories at the same time. Scripture makes up nearly half of Mr. Bonebreaker's references, since he sells it for a living. It makes up more than a third of the bus-driver's, who uses it for oaths.

Where references cluster. The densest chapters are 65, 22, 54, and 29. Chapter 65 alone holds about 120 entries, most of them Mr. Bonebreaker's preaching and the story of Miss MacIntosh's past in Chicago. At the other extreme, chapters 25 and 75 hold almost none. The density follows the catalogs, not the plot: wherever a character begins to list, the references pour in.

Limits. Not every carrier could be settled by reading. Places, historical events, and objects of commerce were assigned by the chapter's point of view and the names nearest them, and those assignments should be treated as approximate. No search can find every allusion either, because some of Young's borrowings are echoes of rhythm or image with no shared wording.

Standards. This volume holds to a few plain rules:

  • Every quotation from the novel or any other source appears in quotation marks, with a chapter for the novel.

  • No reference is counted unless it was found in the text.

  • Connections a reader brings to the novel are welcome, but they are labeled as reader connections and kept apart from Young's own references.

The full index, with every entry, chapter, source, carrier, and category, is kept in a companion spreadsheet alongside this volume. It is built to grow. When a reader finds an allusion the index missed, it can be added as a new line, and the counts update on their own.

intertext-s4-vera:
Vera

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Vera Cartwheel

Characters: Falada · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Allusions: Don Quixote · Greek Mythology

Definition from research

Vera narrates nearly all of the novel, yet she owns surprisingly few references. Most of what she reports belongs to someone else. The references she owns are about seeing without grasping: Don Quixote, whom she guesses at in a stranger, and Tantalus, who names her whole search (chapter 1).

On her fourteenth birthday she rides her pony, "Falada, his dish eyes shining like two moons," and says, "I was the headless rider" (chapter 16). She hopes, early on, that she "would be a Lazarus of these awakening joys" (chapter 4). Late in the book, on a shelf in the old doctor's house, she finds "Poor Richard's Almanack, which I knew so well" (chapter 71). Miss MacIntosh's book has followed her into the world.

Vera's references frame everyone else's. She is the reader in the novel, the one who holds all the other carriers' texts in view.

intertext-s5-6-the-canon-through-its-wou:
6. The Canon Through Its Wounds

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh

Allusions: Milton · Romantic Poets

Definition from research

When the great figures of the past enter the novel, they tend to arrive injured, humiliated, or pitied.

Catherine's bedroom receives "crippled Mr. Alexander Pope, for example, he who had been scorned by Lady Mary Wortley Montagu." Then come "Lord Byron with his club foot" and "blind Milton dictating Paradise Lost to those indifferent daughters" (chapter 2). The house is haunted by "the bloody head of Alcibiades staring through an upper window" (chapter 2). Years later the head of Alcibiades is "in the drainpipe, literally" (chapter 70). Among Catherine's languages is "the language of Volpone who died an imaginary death" (chapter 40).

Miss MacIntosh's adversaries go the same way. For most of the book she scolds Constantine, Franklin, and Edison as "vain" men. Constantine's conversion is remembered through his tears, "shedding his tears of repentance which fell around his feet as pearls" (chapter 22). In chapter 63, undressing at the edge of her own death, her scorn turns to pity: "Oh, my poor Canute who could not stay the tide although he bid the tide stand still! Constantine who changed the calendar but could not change the time."

Canute is the key figure here. The legend of the king who commanded the tide shows the limit of power, and Miss MacIntosh finally hears it that way. The great men become fellow sufferers who also failed at something too large for them.

This strategy explains why Young's allusions rarely feel reverent even when they are learned. She is not interested in the canon as a hall of monuments. She keeps the writers and emperors, but she brings them in through the body and through failure: the club foot, the blind eyes, the tears, the severed head, the tide that would not stop. This fits the principle the notes call "The Margins Reveal the Truth." The greats are seen from the margins of their own lives, where they look most human.

intertext-s4-catherine-cartwheel:
Catherine Cartwheel

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Catherine Cartwheel

Characters: Cousin Hannah · Vera Cartwheel

Philosophy: Spinoza

Allusions: Dante · Milton · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · The History of Opium

Definition from research

Vera's mother holds history as a crowd of houseguests. From her opium bed she receives "crippled Mr. Alexander Pope," Lord Byron, and "blind Milton dictating Paradise Lost to those indifferent daughters" (chapter 2). Her house fills room by room until "Spinoza and Shakespeare and Mrs. Sydington were already in the green" (chapter 24). Her reveries run in alphabetical order, so that "The P's were crowding upon her" (chapter 9), and Pericles stands one step from the penguins (chapter 11).

Much of her cluster is made of calls that go unanswered. "She had called the Bishop of Hippo, but he had always just stepped out" (chapter 24). She left her messages for the Emperor Hadrian, "but Hadrian had stepped out into his garden," and "King Canute had gone on a long voyage." The dead are always almost at home. Her single yellow canary answers to nine names, from Juniper to Dante (chapter 2), which makes her the novel's clearest carrier of a self that is many selves.

Her references keep grief at a distance. Her Latin tag "Sunt lacrimae rerum" (chapter 41) comes with the cold note, "But her tears were never for persons." One exception breaks through. When she asks Cousin Hannah to search the Alps for her lost husband, the list of places ends at the spot "where Childe Roland had blown his horn before a dark tower and where no other sound had ever been heard" (chapter 30). For once the catalog holds a person she misses.

intertext-s7-build-anyway-knowing-its-te:
Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary, and Unfinished Is Honest

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary · Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Characters: Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh

Definition from research

"Since nothing is ever truly final, the honest move is to build anyway, provisionally, and keep revising." And: "The unfinished is not failure. It is honesty."

Every guide in the novel is kept and soaked. Miss MacIntosh's chosen book turns up on the beach as "her Pilgrim's Progress water-logged with marks of sea shells on its pages" (chapter 3). Near her own end she names the journey for what it has become: "a Pilgrim's Progress from nowhere to nowhere" (chapter 63). Still she urges that we must walk "as if we knew where we were walking."

Cousin Hannah, the novel's great quester, is "that Jason who had not found the golden fleece" (chapter 42). Even the stars in Mr. Spitzer's sky have "a letter missing from the boat alphabet of the stars" (chapter 49).

The essay "The Drowned Guide" shows how thoroughly Young keeps her maps while letting the water in. The novel's great length is the length of its unfinished lists, and the unfinished is its honesty.

intertext-s2-a-short-guide-to-intertextu:
Section 2. A Short Guide to Intertextuality

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Falada · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Philosophy: Nietzsche · Plato and Platonism · William James and Pragmatism

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Don Quixote · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Greek Mythology · Sir Walter Raleigh · The Bible · The History of Opium

Definition from research

Every piece of writing is made partly out of earlier writing. A novel borrows words, names, stories, and shapes that its readers already carry, and much of its meaning comes from what those borrowings bring with them. The study of that borrowing is called intertextuality. This section explains the few terms the volume uses, each tied to an example from Miss MacIntosh, My Darling.

Intertextuality

Julia Kristeva coined the word in her 1966 essay "Word, Dialogue and Novel." She described any text as "a mosaic of quotations." By that she meant that a text is built from, and changes, the texts that came before it.

Her idea joined two earlier lines of thought.

  • Saussure. Ferdinand de Saussure, the Swiss linguist, showed that words do not get their meaning from a direct link to things. They get it from their place in a system of other words, each defined by how it differs from the rest.

  • Bakhtin. Mikhail Bakhtin, the Russian critic, showed that a novel is full of many voices in conversation. Every word carries traces of the other places and speakers it has passed through. His name for this conversation was dialogism, and his name for the many kinds of speech inside a single novel was heteroglossia.

Kristeva put the two together. If words mean by their relation to other words, and every word carries its past with it, then a whole text means by its relation to other texts. Meaning does not pass straight from writer to reader. It passes through everything both of them have read.

Young's novel shows this on its first page. Vera sees a stranger driving a bus and reaches for Cervantes to explain him. The bus-driver never becomes Don Quixote, but the name changes how the reader sees him.

Hypotext and Hypertext

The French critic Gérard Genette gave two plain names to the parties in this exchange.

  • The hypotext is the earlier work.

  • The hypertext is the later work that draws on it and transforms it.

John Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress is a hypotext. Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is a hypertext that takes Bunyan's pilgrim and changes where the road leads. This volume uses the two terms sparingly. They are handy when a passage needs to say which book is doing the borrowing.

Three Kinds of Reference

Not every borrowing matters equally. The volume sorts each reference into one of three categories. The category depends on how firmly the reference is anchored in the novel and how much a reader loses by missing it.

Obligatory. The novel builds on the earlier text, and a reader who misses the link misses part of the meaning. Pilgrim's Progress is the clearest case. It is Miss MacIntosh's chosen guide through life. Vera later finds it on the beach, "her Pilgrim's Progress water-logged with marks of sea shells on its pages" (chapter 3). Near the end, Miss MacIntosh herself calls the journey "a Pilgrim's Progress from nowhere to nowhere" (chapter 63). Without Bunyan's straight road to the Celestial City, that phrase loses its weight.

Optional. The link is in the text and enriches the reading, but the passage still works without it. Vera's pony is named Falada (chapter 16). In the Grimm tale "The Goose Girl," Falada is the horse whose severed head, nailed above a city gate, goes on speaking the truth about a princess whose place has been stolen. A reader who knows the tale hears in the pony's name a witness who keeps telling the truth after death. A reader who does not still follows Vera's ride without trouble.

Young never cites them by title, but the novel names a figure, a phrase, or an idea that points straight to each one.

Friedrich Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra is never named, but its central teaching is. Grieving his twin brother, Mr. Spitzer asks, "Should not eternal recurrence be the one law of life" (chapter 42). Nietzsche's other great image, the abyss, appears in thirty-three chapters of the novel and gathers most thickly around the Spitzer brothers. Instead of staring into the abyss, Mr. Spitzer prods the floor with his cane because the abyss is underneath. Zarathustra calls man "a rope over an abyss." Mr. Spitzer pictures his brother's last hours as a long hovering at that edge: "not suddenly had he come to the great abyss, the yawning chasm" (chapter 58). The dwarf in Young’s novel is given a rose in his lapel and a turret on its head.

The ancient Egyptian Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor tells of a sailor who is the lone survivor of a wreck and who lives on among the memories of the drowned. Young brings its figure into Catherine's bedroom as "a drowned Egyptian sailor, gold-turbaned" (chapter 2). His "hieroglyphic language" returns in chapter 40, and in chapter 54 "Some dead Egyptian sailors were unwinding their winding sheets." The tale's pattern returns in the toy salesman, the only survivor of his own wreck.

Thomas Paine's Common Sense lends its title to Miss MacIntosh's creed. The phrase "common sense" appears in eighteen chapters, and she declares, "Common sense is the finest sense" (chapter 1). Her version belongs to the American line that runs from Paine's appeal to plain reason to the pragmatism of William James, whose Pragmatism (1907) gives a whole lecture to "Pragmatism and Common Sense." Like the pragmatists, Miss MacIntosh judges ideas by what they do. She wants Vera to "lead a useful life" and to face "the clear reality of simple things" (chapter 1).

The pastoral poems form a chain of answers. Christopher Marlowe's shepherd invites his love, "Come live with me and be my love." Sir Walter Raleigh's nymph answers that such promises fade. Centuries later William Carlos Williams answers both in "Raleigh Was Right." Young brings Raleigh into Catherine's bedroom, where he "asked that he be addressed by his intimate name, Ocean or Water, for he had crossed many waters" (chapter 11). "Water" was Queen Elizabeth's pet name for him. "Ocean" is the name he takes in his unfinished poem of love and longing to the queen, "The Ocean to Cynthia." The novel's courtships answer one another in the same way, as invitation and sober reply.

Plato's Symposium is not named, but Plato is. Catherine's guests include "Platonists of the period of the intellectual flowering of Athens" (chapter 2), and one of her rooms is "already occupied by Plato's boat" (chapter 24). Her house of voices talking through the night about love and longing is its own banquet of speeches.

Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness is the faintest of these links. The words "heart of darkness" occur as an ordinary phrase in chapters 29, 44, 45, and 53. That is enough to call the echo possible, though not certain.

Accidental. The connection lives in the reader's mind, with no anchor in the text. Max Weber's The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism. Weber is never cited, and the word "Protestant" appears only twice, in passing (chapters 3 and 9). Readers still reach for him because Miss MacIntosh's plain, hard-working, unadorned faith fits his description so closely. That connection is real for those readers and worth exploring, but it belongs to them, not to Young, and the volume labels it that way.

Referential and Typological Borrowing

Borrowings also differ in kind.

Referential borrowing takes a fragment: a name, a phrase, a line. Tantalus is a referential borrowing. Vera names him outright: "All my life I had been reaching for the tangible, and it had evaded me, much like the myth of Tantalus" (chapter 1).

Typological borrowing takes a shape: a pattern or structure carried over from earlier writing, often with no name attached. Young's deepest debts are often of this kind.

  • The pilgrimage. The novel moves like a pilgrimage whose destination keeps receding.

  • The catalog. It gathers material the way an encyclopedia or a litany does. Catherine's opium reveries run in alphabetical order, as when "The P's were crowding upon her" (chapter 9).

The catalog and the pilgrimage are old forms. Young borrows them as surely as she borrows Tantalus, though she never names them.

Iterability and Presupposition

Two last terms describe how borrowing works over time.

Iterability is the capacity of a fragment to be repeated in a new setting and take on new meaning there. Young relies on it constantly. The genealogies of Israel appear in the novel as a schoolroom drill, a barroom lament, and a cry of personal loss. The words stay the same while the speaker and the moment change.

Presupposition is what a text assumes its reader already knows. Young assumes a great deal: the Bible, Mother Goose, Greek myth, the English poets, and American history. A reader of 1965 would have met most of it in school, in church, or at bedtime. Many readers today have not. The names of Issachar's sons, the Moody Bible, and a nursery rhyme carved into a roadside building no longer arrive with the weight Young expected them to carry. That gap between what the novel presupposes and what readers now bring is the main reason a guide like this one is needed.

How the Categories Are Marked

This volume does not use tables to sort its references. Categories are named in the prose where they matter.

  • Each essay on a major source text in Section 6 opens with a sentence stating its category: obligatory, optional, or accidental. A reader knows from the start how firmly that text is anchored in the novel.

  • Elsewhere, when a reference's category bears on the argument, the sentence that introduces it says so.

  • Reader connections are always identified as reader connections, so they are never mistaken for Young's own references.

intertext-s5-5-roles-worn-by-the-wrong-p:
5. Roles Worn by the Wrong People

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Cousin Hannah · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Madge Capehorn · Miss MacIntosh

Philosophy: Hinduism

Allusions: Napoleon and Wellington · Shakespeare

Definition from research

Young keeps handing famous roles to people who do not fit them, and the mismatch carries the meaning. The strategy takes several forms.

Crossed gender. The bus-driver, guarding his uncut hair, "was Penelope weaving this web, not Ulysses" (chapter 5). Cousin Hannah is cast again and again in male heroic roles. She stands "one arm crossed before her bosom like Napoleon" and is "that Jason who had not found the golden fleece" (chapter 42). Looking at her in death, Mr. Spitzer cannot settle even that: "Was she Tristram, or was she the white Yseult?" (chapter 52). Esther Longtree, imagining a virgin birth, decides that "she was Jesus Christ or anybody holy" (chapter 79).

Doubled roles. Two Boston spinsters each believe herself the reincarnation of Cleopatra, and Mr. Spitzer serves as lawyer to both (chapter 26). His brother's house holds "the twin George Washingtons fording the twin Delawares" (chapter 55). Mr. Spitzer cannot distinguish "between the ravings of one imaginary Napoleon and another imaginary Napoleon" (chapter 54).

Great lines in wrong mouths. Calderón's famous line, that life is a dream, never appears on a stage or in a sage's mouth. Miss MacIntosh cries it in her collapse (chapter 18). A drunken country doctor says it after delivering a real baby he believed was a dream (chapter 77).

Parted lovers misread. The same list of lovers turns up three times: Romeo and Juliet, Paul and Virginia, Eloise and Abelard, Tristram and Yseult. Madge remembers her friend as Juliet (chapter 6). Mr. Spitzer uses the list to ask what Hannah was (chapter 52). Miss MacIntosh reads it as a warning, "reminding her of the increase of American divorces" (chapter 65).

In each case the role no longer fits its original shape. A mythic identity, once assigned, turns out to be portable, shareable, and reversible. Young does not treat this as error. The doubled Cleopatras and the crossed Penelope show that identity in her novel is a costume that can be worn by anyone, sometimes by two people at once. The famous role survives the transfer, and the person wearing it becomes stranger and more interesting.

intertext-s6-the-pastoral-poems-marlowe-:
The Pastoral Poems: Marlowe, Raleigh, and Williams

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker

Allusions: Sir Walter Raleigh

Definition from research

Category: optional. Sir Walter Raleigh is named twice and asks to be called "Ocean or Water," which points to his poems of love and longing.

The pastoral poems form a chain of answers. In "The Passionate Shepherd to His Love," printed in 1599, Christopher Marlowe's shepherd invites his beloved: "Come live with me and be my love." Sir Walter Raleigh answered with "The Nymph's Reply to the Shepherd," which begins "If all the world and love were young" and goes on to say that such promises fade with the seasons. Much later, William Carlos Williams answered both in "Raleigh Was Right."

Young brings Raleigh into Catherine's bedroom. When he removed his hat, "removed also his head," and "asked that he be addressed by his intimate name, Ocean or Water, for he had crossed many waters" (chapter 11). "Water" was Queen Elizabeth's pet name for him. "Ocean" is the name he takes in his unfinished poem of love and longing to the queen, "The Ocean to Cynthia." The lost head recalls his execution in 1618. Elsewhere he "had played cards with his executioners" (chapter 53).

The novel's courtships answer one another in the same pattern of invitation and sober reply. Mr. Bonebreaker's "I will make you my wife in Christ's name" (chapter 65) is an invitation, and his flight is the reply. The pastoral scene itself appears on an old wall-hanging, "where the shepherd plays his flute to the sleeping shepherdess" (chapter 16).

intertext-s6-tantalus:
Tantalus

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Tantalus

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Allusions: Greek Mythology

Definition from research

Category: obligatory. Vera names the myth outright and uses it to describe her life.

In Greek myth Tantalus was punished in the underworld by standing in a pool beneath a fruit tree. Whenever he bent to drink, the water drained away. Whenever he reached for fruit, the branch rose out of reach.

Vera says it plainly in the first chapter: "All my life I had been reaching for the tangible, and it had evaded me, much like the myth of Tantalus, much as if the tangible itself were an illusion." That one sentence is the plot of the novel. Vera spends years searching for Miss MacIntosh, the one solid person in a house of dreams, and every time the real seems close enough to hold, it recedes. Young names very few myths as keys to her own book. This is the one she names first.

intertext-s4-cousin-hannah:
Cousin Hannah

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Cousin Hannah

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer

Allusions: Napoleon and Wellington

Definition from research

Cousin Hannah carries conquest and the failed quest. Her references come from the East as a campaign ground: Saladin, "Solymon the Magnificent" (chapter 30), Babylon and Nineveh, a white horse "named El-Burraq after the horse which Mohammed the Prophet had tethered at the Wailing Wall" (chapter 30). She crosses "Al Sirat, delicate as a human hair" (chapter 36), the bridge to paradise in Islamic tradition.

Nearly every reference casts her in a man's heroic part. Catherine sees her as "a Captain Derring-Do" (chapter 30). She stands "one arm crossed before her bosom like Napoleon" (chapter 42). "The Swiss had called her the Black Knight or blackamoor" (chapter 52). Her quests do not end in triumph: "she had not found the Holy Grail or any object of her quest. She was that Jason who had not found the golden fleece" (chapter 42). At her death the conquests return as delirium: "Is that Ur of the Chaldees ... Is that Nineveh, Crete, Babylon?" (chapter 43).

Much of Hannah reaches the reader secondhand, through Catherine's dreaming and Mr. Spitzer's memory. The conqueror is always seen by someone who stayed home.

intertext-s7-language-shapes-whats-possi:
Language Shapes What's Possible

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh

Themes: Music, Sound, and Silence

Philosophy: Spinoza

Allusions: Shakespeare

Definition from research

"Grammar carries a worldview." The principle adds: "Nouns freeze things into fixed identities; verbs keep them moving."

Catherine's catalogs are streams of nouns, yet nothing in them stays frozen. Her alphabet moves: "The P's were crowding upon her" (chapter 9). Her guest rooms fill until "Spinoza and Shakespeare and Mrs. Sydington were already in the green" (chapter 24). Ordering the world by first letter, she lets no name outrank another.

The principle also distrusts any voice that claims to speak from nowhere, in pure objectivity. Miss MacIntosh's voice of plain fact seems to be that voice. She says she never dreams, and "never would she secede her common sense to the illusion" (chapter 63). Then her disguise is uncovered, and she cries, "We each must die and know that this life was all a dream" (chapter 18). The voice from nowhere turns out to stand somewhere after all.

Definition from research

The bus-driver turns Scripture into oaths and barroom litany. "Ach, God and the angels, jumping Jesus, jumping toads, holy Lucifer and Lucifer matches" (chapter 5) is typical of his speech. He recites the tribes of Israel as a lament. He turns the Gospel into a joke about the old doctor: "Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's! Render unto Doc the things that are Doc's!" (chapter 8).

His one extended myth is a reversal. Guarding his uncut hair, he "was Penelope weaving this web, not Ulysses who wandered over the wide seas" (chapter 5). He jokes about the dead having no coin for Charon. He is the novel's first ferryman, driving his passengers through fog toward a river town.

intertext-s4-miss-macintosh:
Miss MacIntosh

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Miss MacIntosh

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Ecclesiastes · Judaism · The Bible

Definition from research

Miss MacIntosh carries reference books, not stories. Her shelf holds Pilgrim's Progress, the genealogies of the Moody Bible, Franklin's almanac maxims, the Farmer's Almanac, and the plain wisdom of Ecclesiastes and Exodus. She prefers Bunyan to Scripture itself, because "the Word of God was that which should be taken with a grain of salt" (chapter 3). Her teaching aims at use: "she would have abjured all learning but what pertained to fact" (chapter 3). So Vera memorizes the sons of Levi and Judah (chapter 9), the Hebrew months, and the stations of the Exodus from Rameses to Elim (chapter 20). She learns "everything that old Benjamin Franklin had ever said about early to bed and early to rise" (chapter 15).

Miss MacIntosh treats the great men of history as personal opponents she would scold to their faces. "Vain man, Benjamin Franklin!" she cries (chapter 23), and she would tell Thomas Edison what she thought of electric lights. She never forgives the Emperor Constantine for changing the day of rest. Nearly every rebuke she delivers turns on time and light, on who decided when people should sleep, wake, and rest.

Her questions about the great are rarely curious. "Who was Martin Luther? Not that she cared for the answers" (chapter 66). Yet her cluster ends in something close to tenderness. At the edge of her own death, the scorn becomes pity: "Oh, my poor Canute who could not stay the tide" (chapter 63). Her guidebook turns into its own negation: "ours is a Pilgrim's Progress from nowhere to nowhere" (chapter 63). The woman who carried the most practical books in the novel ends by admitting, "The Bible exaggerates" (chapter 63).

intertext-s8-the-reference-index:
Section 8. The Reference Index

← Previous · Intertextuality in MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker

Allusions: Dante · Don Quixote · Edgar Allan Poe · Exploration and the Poles · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Milton · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · The Bible

Definition from research

The full index of references is kept outside this volume, in a companion spreadsheet. It holds about two thousand entries covering more than seven hundred and sixty distinct references across all 82 chapters of the novel. For each entry it records the chapter, a line of the surrounding text, the source or tradition, the character who carries it, and its category. A printed table of that size would run to hundreds of pages and would be hard to read. This section explains instead what the index holds and how a reader can use it.

What the Index Holds

The references fall into a handful of broad kinds.

Places make up the largest share. Boston, Chicago, the Arctic, the Alps, Iowa, and What Cheer recur so often that they form the novel's map as much as its setting.

History comes next: kings and emperors, explorers, presidents, generals, and the great wars and crusades.

Scripture follows, from Genesis to Revelation, with the genealogies of Israel as its most repeated thread.

Myth and folklore follow that: the gods of Greece and Rome, the ferryman of the dead, the old woman in her shoe, the talking horse of the Grimm tale.

Literature proper is a smaller share than readers might expect, a little over a hundred entries, though it includes the references that carry the most weight: Bunyan, Cervantes, Calderón, Dante, Milton, and Browning.

A small but telling group of entries is made up of unnamed allusions. These are phrases from the Bible, Shakespeare, Virgil, Coleridge, Poe, and the prayer book that Young weaves into her sentences without naming their source.

How to Use It

The index is most useful for following a single name through the book. A reader who wants to see how the ferryman of the dead travels can find Charon in chapters 3, 5, 8, 30, 46, 51, 52, 53, 59, and 82, and can see from the carrier column that he passes from Catherine to the bus-driver, to Cousin Hannah, to Mr. Spitzer, and back. A reader curious about Miss MacIntosh's quarrel with the calendar can find the Emperor Constantine in chapters 22, 23, 63, 64, 65, and 66. Every one of those entries belongs to her except the one in chapter 65, where Mr. Bonebreaker's sermon seems to have planted the grudge.

The index can also be read one chapter at a time. A reader starting a chapter can see in advance which names will appear there and where they come from. The densest chapters, 65, 22, 54, and 29, reward this most.

How to Add to It

The index is built to grow. When a reader finds an allusion it missed, the new reference can be added as a line, with its chapter, its source, and the character who carries it. The counts in the spreadsheet update on their own. The same standards apply to every addition: the reference must be found in the novel's text, and a connection the reader brings, with no anchor in the text, is marked as a reader connection.

Here is the link to the spreadsheet - MMMD_Intertextual_Index_Phase_Six

philosophy-17-the-past-doesnt-go-away:
Chapter 17. The Past Doesn't Go Away

← Previous · Philosophy of MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Time

Symbols: Clocks and Watches

Chapters discussed: 14, 24, 41, 47

Definition from research

The past is not behind us. It is beneath us, pressed into the present like layers of rock.

Catherine’s house has no single century. The servants say it is “Roman in the morning but Greek in the afternoon” (ch. 24), and the guests sleep “with little regard for century.” For Catherine, “The years collapsed to a moment whenever my mother looked back” (ch. 41).

Young’s image for this is the palimpsest. Under Catherine’s present visions lie “old and precious communications faded or illegible, a palimpsest of many hieroglyphic writings which had been effaced” (ch. 14). The old writing has not vanished. It shows through.

Mr. Spitzer keeps his own palimpsest, a “many-written palimpsest or tally sheet” on which he tries to record every “rose, bird, star, horse, barnacle” (ch. 47). But the tally always leaves someone out, “one lost soul never to be recorded.” Sedimentary time is not a complete archive. It is layer upon layer, and something is always lost between the layers.

The novel’s own structure is sedimentary. Vera rides the bus in the present, but most of the book lies beneath that ride, in layers of memory, and in the memories of others that Vera could never have witnessed. The reader moves down through the layers and back up again. The past does not stay past. It presses up through every scene.

philosophy-12-grief-doesnt-end:
Chapter 12. Grief Doesn't End

← Previous · Philosophy of MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Grief, Loss, and Mourning

Chapters discussed: 1, 41, 63, 72, 82

Definition from research

Grief is not a stage to pass through on the way to recovery. It is permanent weather. Refusing to perform a tidy healing is a way of staying truthful about what was lost.

The whole novel is an act of grief. Vera has spent years searching for Miss MacIntosh, and she describes the loss as “the sudden, terrible shock of that great loss which had divided my heart against my heart” (ch. 1). She does not recover. She searches. The book’s title is the cry of that search.

Every major character carries a grief that the novel will not resolve. Mr. Spitzer mourns Peron for decades and cannot even choose the words for the tombstone. Cousin Hannah built a crusade over the girl whose hand she let go. Esther mourns the stillborn, who come “back to haunt me and tease me” (ch. 72).

Catherine’s life shows what happens when grief is refused. She arranged her whole world to avoid sorrow, and the novel’s verdict is exact: “The lack of sorrow was a sorrow, too” (ch. 41). Miss MacIntosh, at the other extreme, insisted “There is nothing to grieve over” (ch. 63), and her own disappearance became the grief that shaped Vera’s life. Neither avoidance nor dismissal works.

Honest grief is what remains. It does not pretend that the lost can be found. It does not pretend that the loss has been overcome. It keeps walking, and it keeps looking. At the novel’s end, Vera is “in mourning for three deaths” (ch. 82), and she is also in love and carrying a child. The grief has not ended. It has been joined by other things.

philosophy-06-esther-longtree-and-endles:
Chapter 6. Esther Longtree and Endless Hope

← Previous · Philosophy of MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Esther Longtree

Characters: Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Allusions: Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest

Chapters discussed: 72, 82

Definition from research

The Promise

Late in the novel, in the chapters set in the American interior, Vera meets Esther Longtree, a waitress in a small-town restaurant. Esther is the most alive person in the book. The narrator asks, “who could have been more robustly alive than she” (ch. 72). And she is “known for her everlasting pregnancy and her loving heart which knew no lover and her everlasting loneliness” (ch. 72).

Esther’s system is hope. She lives entirely toward the future, toward what will be born. She tells Vera she is “heading toward the coasts of birth where the old ghost babies stand,” while Vera, in her view, is headed “toward the coasts of death” (ch. 72). She promises, “Something will be born. Wait and see.” Her pregnancy is the body of hope itself: a life organized around a birth that is always about to happen.

There is an irony in where Vera finds her. In the first chapter, Miss MacIntosh urged Vera to leave the house of dreams and “see America first, the broad interior, the spacious Middle West,” where she would find “the clear reality of simple things.” Vera follows the advice. And in the broad interior she finds a woman pregnant with nothing that will ever be born.

The Loading

Young loads Esther’s hope with its own history. Esther has had many pregnancies, and all have ended in stillbirth. The salesmen passing through town are “the fathers of her stillborn whom she had hidden everywhere under the leaves and under the buds and under the snow and in the rivers and in the streams and in the still places and in the night” (ch. 72). The list runs on, as Young’s lists always do when experience is entering the argument. “There were as many stillborn as the autumn leaves, the snowflakes, and I could not count them,” Esther says. And she knows what her condition means: “I have been pregnant for an undue long time.”

Hope, lived this way, becomes recurrence. If she laughs too hard, she might lose this pregnancy too, “and then would have to begin it all over again, the great enterprise of her great loneliness” (ch. 72). What Mr. Spitzer proposed as a philosophical doctrine, Esther lives in her body. The eternal return is not the return of a beloved moment. It is the return of the same hope, and the same loss, forever.

The Break

The break comes in Esther’s own voice, and it is a break in the most basic of categories. “It is not true that people are either a success or a failure in life. They could be both and me the failure like the stillborn” (ch. 72). The narrator notes that “This thought had obviously astonished her.” Esther has discovered, in the middle of a conversation about coffee, that the categories by which lives are judged do not divide cleanly. Her hope is both her success and her failure. She is both mother and not a mother. She even says she has the “feeling of not being born myself yet.”

This is the logic of the whole novel stated by its least educated character. The categories of success and failure, born and unborn, living and dead, fail not because a philosopher dismantled them but because a waitress with swollen ankles lived long enough inside them to see them give way.

What Is Left

What is left is Esther’s love, and it proves stronger than her hope. When she first meets Vera, she crushes her hand and introduces herself: “I am me, Esther Longtree, the passive policeman’s only daughter, and you’re you,” and so, she says, they have “our common humanity” in common (ch. 72). It is a plain and almost comic version of the monist vision from the first chapter, stripped of all mystical language. Every heart is not the other heart. But Esther is Esther and Vera is Vera, and that shared separateness is itself a bond.

At the novel’s end, Esther has become the figure through whom Vera sees everything. “She was the mother of the stillborn clapping their hands in clouds, and she loved us all and all things hurt or silent or broken or dead or living” (ch. 82). Hope failed. Love remained, and it extended to everything hope had lost. The final sentence about Esther is a single line: “Esther Longtree would be me.” The woman of endless hope becomes the future of the narrator herself.

philosophy-19-the-sacred-is-here:
Chapter 19. The Sacred Is Here

← Previous · Philosophy of MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer

Allusions: Deafness and Sign Language

Chapters discussed: 82

Definition from research

Meaning is here, in the actual world underfoot, not in a promised beyond.

The novel’s great systems all point elsewhere. Catherine’s dreams point to the dead. Hannah’s crusades point to distant lands and mountaintops. Esther’s hope points to a birth that never comes. Even the monist vision of the first chapter points to “some omniscient eye” that no one possesses.

Against these, the novel keeps returning to small things. The frog musician’s request for a light. Mr. Spitzer’s respect for damaged trunks. Esther’s crushing handshake. And at the end, the deaf man hearing “the fishes whispering at the bottoms of rivers” (ch. 82).

The final wedding in the last chapter gathers this principle into a single list. The guests are to be “little Johnny-jump-up and little jack-in-the-pulpit and the snapdragon and four o’clock and whippoorwill and bluejay and little jenny wren,” the waters and the clouds, “and the old mule that climbed over the fence” (ch. 82). Earlier in the novel, lists were how experience broke systems. Here the list has become an invitation. Nothing is excluded, and nothing is too small.
