philosophy-03-two-utopias-and-twenty-yea:
Chapter 3. Two Utopias and Twenty Years

← Previous · Philosophy of MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh

Themes: Society, Class, and Race

Symbols: Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest

Definition from research

Marguerite Young was born in Indianapolis in 1908 and died there in 1995. Between those dates she published two books of poetry, a work of history, a single enormous novel, and a collection of essays, and she left behind an unfinished biography of the labor leader Eugene V. Debs. On the surface this looks like a scattered career. Seen from the angle of this book, it looks like one long inquiry carried out in several forms.

New Harmony

The ground of that inquiry lies in a small town on the Wabash River in southwestern Indiana. New Harmony was the site of two of the most famous utopian experiments in American history. In 1814 the followers of George Rapp, a German religious leader, founded a community there to await the Second Coming. They lived celibate, worked in common, and prospered, and a decade later they sold the whole town and left. The buyer was Robert Owen, a Welsh industrialist and reformer, who hoped to build a new moral world on reason, science, and cooperative labor. Owen’s community fell apart within a few years.

Young’s mother and stepfather lived in New Harmony, and Young spent years there working on the book that became Angel in the Forest: A Fairy Tale of Two Utopias, published in 1945. The subtitle is exact. She studied two complete systems for organizing human life, one grounded in faith and one grounded in reason, and she watched both of them fail. Rapp’s faith could not survive the passing years in which the promised end did not come. Owen’s rationalism could not survive the actual people who arrived to live in it, with their quarrels and their laziness and their private dreams.

This matters for the argument of this book because of what Young did next. In 1945, the year Angel in the Forest appeared, she began Miss MacIntosh, My Darling. She expected the novel to take two years. It took nearly twenty. She came to it directly from the study of two collapsed utopias, and the novel can be read as that study turned inward. Where the history had examined whole communities organized around a single idea, the novel examines single lives organized around a single idea. The method is the same. Place the system among real people, let time pass, and record what gives way.

The Twenty Years

The long composition is often told as a story of obsession, and it was that. But it also bears on the argument. A novel whose method is accumulation could not be written quickly. Young worked on it daily from 1945 to 1964, and the book’s size is not an accident of temperament. It is structurally necessary. A system can only be shown failing under accumulation if the accumulation actually happens on the page. A short novel could state that common sense is an illusion. Only a very long one could let common sense live for hundreds of pages, grow familiar and beloved, and then break.

The twenty years also placed the novel in history. Young began it in the last year of the Second World War and finished it in the middle of the civil rights movement. Those decades saw the collapse of several grand systems that had promised to explain and order the world, and the rise of leaders who claimed to have the master key. The novel almost never mentions any of this directly. Its politics work at a deeper level, as Part Four will show.

The Political Conscience

Young was clear that her novel had a politics. In the interview with Friedman and Fuchs, she said: “It isn’t that Miss MacIntosh has a social conscience, but the book does. If you understand hallucination and illusion, you don’t blindly follow any leader.” She tied this directly to Mr. Spitzer and to one of the novel’s strangest minor figures: “Mr. Spitzer’s adventures and the passages on the little frog musician investigate the nature of illusion, and if there is no certain reality, the idea of following a leader must be scrutinized.” And she added a sentence that is close to a statement of method: “Some of the poetic writers who insert passages of realism in their texts have no underlying philosophy to uphold them and revert to realism. I don’t believe there can be a poetic novel without political consciousness.”

The phrase “underlying philosophy” is important. Young believed the poetic novel needed one, and she believed she had one. Her charge against other writers was not that they were too realistic but that they fell back on realism because they had nothing else to stand on. Realism, for Young, was not neutral ground. It was one more system, and a writer who retreated into it had simply chosen a comfortable room in the crowded house.

After the novel, Young turned to Eugene V. Debs, the Indiana-born labor organizer and five-time Socialist candidate for president. The Vietnam War years pushed her attention toward labor history and toward the American traditions of mutual aid and common ownership that Debs represented. She worked on the biography for the rest of her life. It was published after her death, edited by Charles Ruas, as Harp Song for a Radical: The Life and Times of Eugene Victor Debs. Even at more than six hundred pages, it covers mainly his early years and the world that formed him, and it stops before the strikes and campaigns that made him famous.

There is something fitting in that. A writer whose philosophy honored the unfinished left her last great work unfinished. The book about Debs grew the way her novel had grown, by accumulation, by digression, by the refusal to reduce a life to its headline events. It became another demonstration of her method, applied this time to history.

One Inquiry

Read together, the three prose books form a single line. Angel in the Forest tests two complete systems against the life of a community and watches them fail. Miss MacIntosh, My Darling tests many systems against individual lives and builds, from their failures, a way of living without a master key. Harp Song for a Radical turns that way of living outward toward politics, toward a leader who, unlike the blind leaders Young warned against, belonged to the people he led. The novel stands at the center of this line, and it is to the novel’s trials that Part Two now turns.

Each chapter in this part follows the same shape. It asks what a lived system promises, how the novel loads that system with experience, where the system breaks, and what is left when it does. The order matters. The trials begin with the most openly illusory life in the book and end with the life built to refute illusion, because only when realism falls is the demonstration complete.

philosophy-04-catherine-cartwheel-and-th:
Chapter 4. Catherine Cartwheel and the Invented World

← Previous · Philosophy of MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Catherine Cartwheel

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Eustace · Joachim Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Philosophy: Empiricism (Locke, Berkeley, Hume)

Allusions: Astronomy · The History of Opium

Chapters discussed: 14, 24, 27, 30, 82

Definition from research

The Promise

Catherine Cartwheel, Vera’s mother, lives in an opium dream in a great house by the sea, and she has built there the most complete system in the novel. Its promise is freedom. In her world nothing is fixed by fact, and so nothing can wound her by being true. The narrator states the principle plainly: “it was this lack of faith which made all things possible to her” (ch. 27). Where a believer is bound to what she believes, Catherine is bound to nothing. She can populate her rooms with anyone from any century.

Her system also promises knowledge. She has, the novel says, “a third eye in her forehead, the eye of her omniscience” (ch. 14). She knows the comings and goings of her guests, the moods of the dead, the thoughts of people she has never met. And the system promises company. Her favorite companion, Eustace, is invisible, and so he can be anything. “Sometimes he was a mocking bird. Sometimes he was an old woman, and sometimes he was an old man bearded like the cypress,” and “he was not confined to any one form by the laws of nature, which had been suspended in his case” (ch. 30).

This is idealism lived all the way through: the view, found in different forms from Berkeley onward, that what exists is what is perceived by a mind. Catherine goes further than any philosopher dared. She is the mind, and the world is what she perceives.

The Loading

Young does not argue against Catherine’s system. She fills it. The house becomes “crowded to the roof” (ch. 24). The guests sleep “tier above tier.” The P’s crowd upon her, planets and petunias and Prussians. Eustace multiplies into “many persons, varying according to her whims” (ch. 30). The more she invents, the more there is to hold, and the house of pure mind becomes a house of pure clutter.

Time loads the system too. Catherine telephones Cousin Hannah for years after Hannah’s death, the telephone “ringing and ringing through empty rooms” of a Boston mansion long since torn down for a highway (ch. 30). The invented world has no way to register loss, and so loss accumulates in it unseen, like water behind a wall.

The Break

The break comes from two directions. The first is a real person. In the fourteenth chapter, among all the imaginary guests, “Only Mr. Spitzer aroused, as she did not like to admit, her feelings of hostile doubt, perhaps because he was flesh and blood and real, making her feel that there was that about him which exceeded her comprehension and might be vastly different from anything either she or God had dreamed.” Idealism cannot hold a real other. The one thing Catherine’s omniscient eye cannot see is a living man who sits beside her bed every day. The narrator notes elsewhere that “The real persons were apparently the only persons who were unreal to my mother” (ch. 30). The system inverts reality so thoroughly that it can no longer find the people who love her.

The second break is sorrow. Catherine has arranged her life so that nothing can make her grieve, and the cost of that arrangement finally comes due. In the forty-first chapter, the narrator says Catherine “had kept herself, at all costs, vastly amused, sacrificing her life to her amusements, just as she remarked when she thought of the infinite sorrows she had missed.” Then comes one of the most important sentences in the novel: “The lack of sorrow was a sorrow, too.” The system promised escape from grief. Lived long enough, it produces a new grief, the grief of a life that has not been felt. In the same passage Catherine admits she “could not tell whether a thing had been a star or a firefly,” and the narrator adds, “Perhaps my mother had never really known anyone.”

At the end of the novel, the invented world is literally destroyed. Vera reports “that the opium paradise had crumbled, that the sea had swept over the dark house with its golden turrets and towers” (ch. 82). But before the flood, something else happens. Catherine, “after many years of sleeping, arose from her bed and walked, not quite sleeping, awake when she died” (ch. 82). The dreamer wakes at the very end. The system that denied death gives way in the one moment that cannot be invented.

What Is Left

Catherine is not simply refuted. The novel says early and plainly that “There was always some right in what my mother said, even when she was wrong” (ch. 27). What was right was her discovery that the world is far more invented than it looks, and that people live inside what they and others have made up. What was wrong was her belief that invention could protect her from what is not made up: another person’s reality, and her own sorrow. Her daughter will inherit both halves of that lesson. Vera never forgets that the world is dreamed. But she will spend the novel searching for the one person she believed was real.

philosophy-15-unfinished-is-honest:
Chapter 15. Unfinished Is Honest

← Previous · Philosophy of MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Philosophy: Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres

Chapters discussed: 21, 51

Definition from research

The unfinished is not failure. It is honesty. Anyone who claims to hold the complete and final answer is usually selling something.

Where the previous principle concerns how to build, this one concerns how to judge. The novel consistently treats claims of completeness with suspicion and treats incompletion with tenderness.

Mr. Spitzer’s unfinished music is the central image. An old piano mender tells him “that there had always been a missing keyboard. There had always been a string missing in the harp of God” (ch. 51). The creation itself is incomplete, and Mr. Spitzer wonders whether the missing string is his.

The opposite figure appears in the sixty-second chapter: the conductor. Mr. Spitzer gives his sympathies “not to the conductor,” and “not to the mad fellow imagining he could conduct all the music of all the singing spheres.” The music of the spheres was the Pythagorean dream, the idea that the whole cosmos sounds one perfect harmony. Pythagoras was a guest in Catherine’s house in the ninth chapter. Here his dream returns as the fantasy of a despot. Whoever imagines he can conduct all the music is, in the novel’s word, mad.

Even Miss MacIntosh, the realist, is described as “this unfinished thing, tentative and unbelievable” (ch. 21), and Vera loves her not in spite of this but because of it. Incompletion is not a flaw to be hidden. It is what a real person looks like in the morning light.

philosophy-11-reality-is-constructed:
Chapter 11. Reality Is Constructed

← Previous · Philosophy of MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh

Allusions: The History of Opium

Chapters discussed: 63

Definition from research

Most of what feels like solid reality is built. Seeing the construction is the first step out from under its spell, but seeing it does not mean escaping it. People go on living in what has been made.

The two great images of this principle are the opium house and the wig. Catherine’s house is invention on a grand scale, a whole world of guests and centuries summoned from a bed. Miss MacIntosh’s wig is invention on the smallest scale, a single disguise worn over a single head. The novel treats them as versions of the same thing. The mother who dreams everything and the nursemaid who dreams nothing both live inside something made.

Miss MacIntosh gives the principle its clearest statement, at the moment her own invention is exposed. “If I warned you against those lies and illusions surrounding us, I meant only those which we ourselves have made. Every man has a porcelain crown like mine” (ch. 63). A porcelain crown is a false tooth, and a crown is also the sign of a king. Every person wears something artificial, and every person is, in some sense, crowned by it.

Young’s own words give the ethic that follows. The mature person, she said, is one who has “examined all the illusions of life” and knows “there isn’t any reality” and yet goes on. Living in the invention is not a failure of nerve. It is the only place there is to live. The difference lies between those who know they are in it and those who mistake it for the granite road.

Chapter 20. The Crossing Point

Characters: Esther Longtree · Vera Cartwheel

Allusions: Deafness and Sign Language

Chapters discussed: 82

Definition from research

Each person stands where everyone who came before meets everyone who will come after.

The novel ends with Vera pregnant, and the last reflective sentence in the book is a statement of this principle: “I do not know the night in which I conceived as I do not know the night in which I was conceived” (ch. 82). Vera stands between the mother she has just lost and the child she has not yet met, and she cannot see the origin of either. She is the crossing point.

The deaf man gives the child a purpose before it is born: “our child will be our ear.” The generation that comes after will supply the sense that the present lacks. And Esther Longtree, the mother of the stillborn, becomes Vera’s future: “Esther Longtree would be me.” The woman whose hope never produced a living child merges with the woman who is about to have one.

This principle gathers all the others. The plural self becomes plural across generations. The invention is handed down. Grief joins with new life. The construction remains open because a child is coming who will build on it. And the time that was sedimentary, layer beneath layer, turns at last toward what is not yet written.

philosophy-05-mr-spitzer-peron-and-the-d:
Chapter 5. Mr. Spitzer, Peron, and the Divided Self

← Previous · Philosophy of MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Joachim Spitzer

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Identity and the Self

Philosophy: Empiricism (Locke, Berkeley, Hume)

Allusions: Gambling and Playing Cards · Suicide in History and Literature

Chapters discussed: 1, 2, 25, 27, 30, 31, 42, 49, 51, 52, 54, 59

Definition from research

The Promise

Mr. Joachim Spitzer, the old attorney who keeps Catherine company, has built a system that looks like the opposite of hers. His is caution. He is “a man so punctual, so unperceptive as himself acting always according to his routines” (ch. 25). He “claimed never to have placed a bet on even that which he had been most certain of” (ch. 2). Where Catherine trusts nothing and so can imagine anything, Mr. Spitzer trusts nothing and so risks nothing. His system promises safety through restraint.

His twin brother Peron embodied the opposite system. Peron was “insolent, a gambler, a spender of borrowed money, a quick suicide” (ch. 2). He bet on everything and lost. Between them, the brothers divide the world into two clean categories: the careful life and the reckless one. It is the old philosophical contest between prudence and passion, reason and appetite, played out by twins.

The Loading

The division does not hold. Cousin Hannah, who disliked them both, always insisted that “they were really identical, not nearly so different as they had supposed” (ch. 30). After Peron’s death, Mr. Spitzer cannot decide what to carve on the tombstone, “never deciding which brother it was, and perhaps he never would decide” (ch. 31). The categories of the careful brother and the reckless brother begin to blur, and the novel keeps adding to the blur for chapter after chapter.

Peron left behind a watch, and Mr. Spitzer wears it. It marks “the recurring years, the unknown flow of time, the backward flow, seasons, days, hours, half-minutes, quarterminutes, seconds as of a hair’s breadth, every conceivable departmentalization” (ch. 27). The instrument of perfect measurement belongs to the man who lived without measure, and it is worn by the man who measured everything. Time itself, divided into the finest categories, runs backward on his wrist.

Mr. Spitzer tries one philosophical system after another in his grief. He proposes eternal recurrence (ch. 42), as Chapter 1 showed, and watches it dissolve into billiard balls that “would not roll twice the same” (ch. 59). He walks the city unsure “whether he would step on nothing” (ch. 25). He comes to feel that “there was no reality, and there was nothingness” (ch. 54). And in the same chapter he reaches a sentence that could stand as a summary of the whole novel’s method: “Distortions seemed to cause distortions, perhaps because one principle had not been correct.”

The Break

The break is the collapse of personal identity itself. In the forty-seventh chapter, he wonders whether he really knows “which brother he was, for had he not lived on both sides, died on both sides.” By the forty-ninth, the novel states it outright: “he did not know which brother he was, and this was the crux of his mystery.” He asks, “Was it Mr. Spitzer who was dead, perhaps living only by that dream which moved and stirred through a dead man’s thoughts?”

Philosophers have argued for centuries about what makes a person the same person over time. Locke pointed to memory. Others pointed to the body, or the soul. Mr. Spitzer tests every candidate and finds that none of them settles the question. His memories are shared with his brother. His body is his brother’s twin. His soul, if he has one, cannot say whose it is.

And then comes the most radical sentence of all. The answer to his question, the narrator says, “would have signified little or nothing, not altering his experience in the least degree or doing so in ways which were unrecognizable” (ch. 49). This is where the category of personal identity truly fails. It is not that the question has no answer. It is that the answer would change nothing about how he lives. The category has become weightless.

What Is Left

What survives in Mr. Spitzer is a stance toward others, and it may be the most humane thing in the book. “Whose illusions could he challenge? He had learned to respect other people’s mirages, especially as he existed only as a mirage himself” (ch. 51). A man who does not know which brother he is cannot sneer at anyone else’s confusion. His own uncertainty becomes the ground of his tolerance.

He is also the one who searches Cousin Hannah’s forty trunks, trying rusted key after rusted key. He could have broken them open, “but he was not violent,” and he proceeded “carefully as one whose own violences were suppressed” (ch. 52). He had “a due respect for damaged properties which should not be further damaged by him.” When he concludes that “There was no master key,” he does not force the locks. He leaves the mysteries their dignity.

His music, which no one ever hears, carries the same lesson. An old piano mender tells him “that there had always been a missing keyboard. There had always been a string missing in the harp of God,” and Mr. Spitzer wonders if that missing string is his own (ch. 51). The divided self is not a flaw in an otherwise complete creation. It is part of a creation that was never complete.

In the last chapter, Vera reports that Mr. Spitzer finally knew, “for what might seem only a shining moment in the long darkness of time or timelessness, which brother he truly was.” The answer is “the dead.” Even this resolution is framed as a moment, not a conclusion, and it arrives only at the point where identity no longer matters to anyone but the one who dies.

Chapter 16. The Margins Reveal the Truth

← Previous · Philosophy of MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Characters: Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · The Stone Deaf Man

Allusions: Deafness and Sign Language

Chapters discussed: 61, 62, 82

Definition from research

The people who do not fit the categories see the categories most clearly. The margins are where the seams show.

The novel is full of people at the edges: the deaf, the mute, the addicted, the unmarried, the poor, the half-mad. Young gives them the clearest sight in the book.

Mr. Spitzer states the principle in musical terms. “The man kicked out of an orchestra knew more about music than any playing in an orchestra, for the player was under the powers of the despotic conductor and could play only his own part” (ch. 62). The one inside the system hears only his part. The one outside it hears the whole.

The frog musician, a derelict who haunts Mr. Spitzer’s city, speaks only in scraps. He asks for a light, and “this simple question” seems to Mr. Spitzer “the real miracle” (ch. 61). The mute who stands with Mr. Spitzer in the rain says nothing at all. Esther Longtree cannot spell. The stone deaf man cannot hear. And in the last chapter it is an old Black woman on a country road, a figure at the far margin of the society the novel describes, who gives the deaf boy the words that could stand as the book’s creed: “life is imaginary, and this be an imaginary world” (ch. 82).

In a novel whose memories begin in a New England mansion of inherited wealth and whose present ends among the poor of the American interior, the movement itself is an argument. The truth is not at the center, where the systems are built. It is at the edges, where they fail to reach.

philosophy-22-the-ethics-of-going-on:
Chapter 22. The Ethics of Going On

← Previous · Philosophy of MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · The Stone Deaf Man · Vera Cartwheel

Symbols: Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Nietzsche

Allusions: Deafness and Sign Language

Chapters discussed: 1, 32, 54, 59, 63, 72

Definition from research

The sentence of Young’s that this book has returned to most often is an ethical one. “When you have examined all the illusions of life and know that there isn’t any reality, but you nevertheless go on, then you are a mature human being.” The important word is “nevertheless.” Young’s system does not end in despair or in a triumphant affirmation. It ends in continuation.

Against Two Easy Endings

There are two easy ways out of the collapse of every system, and the novel refuses both.

The first is despair. If nothing is certain, nothing matters. Mr. Spitzer comes close to this. He feels at times that “there was no reality, and there was nothingness” (ch. 54). But he does not stop. He keeps walking the city, keeps searching trunks, keeps writing music no one will hear. The nothingness does not become a reason to stop.

The second easy ending is heroic affirmation, and it belongs to Nietzsche. Nietzsche’s answer to the collapse of all values was the thought of eternal recurrence: the demand that a person live so as to will every moment to return forever. The novel takes this thought seriously. Mr. Spitzer proposes it in the forty-second chapter. But the novel’s experience undoes it. The billiard balls “would not roll twice the same” (ch. 59). Esther lives recurrence as endless loss, beginning “it all over again, the great enterprise of her great loneliness” (ch. 72). Vera sees in her own life only “the dream of chaos repeating chaos” (ch. 1). The eternal return, lived, is not glorious. It is either impossible or unbearable.

What Young offers instead is quieter. If no moment can ever exactly repeat, then each moment is unrepeatable. Going on does not require willing the return of everything. It requires only willing the next step, over the abyss that has always been the floor.

The Virtues That Survive

The trials of Part Two each left something behind when their systems broke, and these remnants form an ethics.

From Catherine comes the knowledge that the world is invented, and the warning that invention cannot shield a person from sorrow. From Mr. Spitzer comes respect for other people’s mirages, and the patience to leave locked trunks unbroken. From Esther comes love that outlives hope. From Cousin Hannah comes the discovery that action and meditation are not opposites, and that the greatest battles may be “fought in the domestic wars by those who had never left home” (ch. 32). From Miss MacIntosh comes courage: “Be not afraid of life” (ch. 63).

None of these is a rule. Each is a disposition, a way of standing in the world once the world has stopped offering solid ground. Together they describe a person who knows she lives in illusion and treats others with the tenderness that knowledge makes possible.

Going On as Search

Vera’s whole story is the ethic of going on made visible. The novel opens with her riding a bus through fog, searching for a woman she knows is probably dead. She asks, “Where should I go? Where should I turn?” (ch. 1). She has no system to answer. She goes anyway.

The search does not find its object. Vera never finds Miss MacIntosh. What she finds instead are people she was not looking for: Esther, the stone deaf man, a life. This is the shape of going on in Young’s philosophy. The search is not justified by its success. It is justified because it keeps a person moving among other people, where love can happen.

philosophy-10-not-one-self:
Chapter 10. Not One Self

← Previous · Philosophy of MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Pillar 1 Not One Self

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Esther Longtree · Eustace · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Identity and the Self

Chapters discussed: 1, 30, 47, 63, 72

Definition from research

A person is a crowd, not a single fixed identity. The many selves are not a malfunction to correct. They are the normal condition of being alive.

The novel announces this principle before it states any idea. The first philosophical passage begins with “a double-headed man” by the side of the road, a man carrying a child on his shoulders (ch. 1). From there, the doubling spreads through every major character. Mr. Spitzer cannot tell whether he is himself or Peron, and he wonders whether he “lived on both sides, died on both sides” (ch. 47). Cousin Hannah could be “both herself and a gentleman” (ch. 30). Miss MacIntosh tells Vera, “My elder brothers called me George,” and wishes she had been “an honest woman or an honest man” (ch. 63). Catherine’s Eustace “might be simultaneously many persons” (ch. 30). Even Esther Longtree says she has the “feeling of not being born myself yet” (ch. 72).

The trials showed what happens when a person tries to be one thing. Miss MacIntosh insisted on being plain and simple and had to hide half of herself under a wig. Mr. Spitzer tried to be the careful brother and found he could not say which brother he was. The plural self is what remains when the demand for a single identity breaks.

The principle is also a kind of mercy. When Vera, in the twenty-first chapter, finally sees her nursemaid without disguise, she finds “no identity but the individual stripped bare of individuality and vain pretence.” The individual is still there. What is gone is the pretence that the individual is one simple thing.

philosophy-08-miss-macintosh-and-the-fal:
Chapter 8. Miss MacIntosh and the Fall of Common Sense

← Previous · Philosophy of MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Miss MacIntosh

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Order, Chaos, and Discipline

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology

Allusions: The History of Opium

Chapters discussed: 1, 3, 17, 18, 22, 63, 64

Definition from research

The Promise

Every trial so far has tested a system that a reader might already suspect of illusion: an opium dream, a man who cannot tell himself from his brother, a pregnancy that never ends, a crusade built over a secret grief. The last trial is different. Miss MacIntosh, Vera’s nursemaid, is the character the novel builds to refute illusion. She is the realist, and her fall is the decisive case. If realism survives, then Young has only shown that some lives are deluded. If realism falls, then no position is left standing outside the test.

Her doctrine is stated in the first chapter. She taught Vera “that no one must dream of what was not, of what would never be,” that Vera must “lead a useful life,” that “reality was very good and could be found by those who lived, could be seen even with the naked eye.” She had always said that common sense was the finest sense, and that the way of life “was very plain, quite direct. It was a granite road and not the sea road taken by the ships falling beyond a far horizon.” In the third chapter, “she did not believe in things invisible.” She is the voice of plain fact against the opium house.

Her doctrine has philosophical ancestors. A tradition of common sense philosophy, most closely tied to Scotland and to Thomas Reid, held that ordinary perception gives direct access to the world and that philosophical doubt is a kind of madness. Miss MacIntosh claims descent from Scotland, as the novel shows later. Whether Young had Reid specifically in mind is a question for further research, but the fit is striking.

The Loading

Young loads the realist with small details that do not quite fit. In the very passage that states her creed, her “knitting needles of ivory bone” are “clicking like her false teeth” (ch. 1). The voice of natural fact speaks through artificial teeth. In the storm lessons of the sixty-sixth chapter, she dresses for a sea voyage in the nursery, insisting “that common sense demanded we should be dressed for the gale,” although “We were not going anywhere.” Her common sense requires costume.

Her theology, too, has a gap in it. She holds that God “had God’s limitations” and “had not created everything. He had left many things uncreated” (ch. 3). On the beach she teaches that God made two mistakes: “The first was to have begun what He could not finish. The second was not to have finished what He had begun” (ch. 22). The realist’s world is not complete. Her creed of plain fact already contains the idea of the unfinished.

Even her ancestry is a romance. She tells Vera she is “descended from a Gaelic prince who was lost at sea and who was bald as she was” (ch. 64), a prince whose golden crown floated away while he washed ashore in Scotland and founded a family of sheep herders and coffin makers. The woman who forbade dreaming carries a legend at the root of her identity.

The Break

The break comes when Vera, as a child, enters Miss MacIntosh’s bedroom and sees her without her wig. “She was only this old man who had only one breast and no hair and no future prospect. Her baldness gave her away, coldly and utterly” (ch. 17). Vera writes, “She was other than herself, and she had deceived me.” The realist was wearing a disguise the whole time.

Then comes the most important detail in the scene. In the next chapter, Vera sees “one breast of milky whiteness lighted even as she tried to explain that what I saw, I did not see, that it would be banished with the honest dawn which should dispell these vagrant, foolish dreams” (ch. 18). This is where realism falls. Miss MacIntosh’s whole creed rested on the reliability of the naked eye. Now, to preserve herself, she must tell Vera that what Vera sees is not there. The doctrine of common sense can survive only by denying perception. The realist has become the dreamer, and the child who was taught to trust her eyes is told to disbelieve them.

In the sixty-third chapter, Miss MacIntosh speaks for herself, and her words complete the collapse from the inside. “Perhaps I have seemed deceiving, but you should have recognized me long ago, just by all that I was not and could not be, just by what was missing from these features!” She reflects on love: “what is the love of one person for another? It is a system of mutual deception.” She regrets: “I should have been an honest woman or an honest man.” And she clarifies her lifelong warnings: “If I warned you against those lies and illusions surrounding us, I meant only those which we ourselves have made. Every man has a porcelain crown like mine.”

Then she says the sentence that may be the novel’s deepest statement of its own philosophy, spoken by the one character who spent her life denying it: “There is one dream we do not awaken from. That, my dear, is life.”

In time she disappears into the mist by the sea and is believed drowned.

What Is Left

What is left is the most surprising thing in the novel. The realist, once exposed, becomes the object of a lifelong dream. Vera spends years searching for her, and the novel’s title is her cry. “For there had been no one else so true, so good, and, even in her unkindness, so kind” (ch. 1). In the seventieth chapter, Vera admits that Miss MacIntosh forbade all dreaming, “and then it was of her I dreamed the most when she was dead, in fact, of her only.”

Miss MacIntosh did not stop being true when her baldness was revealed. She became true in a different way. Her advice outlived her creed. “Be not afraid of life,” she told Vera (ch. 63), and Vera took it, traveling into the broad interior her nursemaid had recommended. The realism fell. The courage it was meant to protect survived. And this, finally, is the pattern of every trial in Part Two. Each system breaks, and something that was carried inside it, love, patience, respect, courage, walks on without it.

Chapter 13. Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

← Previous · Philosophy of MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Chapters discussed: 31, 51, 52, 82

Definition from research

The hardest and most honest stance is to stay in the room with something painful and complicated without rushing to fix it or wrap it up.

Mr. Spitzer is the novel’s witness. He sits for years beside Catherine’s bed, listening to her conversations with the dead. He does not correct her. The narrator explains that “he indulged my mother’s moods so long as they were not of reality, he being profoundly, ever and increasingly convinced that reality would kill her as it had killed her canary” (ch. 31). He is not a believer in her dreams. He simply refuses to be the one who destroys them.

His stance is summed up in a single line: “He had learned to respect other people’s mirages, especially as he existed only as a mirage himself” (ch. 51). The witness does not stand above the scene as a clear-eyed judge. He stands inside it, as unsure of his own reality as anyone else, and that uncertainty is what makes his respect possible.

The forty trunks show the witness at work. He could break them open, but he does not, because he has “a due respect for damaged properties which should not be further damaged by him” (ch. 52). He accepts that “There was no master key” and leaves the locks unbroken. A lesser searcher would have forced the answer. The witness lets the mystery stand.

Vera learns this stance by the end. When she meets Esther Longtree, she listens to the waitress’s long story of stillbirths and does not correct her, pity her, or try to cure her. She hears. And in the last chapter she imagines telling Esther all her own losses and hearing Esther reply, “So had not everyone lost something?” (ch. 82). The witness is witnessed in return.

philosophy-07-cousin-hannah-and-the-life:
Chapter 7. Cousin Hannah and the Life of Action

← Previous · Philosophy of MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Cousin Hannah

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer

Philosophy: Nietzsche

Allusions: Exploration and the Poles · The History of Opium · Women's Suffrage

Chapters discussed: 30, 31, 32, 41, 43, 45, 52

Definition from research

What Her Life Proposes

Cousin Hannah Freemount-Snowden never appears in the novel alive. She is remembered by Catherine and investigated by Mr. Spitzer after her death, and her story fills much of the middle of the book. A close reading shows that her life proposes a system distinct from all the others: the life of action. She is a suffragette, an explorer, a mountain climber, a duelist, a marksman. She “had gone by camel into places where no woman had ever gone before” (ch. 30). Where Catherine dreams and Mr. Spitzer hesitates, Hannah acts.

Her system rests on certainty. “She had compensated for her superficial views by a marvelous certainty that was set above the peaks of time” (ch. 30). She lived “by her inscrutable choices as if there had been no alternative, no road except the road she had taken, no ship except the ship in which she had sailed.” She “had always believed in being direct” (ch. 31). And her certainty made further inquiry unnecessary. She acted as if she had “already seen into all the dark abysses of human nature,” and “so she had had no use for further experience or knowledge” (ch. 30).

This is the philosophy of the deed: the conviction that thought is secondary, that the world is changed by those who move rather than those who wonder. It has noble forms, and Hannah’s cause, the vote for women, was a just one. The novel never mocks the cause. It tests the certainty.

The Loading

Young loads Hannah’s life with a secret that her certainty was built to cover. The narrator hints at it early: “Because of the loss of a skirt, it was known now, her entire life had been perhaps an act of sorrow and redemption” (ch. 30). As Mr. Spitzer’s researches continue, the story comes into view. On a mountain long ago, Hannah climbed with a young woman she loved, and in a snowstorm she “had let go her girl’s hand, her dove-white fluted hand in a snow storm long ago as in another life” (ch. 45). The girl was lost. The crusade that followed, the forty voyages and the battles against men, grew from that one moment of letting go.

The loading also comes from her own divided nature. Catherine calls her “a soul of vast duplicity” and imagines she could play two hands at cards, being “both herself and a gentleman” (ch. 30). The woman who lived by directness was never simple. And her certainty about the future turns out to be dreamlike too. She was said to have “known of the murder of the archduke at Sarajevo several hours before the news had reached the rest of the world” (ch. 30), knowledge as uncanny as anything in Catherine’s opium visions.

The Break

The break comes at her death, and it comes twice. First, there is the reported deathbed confession: “that she no longer believed in the glory of these foreign conquests” and that “The greatest battles were fought in the domestic wars by those who had never left home” (ch. 32). The woman of action, at the end, turns against action. But the novel immediately undercuts even this: “it was impossible to know how the great captain could have made this death-bed confession,” since she had not answered her telephone in years. The confession may be Catherine’s invention. Even the collapse of the system cannot be verified.

Second, there is the delirium Mr. Spitzer overhears as she dies, and here the Nietzschean images gather. She cries, “Shall I fall into the great abyss of which there is no floor, no ceiling? Shall I fall into love or death? Are both one?” (ch. 43). And in the forty-fifth chapter, climbing in her fever through mountains of snow, she sees the dwarf “a turret on his head.” Nietzsche’s Zarathustra climbed with the spirit of gravity on his back and, at the summit gateway, overcame it with the thought of eternal return. Hannah climbs with her grief and her lost girl, and the dwarf she meets wears the tower of the house of illusion. The heroic ascent ends not in affirmation but in the question of whether love and death are one.

Catherine delivers the final verdict, and it is devastating in its gentleness. “Cousin Hannah’s life, just like her own, had been largely imaginary, transient, unknown, unexplored, passing like a dream” (ch. 41). Then comes the question that dissolves the whole distinction on which Hannah built her life: “how should action differ from meditation?” The woman who acted and the woman who dreamed turn out to have lived in the same condition. Time and sorrow, the narrator adds, were “all she had ever denied.”

What Is Left

Mr. Spitzer’s researches uncover one more image, and it carries Young’s politics. According to an old newspaper story, Hannah once “skied, according to one old newspaper reporter dreaming of her,” with “blind skiers following a leader’s bell, and none had known that which Mr. Spitzer knew, that the leader was blind” (ch. 52). The leader of the crusade was as blind as the followers. This does not make the cause wrong. It makes the certainty dangerous.

What remains of Hannah is her love, which her crusade never mentioned and never healed, and her forty unopened trunks. Mr. Spitzer tries every key and opens none, and he does not break them. The life of action leaves behind a store of experience that no single key can open, and a man patient enough to leave it closed.

philosophy-14-build-anyway-knowing-its-t:
Chapter 14. Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

← Previous · Philosophy of MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Chapters discussed: 22, 59

Definition from research

Since nothing is ever truly final, the honest move is to build anyway, provisionally, and keep revising. The frozen, finished blueprint is the thing to distrust.

The image for this principle comes from the beach where Miss MacIntosh raised Vera. Because God stopped too soon, they refused to rest. “We worked on both Sunday and Saturday as well as all the other days, observing no period of rest” (ch. 22). And their work was strange. On Saturdays they “nailed old boards or unnailed old boards.” Building and unbuilding are the same activity. Nothing on that beach is finished, and nothing is meant to be.

Mr. Spitzer’s music follows the same law. He tries to compose from the movements of billiard balls and discovers that “no game could doubtless ever exactly repeat itself” (ch. 59). The music can never be fixed in a score. It must be made again each time, differently.

Young’s own practice embodies the principle. She expected to finish the novel in two years and kept building for twenty. The Debs biography never reached its planned end. The construction was left open because the life it described was open.

The opposite of this principle is the utopia. Rapp’s New Harmony and Owen’s New Harmony were both finished blueprints, complete plans for human life imposed on real people. Young watched both fail before she began her novel. Keeping the construction open is her answer to them.

philosophy-18-language-shapes-whats-poss:
Chapter 18. Language Shapes What's Possible

← Previous · Philosophy of MMMD Home · Next →

See also: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Characters: Esther Longtree · Miss MacIntosh · The Stone Deaf Man · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Music, Sound, and Silence

Allusions: Deafness and Sign Language

Chapters discussed: 2, 63, 72, 82

Definition from research

Words build the world they describe. Nouns freeze things into fixed identities. And any voice that claims to speak from nowhere, in pure objectivity, is hiding where it really stands.

Miss MacIntosh, for all her faith in plain fact, distrusted words. “Words do not harness the winds,” she told Vera. “Love has shut many a woman’s mouth” (ch. 63). The realist knew that language was a construction, even if she did not know that her realism was one too.

Young’s own prose is the strongest demonstration of this principle. As Chapter 2 showed, her sentences do not state ideas and then move on. They build an idea, add to it, and let it collapse, all within the grammar. The long sentence is itself a construction that shows its own seams.

At the edges of the novel, language breaks down into something more honest. Esther Longtree was “learning the alphabet all over again because she was teaching it to the stillborn” (ch. 72). The stone deaf man speaks of words “not in the alphabet of the stars. Flowers spell them out on the earth, and grasses talk” (ch. 82). There is a language older than the alphabet, and it cannot be fixed in spelling.

The last words of the novel are a misspelled sign in a restaurant window: “Owt to luntsch. bee bak in a whale.” Then the narrator adds, “For she could not spell either.” A book of more than a thousand pages of the most elaborate English prose ends with a sentence no dictionary would accept, and it is perfectly clear. Language is a construction, and a broken construction can still carry love and a promise to return.

philosophy-23-the-ending-as-demonstratio:
Chapter 23. The Ending as Demonstration

← Previous · Philosophy of MMMD Home

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · The Stone Deaf Man · Vera Cartwheel

Themes: Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality

Allusions: Deafness and Sign Language · The History of Opium

Chapters discussed: 2, 82

Definition from research

The last chapter of Miss MacIntosh, My Darling performs everything the novel has argued. It is worth reading slowly, in the same way Chapter 2 read the monist passage, as a proposal, an accumulation, and a collapse. But this time the pattern turns in a new direction.

The Inventory

The chapter opens with a list of losses. Vera reflects on what she could have confessed to Esther Longtree: “that my mother was dead, that the opium paradise had crumbled, that the sea had swept over the dark house with its golden turrets and towers,” that “the only property which was left to me was this string of pearls I wore, that I was in mourning for three deaths, that I was in love with an older love than memory provided” (ch. 82).

This is accumulation of the familiar kind. Each system in the novel has now ended. Catherine is dead and her invented world has been swept away. Mr. Spitzer has learned which brother he was, and the answer is “the dead.” Miss MacIntosh is remembered “with her bald head upon the waves.” Everything the novel built has been loaded until it gave way.

Vera imagines telling all this to Esther and imagines Esther’s reply: “So had not everyone lost something? Think, she might say, of those who do not see, those who do not hear!” Loss itself becomes common ground.

The Final Proposal

Then Vera states the novel’s last philosophical proposal. She faces “that reality which had been a dream and which had crumbled, perhaps into reality, perhaps into a dream if nothing was real.” And she offers a thought that gathers all the trials into one: “Perhaps there is always a sense missing, that sense which would make the world real.”

This is a new and precise claim. The novel has shown that every system fails. Here it suggests why. Every person, every philosophy, is missing a sense. The deaf lack hearing. The blind lack sight. But even those with all five senses lack the one sense that would make the world fully real. No system has it, and so every system is partial. The missing sense is the novel’s name for the gap that no master key can close.

The Collapse of Illusion Itself

And then comes the turn that completes Young’s philosophy. Vera has spent the night listening to a voice she half believes she dreamed, a man singing of silence and of “the things awakening not.” She thinks it may have been imagined. Then she writes: “But I was wrong, for all was real, and he was real. He was the stone deaf man whom I saw in the dim corridor at dawn.”

For more than a thousand pages, the novel has tested every category against experience and watched it fail. Here, at the very end, the last category fails too. The category of illusion itself gives way. After all the dreams and mirages, Vera finds a real man. The novel does not return to naive realism. Miss MacIntosh’s granite road is gone for good. But neither does it rest in the easy conclusion that everything is illusion. That conclusion, too, is a system, and it too breaks under the weight of a real person standing in a corridor at dawn.

This is why Young’s philosophy is complete in the only way it can be. The method of accumulation, applied long enough, undoes even the doctrine that nothing is real. What remains is neither reality nor illusion but a person, met.

What Is Left

The stone deaf man is himself a portrait of Young’s ethics. He lost his hearing at fourteen. “It took him a long time to learn to dream. He became a painter, and he was also the artist of his life.” He “heard with his eyes.” Missing a sense, he built a life from the senses he had. An old woman on a country road told him the words that could stand as the novel’s last teaching: “life is imaginary, and this be an imaginary world. And the silence had its tongues, and love came before words were or ever will be” (ch. 82).

Vera loves him “as a mother might love a child,” “as a woman loves a man,” and “for the silences and for all the tongues of silence speaking the name of love.” She is carrying his child, and he gives the child its purpose: “our child will be our ear.” What one generation lacks, the next may supply.

Then comes the crossing point: “I do not know the night in which I conceived as I do not know the night in which I was conceived.” Vera stands between two unknowns, her origin and her child’s, and she does not need to know either.

She lets go of her last possession. “My pearls were lost,” she writes, “and never would I find my pearls in the morning light, never even look for them.” The inheritance from the opium house is scattered over the bluffs, and she does not search. After a whole novel of searching, this refusal to search is itself a form of peace.

The two lovers plan a wedding, and the reason given is disarming: “We would be married, for legality helped.” A legal marriage is a construction, and they know it. They will use it anyway, because it helps. This is living in the invention with open eyes.

The guest list follows, and it is the last of Young’s great accumulations. Wildflowers, birds, waters, clouds, moon and sun and stars, “and the old mule that climbed over the fence and Esther Longtree, for she was also our love.” In every earlier list, experience piled up until a system broke. In this list, experience piles up and nothing breaks, because there is no longer any system to break. The accumulation has become a celebration. Everything is invited.

“Esther Longtree would be me.” The narrator and the waitress, the searcher and the one who waits, the mother who will bear a child and the mother of the stillborn, become one. It is the monist vision of the first chapter, “Every heart is the other heart,” returned in a new form. Not as a doctrine seen by an omniscient eye, but as a plain statement about two women in a small town who will share a future.

The Last Words

The novel ends with a sign. Esther hangs it in the restaurant window: “Owt to luntsch. bee bak in a whale.” And then: “For she could not spell either.”

After more than a thousand pages of some of the most elaborate prose in American literature, the last words are misspelled. The sign still works. Everyone who reads it will know what it means. And the misspelling opens a second meaning. “Bee bak in a whale” is a joke on “be back in a while,” and it is also Jonah, swallowed by the great fish and returned to the world. The promise of return, which eternal recurrence could not keep, comes back as a waitress’s spelling error. It is a small, comic, human return, not the cosmic cycle of the philosophers.

The word “either” is quietly important. Esther could not spell either, just as the deaf man could not hear, just as Vera could not know the night of her conception, just as every person lacks the sense that would make the world real. Everyone is missing something. The sign goes up in the window anyway.

That is the system’s final demonstration. Every category has failed. Every master key has been tried and found wanting. And a woman who cannot spell hangs a sign that everyone can read, promising to be back.

Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality
philosophy-21-the-politics-of-distrustin:
Chapter 21. The Politics of Distrusting Leaders

← Previous · Philosophy of MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer

Themes: Music, Sound, and Silence

Symbols: Eyes and Blindness · Music and Instruments

Philosophy: Nietzsche · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres

Chapters discussed: 9, 30, 42, 49, 52, 61, 62

Definition from research

Young insisted that her novel had a politics, and she located it exactly. “If you understand hallucination and illusion, you don’t blindly follow any leader,” she told Friedman and Fuchs. “You must know if the person is sane or insane, over the abyss.” The last phrase deserves attention. In Nietzsche, the abyss was something the solitary thinker looked into. In Young’s interview, it is the place where a leader stands. And in her novel, as Part One showed, it is the floor everyone walks on. A leader who claims solid ground is either deceived or deceiving.

The argument that runs through the trials of Part Two now becomes political. If every system fails under the accumulation of lived experience, then every leader who offers a complete system is offering something that will fail. The danger is not only that the leader might be wrong. It is that followers, trusting the system, will stop looking at the experience that would show them the failure.

The Blind Leader

The novel’s sharpest political image comes from Cousin Hannah’s past. According to an old newspaper story, she once skied “with blind skiers following a leader’s bell, and none had known that which Mr. Spitzer knew, that the leader was blind” (ch. 52). The image works on two levels. On the surface it is simply strange, a feat of mountain daring. Beneath it is a parable. The followers are blind and know they depend on the bell. What they do not know is that the one ringing it is blind too.

Hannah was a leader herself, “the leader of those great armies riding thunderously into war, flying their silken petticoats as flags” (ch. 42), and her cause was just. The novel does not suggest that causes are false or that action is worthless. It suggests that certainty is the danger. Hannah acted as though she had “no use for further experience or knowledge” (ch. 30). A leader who needs no further experience is a leader who cannot learn that the path has changed.

The Despotic Conductor

The second political image is musical. Mr. Spitzer, a musician who never plays, reflects on the orchestra. “The man kicked out of an orchestra knew more about music than any playing in an orchestra, for the player was under the powers of the despotic conductor and could play only his own part” (ch. 62). The player may even be led astray “if the leader should misread the score and turn South instead of North.” Mr. Spitzer gives his sympathies “not to the conductor” and “not to the mad fellow imagining he could conduct all the music of all the singing spheres.”

Here the thread from Part One comes full circle. Pythagoras entered the novel as a guest in Catherine’s house, the man who “had discovered heaven’s harmony” (ch. 9). The dream of a single cosmic harmony was a philosopher’s dream. In the conductor, it becomes a political fantasy: one man who believes he can direct all the music there is. The novel names that belief madness. Young’s politics begin here, in the refusal of any total harmony imposed from a podium.

The Frog Musician

Young named the frog musician as one of the passages that “investigate the nature of illusion,” and his scenes show how the voice of guidance can arrive from anywhere. He is a derelict who steps from doorways in the fog. He asks Mr. Spitzer for a light, for a nickel, for a coin. Then he begins to give advice. “Watch out for the butterflies. Watch out for the weeds in the garden.” Later: “Watch out for the pickpockets. Watch out for the glass-smashers.” And later still, he tells Mr. Spitzer to “Put your money on the Robins” (ch. 61).

Mr. Spitzer, “very much agitated,” cannot tell what the tip means, and for a moment it is “almost as if he had heard his brother’s voice.” This is the psychology of the follower in miniature. A voice speaks with confidence out of the fog. It warns of dangers and promises winners. And the listener, lonely and grieving, begins to hear in it the voice of someone he loved. Mr. Spitzer does not follow the tip. He wonders about it. That wondering is Young’s politics in its smallest unit.

The Unelected Representative

Against the blind leader and the despotic conductor, the novel offers Mr. Spitzer himself as a model of public life. He was, the narrator says, “the pleader of lost causes,” causes “of which he had been an unsolicited and unelected representative, a minority representing a majority, a hidden majority like those sleeping in the churchyard” (ch. 49). He represents the dead and the forgotten. He holds no office. He claims no system. He simply refuses to let the lost be erased.

This is close to the figure Young would spend her last decades writing about. Eugene V. Debs was a leader, but a leader of an unusual kind, one who said he would not lead people into a promised land because others could lead them out again. Young’s long biography of him grew from the same conviction that runs through her novel: that the only trustworthy public figure is one who belongs to the people rather than standing above them with a master key.

What the Politics Requires

The politics of the novel is not a program. It does not tell readers what to vote for. It tells them how to hold their beliefs. Every system is a room in a crowded house. Every leader rings a bell in the fog. The task is not to stop following all bells, which would leave a person alone on the mountain. The task is to remember that the one ringing may be blind, and to keep listening to the experience that no system has yet absorbed.

philosophy-01-the-house-is-full:
Chapter 1. The House Is Full

Philosophy of MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Symbols: Keys, Doors, and Locks · The House

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Nietzsche · Plato and Platonism · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres · Spinoza

Allusions: Astronomy · Exploration and the Poles · Music and Composers · Napoleon and Wellington · Shakespeare · Women's Suffrage

Chapters discussed: 45, 47, 52, 59, 82

Definition from research

In the twenty-fourth chapter of Miss MacIntosh, My Darling, the servants in Catherine Cartwheel’s seaside house sit arguing about where and when they are. “One would say that it was Roman in the morning but Greek in the afternoon or that the Duke of Wellington was surely expected.” Then the rooms are assigned. “Admiral Peary was to be put into the blue room which was already occupied by Plato’s boat, et cetera. Sir Christopher Wren and Jenny Lind were to be put into the rose. Spinoza and Shakespeare and Mrs. Sydington were already in the green.” The house, the narrator says, “was always crowded to the roof,” its bedrooms “filled with famous guests sleeping tier above tier according to rank and station but with little regard for century.”

This is one of the few places in a novel of more than a thousand pages where philosophers appear by name, and it is worth noticing what happens to them. Plato does not arrive with an argument. He arrives as a boat, taking up space in a room that must also hold an Arctic explorer. Spinoza shares the green room with Shakespeare and with a Mrs. Sydington whom no history remembers. The phrase “et cetera” does quiet, devastating work. The great systems of Western thought are filed alongside a soprano, an architect, and a duke, and the filing is done by servants who cannot agree on the century.

The same thing happens earlier. In the ninth chapter, Catherine lies in “an unearthly coma,” receiving “her distinguished circle which never diminished and which included Pythagoras who had a golden thigh and had discovered heaven’s harmony, the symphonious music of the silver-toned spheres.” Pythagoras is given his legend and his great idea in a single breath, and then the circle keeps expanding. “The P’s were crowding upon her,” the passage continues, “planets, Pythian games, polygons, Prussians, petunias, pseudopsias which are the delusions of sight.” The mathematician who heard the music of the spheres is one P among petunias, and right beside him stands a medical term for seeing what is not there. The placement is a verdict. The sentence does not say Pythagoras was wrong. It says he is one more guest in the house of illusion, and that the house has room for everyone.

In the fourteenth chapter, Catherine “would ordinarily not ask for the appearance beyond the appearance, mainly because she was aware of it and knew that the dog was Socrates.” The joke runs deep. Pythagoras taught that souls pass from body to body, and here the most famous questioner in philosophy has been reborn as a household pet. The phrase “the appearance beyond the appearance” names the move Plato made at the foundation of Western metaphysics, the claim that behind the shifting world of appearances stands a truer world of forms. Catherine does not refute this. She simply declines to ask, because she already knows what she would find. Behind every appearance there is only another appearance, and the dog is Socrates.

Even Copernicus appears, in the same chapter, as “the author of that great celestial revolution which had exiled the dear God to the void and had robbed us of the evidence of our senses.” In a single phrase, the scientific revolution becomes one more event in the long history of illusion. The senses were wrong about the sun, and so the senses cannot be trusted, and so the ground under every realist falls away.

When readers first meet these passages, it is natural to think Young is arguing with the philosophers, or gathering them up, or trying to illuminate what they meant. The scenes suggest something else. An argument requires two parties standing on the same ground. In Catherine’s house, no one stands on ground at all. Young is not in conversation with philosophy. She is housing it. She gives each system a room, lets it sleep beside the others, and waits to see what happens when the house becomes crowded to the roof.

The Second Door

If named philosophers were the only evidence, the claim would be thin. A dozen mentions in a book of this size could be decoration. But the named guests are only the first of two ways philosophy enters the novel. The second way is quieter and far more pervasive. Young takes a philosopher’s central image, removes the name, and gives the image to a character to live inside.

Friedrich Nietzsche is never named in the novel, but his images run through it. His most famous line warns that whoever gazes long into an abyss will find the abyss gazing back. In the twenty-fifth chapter, Mr. Spitzer, the careful old attorney, walks through the world never knowing “what the next step would bring, whether he would step on nothing, whether it would be a stairway or a dissolving stairway or a chasm filled with the songs of dead birds, whether he would stare at that wild, precipitous abyss which would stare at him.” Nietzsche’s abyss sat before the heroic thinker who dared to look. Young moves it underfoot. It becomes the floor of an ordinary walk to the office. Later Mr. Spitzer fears he has “stepped upon a pulsing cloud where he had thought there was no pavement” (ch. 45), and elsewhere “Every crack might suddenly be the abyss” (ch. 52). There is nothing to stare into from a safe height, because everyone has been walking on the abyss all along.

In Thus Spoke Zarathustra, the prophet climbs a mountain path with a dwarf, the spirit of gravity, riding on his shoulders, and at the gateway called Moment he first proposes the thought of eternal recurrence. In the forty-fifth chapter of Young’s novel, Cousin Hannah, the old suffragette and mountain climber, lies dying and raves that she is “climbing naked through mountains of snow.” Then she cries out, “Who is that dwarf, a turret on his head, a rose at his collar? It is the rose of consciousness.” The mountain, the climber, and the dwarf are all present. But the dwarf now wears a turret, and the turret belongs to the novel’s own house, which Vera later describes as “the dark house with its golden turrets and towers” (ch. 82). The spirit of gravity has put on the architecture of illusion as a hat.

Eternal recurrence itself appears openly. In the forty-second chapter, Mr. Spitzer, mourning his brother, asks: “Should not eternal recurrence be the one law of life, and should not the great lamp-lighter going his rounds through darkened heavens light that lamp which had gone out and was himself shining through clouds?” The doctrine that Nietzsche offered as the supreme test of a life is proposed here by a grieving man who wants his brother back. And the novel does not leave it there. Five chapters later the idea returns, softened, as “life forever repeating itself as the rain recalls the rain and the star recalls the star,” followed by a telling qualification: “This tendency of an image to repeat an image, perhaps with variations, was something to be considered, weighed, taken into account” (ch. 47). By the fifty-ninth chapter it has broken. Mr. Spitzer tries to compose music from the paths of billiard balls, only to discover that “no game could doubtless ever exactly repeat itself. The ivory balls would not roll twice the same.” (ch. 59)

Across seventeen chapters, a philosophical doctrine is proposed, qualified, and undone, and it is undone by nothing more than lived experience piling up. No one refutes eternal recurrence. It simply cannot survive the accumulation of one man’s actual days.

What Kind of Book This Is

These two doors, the named guests and the unnamed images, point to the argument of this book. Marguerite Young did not write a novel that comments on philosophy. She built a philosophical system and used fiction as its demonstration. Her method is to take a way of understanding the world, place it inside a human life, and then keep adding experience until the understanding gives way. She does this to religious faith, to romantic imagination, to heroic action, to hope, to common sense, and to the doctrines of the philosophers themselves. Every category fails under the weight of what keeps arriving.

A skeptical reader will object at once. If every system fails under accumulation, then Young’s system must fail too, and the phrase “complete philosophical system” contradicts itself. This book takes that objection as its center rather than its weakness. Young’s system is complete precisely because it includes its own undoing. It is not a set of doctrines to be believed. It is a way of seeing how every doctrine breaks, joined to a way of living after the break. Young said as much, late in her life, to the interviewers Ellen G. Friedman and Miriam Fuchs: “When you have examined all the illusions of life and know that there isn’t any reality, but you nevertheless go on, then you are a mature human being.”

The chapters that follow set out that system in four movements. The rest of Part One teaches how to read Young’s sentences as arguments and lays the biographical ground from which the novel grew. Part Two follows the trials, one lived system at a time. Part Three states the principles that remain once the trials are over. Part Four turns to consequences: politics, ethics, and the novel’s ending, which is the system’s final demonstration.

The novel itself supplies the book’s title. In the fifty-second chapter, Mr. Spitzer searches the forty trunks that Cousin Hannah brought back from forty voyages, trying rusted key after rusted key, and understands at last that “never would that lock open which should open upon all mysteries at once.” A few lines later the thought is completed: “There was no master key.” Every philosopher in Catherine’s crowded house arrived carrying a master key. Young’s achievement was to show, one life at a time, that none of them fits every lock, and then to ask what a person does with a ring of keys that only open some doors.

philosophy-09-youngs-own-words:
Chapter 9. Young’s Own Words

← Previous · Philosophy of MMMD Home · Next →

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology

Allusions: The Bible · The History of Opium

Chapters discussed: 14, 21, 47

Definition from research

Before the principles can be stated, it helps to notice the words Young herself returns to. A philosopher’s system can often be read in the vocabulary she cannot stop using. In Miss MacIntosh, My Darling, “dream” and its forms appear well over a thousand times, and “illusion” and its forms close to two hundred. These are not decorative words. They are the novel’s basic terms, and a few others gather around them.

Illusion, in Young’s usage, does not mean simple error. It means whatever a person lives inside and takes for solid. Catherine’s opium house is an illusion, but so is Miss MacIntosh’s common sense, so is Hannah’s certainty, and so, the novel suggests, is the separate self. Illusion is the condition of being human, not a mistake that clearer thinking could correct.

The unfinished is Young’s word for the condition of the world. God, in Miss MacIntosh’s beach theology, began what He could not finish. Mr. Spitzer’s music is never completed. Vera, seeing her nursemaid bald in the morning light, calls her “this unfinished thing, that which had no business in creation” (ch. 21).

The palimpsest is Young’s image for time and memory. A palimpsest is a manuscript scraped clean and written over, with the old writing still faintly visible beneath the new. Catherine’s world is “a palimpsest of many hieroglyphic writings which had been effaced” (ch. 14), and Mr. Spitzer keeps a “many-written palimpsest or tally sheet” of everything he has seen (ch. 47).

Deep calling to deep is Young’s phrase, borrowed from the Psalms, for the hope that souls might truly answer one another. It appears in the monist passage of the first chapter, first as a promise and then as a lack.

Other people’s mirages is the phrase for Mr. Spitzer’s hard-won tolerance. Once a person knows that everyone lives inside some illusion, including himself, the only decent response is respect.

The principles that follow are drawn from this vocabulary and tested against the trials of Part Two. They owe a debt to an earlier attempt to state a philosophy of radical immanence in plain language, whose categories fit Young’s novel remarkably well. But they are stated here as what remains after the trials, not as a frame laid over them. Each principle is something that survived the breaking of a system. None is offered as a master key.
